Aberdeen.text: Known as the offshore oil capital of Europe ever since North Sea oil was discovered in 1969.
Its grey granite buildings can sparkle like silver, thanks to flecks of mica in the stone.
Home to a university founded in 1495, the fifth oldest in the English-speaking world.
Its heliport is one of the busiest commercial heliports anywhere in the world.

Aberystwyth.text: Wales's first UNESCO City of Literature, even though it isn't actually a city.
Home of the National Library of Wales, and often called the unofficial capital of Mid Wales.
A Victorian cliff railway, opened in 1896, hauls visitors up a 50% slope to a camera obscura on top of Constitution Hill.
Its name simply means "the mouth of the Ystwyth", a river that skirts the town.

Abu Dhabi.text: Capital of the United Arab Emirates, sitting on a T-shaped island that pokes out into the Persian Gulf.
Its name means 'Father of the gazelle', and a popular story says hunters chasing a gazelle found fresh water here in 1761.
Before oil, pearl divers here plunged for one to three minutes at a time, up to thirty times a day, with no air tanks.
Its Gulf waters are home to one of the world's largest known populations of humpback dolphins.

Abu Simbel.text: Two temples carved straight into a mountainside for Pharaoh Ramesses II over 3,200 years ago.
In the 1960s, both temples were cut into huge blocks and rebuilt on higher ground to escape Lake Nasser's rising water.
Twice a year, around 22 February and 22 October, the rising sun lights statues deep inside, all except Ptah, a god linked with the dead.
By the time a Swiss explorer found it in 1813, the Great Temple was mostly buried under a sand dune.

Abuja.text: Took over from Lagos, Nigeria's most populous city, as the capital in 1991.
A purpose-built capital, chosen partly because it sits near the middle of Nigeria.
Much of the city, including the presidential complex, spreads out south of Aso Rock, a 400-metre rock shaped by water erosion.

Accra.text: Ghana's capital on the Gulf of Guinea, and capital of the British Gold Coast colony from 1877 to 1957.
The city grew from settlements around three forts built by the British, the Dutch and the Danes.
Its name comes from the Akan word 'Nkran', meaning ants, after the anthills dotting the countryside around it.

Addis Ababa.text: At about 2,355 metres above sea level, it's the highest capital city in Africa.
Called "the political capital of Africa", it hosts the headquarters of the African Union.
Lucy, the famous fossil skeleton of an early human relative, is kept at the National Museum here.

Afghanistan.text: Mostly mountainous and rugged, it is dominated by the Hindu Kush, the western extension of the Himalayas.
Hidden in a remote valley stands the Minaret of Jam, a soaring medieval tower and UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The silky-coated Afghan Hound was bred here in the cold mountains to hunt game at speed, even wolves.
In buzkashi, the national sport, two teams on horseback compete to grab and hold a goat carcass, a bit like polo.

Ahu Tongariki.text: The largest ahu, or stone platform, on Easter Island, lined with fifteen restored moai statues.
One of its statues weighs about 86 tonnes, the heaviest moai ever raised upright on the island.
A Japanese crane maker teamed up with Chile to restore the site in a five-year project during the 1990s.

Al-Khazneh.text: Carved straight out of a sandstone cliff about 2,000 years ago, it is thought to have been built as a grand tomb.
Movie fans know it as the Holy Grail temple entrance in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989).
Its name means "The Treasury" after legends of riches hidden in the stone urn up top, which is actually solid sandstone.
So many hands have touched its walls that the surface wore away by 40 mm in under ten years.

Alabama.text: Mobile is known for the oldest organised Mardi Gras celebration in the United States, dating back to 1703.
NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center opened in Huntsville in 1960 and helped develop the giant Saturn rockets.
Nicknamed the Yellowhammer State, after its state bird: a woodpecker called the yellowhammer or northern flicker.
About 80 million years ago, a meteorite blasted a crater nearly 8 km wide just north of today's Montgomery.

Alaska.text: By far the largest US state by area, bigger than Texas, California and Montana put together.
Home to Denali, the highest mountain in North America.
The USA bought it from Russia in 1867 for $7.2 million, a deal some critics mocked as "Seward's Folly".
Its Aleutian Islands cross 180 degrees longitude, making it the most northerly, most westerly and, by longitude, most easterly US state.

Albania.text: Albanians call their homeland Shqipëria, popularly said to mean "Land of the Eagles", though scholars debate its origin.
The ancient city of Butrint, near the Ionian coast, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992.
By 1983 roughly 173,000 concrete bunkers had been built across the country to guard against invasion.
Grapevines grew wild here even during the Ice Age, one of only a few places where they survived.

Alcatraz Island.text: Its federal prison (1934–1963) was famous because cold water and strong currents made escape nearly impossible.
Its first lighthouse, lit in 1854, was the very first on the US West Coast.
The Spanish name, likely meaning 'pelicans', was first given to nearby Yerba Buena Island before moving to this rock.
Today the island is shared by tourists and a seabird colony of gulls, cormorants and egrets.

Alexandria.text: Named after Alexander the Great, who founded it in 331 BC.
Home of the ancient Lighthouse of Alexandria, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.
The seaside Citadel of Qaitbay, built in the 1470s, stands on the very spot where the great lighthouse once rose.
A modern library, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, opened in 2002 near the site of the legendary ancient Library.

Algeria.text: Africa's largest country by area since Sudan split in two in 2011, and the tenth largest in the world.
Its Roman ruins at Timgad and Djémila are both UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
The name comes from Algiers, whose Arabic name al-Jazāʾir means "the islands", after islets off its coast.
More than 15,000 prehistoric rock artworks on the Tassili n'Ajjer plateau show crocodiles and cattle from when the Sahara was green.

Algiers.text: Nicknamed 'Algiers the White' for its gleaming whitewashed buildings rising above the Mediterranean.
Its hillside Casbah, mixing Algerian, Ottoman and Andalusian architecture, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Under Ottoman rule the city's name spread to the whole country, which is how Algeria got its name.
Ancient Greeks called it Ikosion and told a legend that it was founded by 20 companions of Hercules.

Alhambra.text: The only well-preserved palace surviving from the medieval Islamic world.
Its name comes from Arabic for 'the red one', after the reddish colour of its earthen walls.
Some ceilings drip with honeycomb-like 'stalactite' carvings called muqarnas.
American writer Washington Irving made it world-famous with his 1832 book Tales of the Alhambra.

Amman.text: Plaster statues found at 'Ain Ghazal, now part of the city, are among the oldest large-scale human figures ever made.
Ptolemy II, a Greek king of Egypt, renamed it Philadelphia, meaning "brotherly love".
First built on seven hills, the city now spreads over more than 19 of them.
A Roman theatre built in the second century AD still stands in the city, facing the modern Hashemite Plaza.

Amsterdam.text: Nicknamed the 'Venice of the North', its historic canal network is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
It's the Netherlands' official capital, yet the government and royal family are based in The Hague.
The city is named after a dam on the River Amstel, first recorded in 1275 as 'Amestelledamme'.
The Rijksmuseum here houses Rembrandt's masterpiece The Night Watch.

Andorra.text: Two co-princes share the role of head of state: the Bishop of Urgell, across the border in Spain, and the president of France.
The largest of Europe's tiny microstates, though still only the sixth-smallest country in Europe.
Has no armed forces of its own.
Said to have been founded by Charlemagne, and its national anthem is called "The Great Charlemagne".

Angel Falls.text: Widely listed as the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall at 979 metres, though South Africa's Tugela Falls may rival it.
Named after US pilot Jimmie Angel, whose plane got stuck in marshy ground on the mountaintop above it in 1937.
Jimmie Angel's stranded plane sat on the mountaintop for 33 years before military helicopters lifted it down in 1970.
It was the main inspiration for Paradise Falls in Pixar's film Up.

Angel of the North.text: Beside the A1 and the East Coast Main Line, it's seen by an estimated 33 million people every year.
Its rust-coloured steel wings span 54 metres, and its ribbed frame can withstand winds of over 100 mph.
Its wings stretch wider than those of a Boeing 757 jet airliner.
Sculptor Antony Gormley based the Angel on a cast of his own body.

Angkor Wat.text: By area, the world's largest religious structure, says Guinness World Records, set in the old Khmer capital, Angkor.
Cambodia has shown the temple on almost every version of its national flag since 1863.
Unlike most Khmer temples, it faces west rather than east, possibly because Vishnu was linked with the west.
At the spring and autumn equinoxes, the sun rises right over the central tower when seen from the western causeway.

Angola.text: After Brazil, the second-largest Portuguese-speaking country in both area and population.
Africa's largest country by area lying entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.
Its Cabinda province is cut off from the rest of the country by a strip of DR Congo about 60 km wide.
Portuguese explorers took the name from ngola, the title held by the kings of Ndongo.

Ankara.text: Became the capital of the new Republic of Turkey in 1923, taking over from Istanbul.
Over 2,000 years ago it was the capital of Galatia, a state ruled by Celts.
Angora cats, goats and rabbits are all named after the city's old name, Angora.
In Ancient Greek its name, Ánkyra, meant "anchor".

Antananarivo.text: At about 1,280 m, the highest national capital by elevation of any island country.
Its name means "City of the Thousand", honouring King Andrianjaka's soldiers.
Rice paddies built by early Merina kings still surround the city and still grow rice.
Its zoo shows a complete skeleton of the extinct elephant bird, a giant flightless bird.

Arc de Triomphe.text: Twelve avenues radiate from it in a star shape, which is why its square was once called Place de l'Étoile.
It was the world's tallest triumphal arch until Mexico City's Monument to the Revolution was finished in 1938.
Long before it was finished, Napoleon had a wooden mock-up built in 1810 to welcome his new bride to Paris.
In 1919 pilot Charles Godefroy flew a biplane straight through the arch's main vault.

Argentina.text: Its Aconcagua, almost 7,000 m tall, is the highest point in both the Southern and Western Hemispheres.
Its name comes from the Latin argentum, meaning "silver", after early explorers heard of silver in the region.
Its Orcadas Base, staffed without a break since 1904, is the oldest research station still running in Antarctica.

Arizona.text: Known as the Grand Canyon State, it holds the famous steep-sided gorge carved by the Colorado River.
Along with Hawaii, one of only two states that skip daylight saving time, though the Navajo Nation within it does change its clocks.
Became a state on Valentine's Day 1912, the last of the 48 contiguous states to join.
Lake Havasu City is home to London Bridge, moved here from London, England.

Arkansas.text: At Crater of Diamonds State Park, visitors can dig for real diamonds and keep whatever they find.
Walmart, founded by Sam Walton in 1962, has its headquarters in Bentonville.
In 1881 lawmakers settled a dispute by declaring the final "s" silent, so it's said "AR-kan-saw".
Its Ozark and Ouachita mountains form one of the few mountain regions between the Rockies and the Appalachians.

Armenia.text: Often called the first state to adopt Christianity as its official religion, traditionally in AD 301.
Writes in its own alphabet, invented by the scholar Mesrop Mashtots around 405.
The world's earliest known leather shoe was discovered in its Areni-1 cave, along with an ancient winery.
Mount Ararat, just across the border but clearly visible from Armenia, is a national symbol and appears on its emblem.

Ashgabat.text: In 2013 Guinness World Records named it the city with the most white marble buildings in the world.
In modern Persian its name reads as "city of love", though the name may really go back much further.
Buildings here take playful shapes: the dental hospital looks like a tooth, and the airport's international terminal like a falcon.
When it opened in 2012, its Alem centre held the world's tallest Ferris wheel in an enclosed space, according to Guinness.

Astana.text: Became Kazakhstan's capital in 1997, taking over from Almaty.
Its modern plan was shaped by Japanese architect Kisho Kurokawa, who won a design competition in 1998.
Its name simply means "capital" in Kazakh.
It has gone by many names, including Akmolinsk, Tselinograd and Aqmola.

Athens.text: Hosted the very first modern Olympic Games in 1896, and welcomed the Summer Olympics back in 2004.
Often regarded as the birthplace of democracy and a cradle of Western civilisation.
In one version of the legend, Athena won the city by offering the first olive tree, beating Poseidon's salt-water spring.
The 1896 Games were held in the Panathenaic Stadium, which dates back to the 4th century BC.

Atomium.text: Its nine giant spheres show the atoms of an iron crystal, magnified 165 billion times.
Built for the 1958 World's Fair, it was only meant to last six months.
Its name blends 'atom' and 'aluminium', the metal that first covered its spheres.
Its central lift, Europe's fastest when built, carries 22 people to the top in just 23 seconds.

Auckland.text: New Zealand's most populous city, though Wellington took over as the capital back in 1865.
Its narrow isthmus sits between two harbours, one opening onto the Tasman Sea and the other onto the Pacific Ocean.
About 53 volcanoes dot its landscape, together making up the Auckland volcanic field.
Its nickname, the "City of Sails", comes from its residents' love of sailing.

Australia.text: Off its north-east coast lies the Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef, stretching over 2,300 km.
Aboriginal Australian culture is one of the oldest continuous cultures on Earth.
About 150 kinds of marsupial, pouched mammals like kangaroos and koalas, live here, nearly half the world's species.
The mainland is remarkably flat, averaging just 325 m above sea level, against 870 m for all continents.

Austria.text: The Alps cover about 62% of the country, and only about a quarter of it is low-lying.
Haydn, Schubert and the waltz-writing Strausses were born here, and Mozart in Salzburg, which later became part of Austria.
Its German name, Österreich, comes from Ostarrîchi, meaning "eastern realm", first written down in 996.
PEZ sweets were first sold in Vienna in 1927; the name is short for Pfefferminz, German for peppermint.

Azerbaijan.text: Its traditional carpet weaving joined UNESCO's list of the world's Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2010.
On a hillside near Baku, Yanar Dag, the "burning mountain", is a natural gas fire that blazes continuously.
Its traditional mugham music is so full of improvisation that musicians here blended it with jazz to create jazz mugham.

Badaling.text: The most visited section of the Great Wall of China, about 80 km northwest of central Beijing.
It was the first stretch of the Great Wall opened to the public in the People's Republic of China.
US President Richard Nixon walked here in February 1972, during his historic visit to China.
After nearly 10 million visitors in 2018, a daily limit of 65,000 people was brought in the next year.

Baffin Island.text: Canada's largest island and the fifth-largest island in the world by area.
Iqaluit, the capital of Nunavut, sits on Frobisher Bay at its southern tip.
Its Inuktitut name, Qikiqtaaluk, means "very big island".
The James Bond film The Spy Who Loved Me opens with a ski-and-parachute jump filmed off its Mount Asgard.

Bagan.text: Over 10,000 temples, pagodas and monasteries were built on these plains between the 11th and 13th centuries.
Capital of the Pagan Kingdom, the first kingdom to unite the lands that became Myanmar.
More than 2,000 of its temples and pagodas still stand, scattered across the dry plain.
Old Pali names for the area mean "parched land" and "bronzed country", thanks to its very dry climate.

Baghdad.text: Founded in 762 as the Abbasid capital, it grew into one of the world's largest cities, with perhaps over a million people.
Home to the great House of Wisdom library, medieval Baghdad earned a worldwide reputation as the 'Center of Learning'.
The original city was laid out as a circle about 2 km across, earning it the name the Round City.
Many tales from the One Thousand and One Nights, or Arabian Nights, are set in Baghdad's golden age.

Bahrain.text: Its Arabic name means "the two seas".
Home of ancient Dilmun, a Bronze Age trading hub linking Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley.
Famous since ancient times for its pearls, once considered the finest in the world.
Since ancient times, visitors have marvelled at fresh water bubbling up through the salty sea north of the island.

Baku.text: At about 28 metres below sea level, it is the lowest-lying national capital in the world.
Around 1900, its oil fields produced about half of the world's oil.
Nicknamed the "City of Winds", it is blasted by a cold northern wind called the khazri and a warm southern one called the gilavar.
Its walled Old City, home to the Maiden Tower, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

Bali.text: The only province of Indonesia where most people are Hindu.
On Nyepi, the Balinese New Year's 'Day of Silence', even the island's only airport closes for the whole day.
Its subak system for watering rice fields dates back to the 9th century and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Wallace Line, an invisible boundary where animal species change, runs through the narrow strait between Bali and Lombok.

Baltic Sea.text: One of the world's largest brackish seas, its water a salty-fresh mix fed by many rivers.
From the 1200s to the 1500s, the Hanseatic League of merchant cities around the Baltic and North Sea was northern Europe's biggest trading power.
Its southern shores are famous for amber, the fossilised tree resin used in jewellery.
At its winter peak, ice covers about 40% of the sea on average; in severe winters it reaches the Danish straits.

Bangkok.text: Its full ceremonial name is listed by Guinness World Records as the longest place name in the world.
Thais call it Krung Thep, a name usually translated into English as "City of Angels".
Its canals once carried most of its traffic, earning it the 19th-century nickname "Venice of the East".
Its historic heart, Rattanakosin Island, is home to the glittering Grand Palace.

Bangladesh.text: Home to most of the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest and a refuge of the Bengal tiger.
Of all countries with large populations, it is the most densely packed, with well over 1,000 people per square kilometre.
Its 21 February Language Movement Day, honouring the Bengali language, was declared International Mother Language Day by UNESCO in 1999.
Nicknamed the "Land of Rivers", it has around 700 rivers, dozens of them flowing in from India and Myanmar.

Banks Island.text: Over 68,000 muskoxen once lived here, the majority of all the muskoxen in the world.
The world's 24th-largest island by area, in Canada's icy Arctic Archipelago.
The first confirmed wild grizzly–polar bear hybrid was found here in 2006.
Everyone on this huge island lives in one tiny hamlet, Sachs Harbour.

Barbados.text: Sticking out into the Atlantic, it's the easternmost island of the Caribbean region.
In 2021 it became a republic, swapping the British monarch for its own ceremonial president.
Its name means "the bearded ones" – perhaps after the hanging roots of its bearded fig trees, though nobody is sure.
A young George Washington visited in 1751, believed to be his only trip outside what is now the United States.

Barcelona.text: Spain's second most populous city after Madrid, and the capital of Catalonia.
Gaudí's Sagrada Família church has been under construction since 1882, paid for by donations and visitors' tickets.
For the 1992 Olympics, old seafront factories were knocked down and new city beaches created in their place.
Its Eixample district is a grid of octagonal blocks whose corners were cut off so people could see round them.

Bay of Kotor.text: A winding Adriatic bay ringed by medieval towns, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.
The mountains rising above the bay are among Europe's rainiest places, with villages there soaking up about 5 metres of rain a year.
At the Verige Strait, ships squeeze through a channel only about 340 metres wide.
In the 18th century its fleet peaked at 300 ships, rivalling Venice and Dubrovnik.

Beijing.text: The first city ever to host both the Summer Olympics (2008) and the Winter Olympics (2022).
Its name simply means "Northern Capital" in Chinese.
At its heart lies the Forbidden City, the enormous palace where the Ming and Qing emperors lived.
Fossils of Peking Man, an early human relative who lived hundreds of thousands of years ago, were found in caves near the city.

Beirut.text: People have lived here for more than 5,000 years.
The name comes from an old Phoenician word meaning "wells".
In Roman times its famous law school was named one of the empire's three official law schools.
The city's Latin motto, Berytus Nutrix Legum, means "Beirut, mother of laws".

Belarus.text: About two-fifths of the country is covered by forest.
Shares the Białowieża Forest, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with neighbouring Poland.
Landlocked, yet dotted with thousands of lakes scooped out by Ice Age glaciers.
Crispy potato pancakes called draniki are often called the national dish.

Belfast.text: The RMS Titanic was built in its Harland & Wolff shipyard, and was the largest ship afloat when she entered service in 1912.
When it became a city in 1888, it was the world's largest centre of linen-making.
Two giant yellow shipyard cranes, Samson and Goliath, have towered over the docks since 1969 and 1974.
Its name comes from the Irish Béal Feirste, meaning "mouth of the Farset", a small river.

Belfry of Bruges.text: A steep staircase of 366 steps leads to the top of this 83-metre medieval tower, which leans 87 cm to the east.
Part of UNESCO's World Heritage listing of the Belfries of Belgium and France since 1999.
It once wore a wooden spire, but after fire destroyed it in 1741 it was never replaced, shrinking the tower from 102 to 83 metres.
Its carillon has 47 bells that together weigh about 27.5 tonnes.

Belgium.text: Its capital, Brussels, is the unofficial capital of the European Union.
The first country in continental Europe to become industrialised, back in the 19th century.
Tintin and the Smurfs were both created by Belgian comic artists.
Belgian instrument maker Adolphe Sax invented the saxophone in the early 1840s and patented it in 1846.

Belgrade.text: Its Serbian name, Beograd, means 'White City'.
Built where the Sava river flows into the Danube, watched over by the old Kalemegdan fortress.
One of Europe's oldest continuously inhabited cities, with farming villages here over 7,000 years ago.
In hot summers, locals flock to the beaches of Ada Ciganlija, a former river island.

Belize.text: The only Central American country where English is the official language.
Its barrier reef is part of the Mesoamerican Reef, the largest barrier reef in the Western Hemisphere.
The Cockscomb Basin, founded in 1986, was the first wilderness sanctuary for jaguars.
The capital, Belmopan, is a planned city built about 80 km inland, away from coastal storms.

Bengaluru.text: Known as the 'Silicon Valley of India', it is the country's biggest hub and exporter of IT services.
One legend says a lost, hungry king was fed boiled beans here and named the place 'town of boiled beans'.
Nicknamed India's 'Garden City' for its many parks and greenery.
In 1906 it became one of the first cities in India to have electricity.

Benin.text: Called Dahomey until 1975, after the powerful Kingdom of Dahomey that once ruled its south.
Pendjari National Park, with neighbouring parks in Burkina Faso and Niger, is a West African stronghold for lions.
Porto-Novo is the official capital, but the government sits in Cotonou, the biggest city.
Cotton is the country's main export crop.

Berlin.text: Germany's capital is the most populous city proper in the European Union.
Museum Island in the River Spree holds five museums built between 1830 and 1930 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Tempelhof Airport closed in 2008, and its old airfield became a huge public park, Tempelhofer Feld, in 2010.
Locals call the jam-filled Berliner doughnut a 'Pfannkuchen'.

Bern.text: Switzerland deliberately has no official capital, so Bern is called the 'federal city' instead.
Legend says its founder named it after the first animal he met on a hunt: a bear.
About 6 km of arcades make its old town one of Europe's longest covered shopping streets.
Albert Einstein lived in a flat here in 1905, the year he published his most famous papers.

Bhutan.text: Gangkhar Puensum, its highest peak, is the highest unclimbed mountain in the world.
Its forests absorb more greenhouse gas than the whole country gives off.
Television and the internet were only allowed in 1999, making it one of the last countries in the world to get TV.
In archery, the national sport, rivals may stand near the target poking fun at the shooter.

Big Ben.text: Strictly, "Big Ben" is the nickname of the Great Bell; the tower itself was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
Its clock is fine-tuned with old pennies on the pendulum: each one changes its speed by 0.4 seconds a day.
The first great bell cracked beyond repair during testing, so a new one had to be cast in 1858.
A lantern above the belfry, the Ayrton Light, shines whenever Parliament is sitting after dark.

Birmingham.text: Britain's second-largest city, nicknamed the "City of a Thousand Trades".
The sizzling balti curry is widely believed to have been invented here in the 1970s, and one district is called the "Balti Triangle".
A cradle of heavy metal: Black Sabbath and Judas Priest both came from here.
J. R. R. Tolkien grew up here, and a Tolkien Trail links local spots said to have inspired his stories.

Bishkek.text: One story says its name comes from a paddle used to churn kumis, a fermented milk drink.
It began as a caravan stop on a branch of the Silk Road through the Tian Shan mountains.
For 65 years, from 1926 to 1991, it was named Frunze after a Soviet military leader born there.
Many streets are lined with little irrigation channels that water the shady trees in the hot summers.

Black Sea.text: Only six countries touch its shores, but rivers such as the Danube bring it water from more than 20 countries.
Its deep water barely mixes and has almost no oxygen, which has preserved ancient shipwrecks remarkably well.
One of four seas named in English after a colour – along with the Red, White and Yellow seas.
Its earliest known name is the "Sea of Zalpa", used by the ancient Hattians and Hittites.

Blackpool Tower.text: When it opened in 1894, it was the tallest building in Britain.
Its builders set out to give the seaside its own copy of Paris's Eiffel Tower.
Usually dark red, it was painted gold by abseiling painters for its 100th birthday in 1994.
The circus between its four legs opened with the tower in 1894 and hasn't missed a season since.

Blue Lagoon (geothermal spa).text: This famous hot lagoon is man-made, filled with water used by a nearby geothermal power station.
Silica turns the water milky blue and forms soft white mud that bathers smear on their skin.
Bath-warm in a chilly land: the water averages a toasty 37 to 39 °C.
Its story began in 1981, when a man with the skin condition psoriasis bathed in the power plant's runoff pool and felt better.

Blue Mosque, Istanbul.text: Thousands of Iznik tiles and blue painted flowers inside gave this 400-year-old Ottoman mosque its famous nickname.
One of only a handful of mosques in Turkey crowned with six minarets.
Sultan Ahmed I wanted so many tiles that in 1613 he banned making or selling Iznik tiles for anything else.
The whole surrounding Istanbul neighbourhood, Sultanahmet, is named after the mosque.

Bogotá.text: Averaging about 2,640 metres above sea level, it's one of the highest capital cities in the world.
Founded in 1538 as the capital of the Spanish New Kingdom of Granada.
On Sundays and public holidays, main roads close to cars for the Ciclovía, so people can cycle the city.
Simón Bolívar gave the city its name, Bogotá, to honour the Indigenous Muisca people.

Bolivia.text: Home to the Salar de Uyuni, the world's largest salt flat.
Sucre is the constitutional capital, while the government works from La Paz.
Although landlocked, it still keeps a navy.
Named after Simón Bolívar, the Venezuelan-born 'Liberator' who led much of South America to independence from Spain.

Bondi Beach.text: One of the most visited tourist sites in Australia, and the setting of the TV series Bondi Rescue.
Its name comes from an Aboriginal word for a loud thud, like waves crashing over rocks.
Beach volleyball at the Sydney 2000 Olympics was played right here on the sand.
Its surf club, founded in 1907, claims to be the world's first surf lifesaving club.

Bora Bora.text: An old extinct volcano ringed by a lagoon and a barrier reef with just one opening to the ocean.
Its lagoon shifts from dark indigo in the deep channels to pastel blues and greens in the shallows.
Until 1960, its little airstrip was the only international airport in all of French Polynesia.
Legend says the war god Oro came down from the sky on a rainbow, landing on the island's Mount Pahia.

Borneo.text: The third-largest island in the world by area (not counting Australia), and the largest in Asia.
Shared by three countries: Indonesia, Malaysia and tiny Brunei.
The equator runs right across the island, cutting it roughly in half.

Borobudur.text: Guinness World Records names it the largest Buddhist temple in the world.
Its walls are carved with 2,672 relief panels, and it originally held 504 Buddha statues.
For centuries the temple lay hidden under layers of volcanic ash and jungle.
Its stones were laid without mortar, locked together with knobs, notches and dovetail joints.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.text: Mostar's graceful Old Bridge was commissioned by the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent in 1557.
Its capital, Sarajevo, hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics.
Almost landlocked: its entire coastline is a stretch of about 20 km around the town of Neum.
Perućica, in Sutjeska National Park, is one of Europe's last remaining primeval forests.

Boston.text: In the 1773 Boston Tea Party, protesting colonists tipped a whole shipment of tea into the harbour.
The Boston Marathon is the world's oldest annual marathon.
North America's oldest subway tunnel, the Tremont Street subway, opened here in 1897.
Fenway Park, built in 1912, is the oldest stadium still used by a major US pro sports team.

Botswana.text: In the Okavango Delta, a river spreads out across the Kalahari instead of flowing into the sea.
The discovery of diamonds in 1967 transformed the country's economy.
Much of the country lies in the Kalahari, which is really a dry, sandy savanna rather than a true desert.
The currency, the pula, means "rain" in Setswana, because rain is so scarce and precious here.

Bran Castle.text: Sold to tourists as 'Dracula's Castle', though there's no evidence Bram Stoker knew anything about it.
Built by Saxon townsfolk from 1377, it later served as a customs post on a mountain pass.
Queen Marie of Romania made it her favourite home and retreat, and had it lavishly renovated.
Handed back to Queen Marie's grandchildren, it reopened in 2009 as a privately owned museum.

Brandenburg Gate.text: Blocked by the Berlin Wall for almost three decades, it is now a symbol of European unity and peace.
Built from 1788 to 1791 for the Prussian king, it was modelled on the gateway to the Acropolis in Athens.
The goddess driving its four-horse chariot began as Eirene, goddess of peace, and was later renamed Victoria, goddess of victory.
Ordinary citizens were originally only allowed through the outer passageways.

Brasília.text: Built from scratch and opened in 1960 to replace Rio de Janeiro as Brazil's capital.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site, honoured for its modernist architecture and artistic city planning.
Its main buildings went up in just 41 months, ready for the grand opening in 1960.
Often said to be shaped like an airplane, but planner Lúcio Costa said his design was a cross adjusted to the landscape.

Bratislava.text: The only national capital that borders two other countries: Austria and Hungary.
For almost 300 years, Hungary's kings and queens were crowned in its Gothic St. Martin's Cathedral.
The name Bratislava only became official in 1919; German speakers had long called the city Pressburg.

Brazil.text: The largest country in South America, and the fifth-largest in the world by area.
The only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas.
Its men's football team has won the World Cup a record five times.
Probably named after brazilwood, a tree prized in Europe for its deep red dye.

Brighton.text: A fashionable seaside resort since Georgian times, where the Prince Regent built the Royal Pavilion.
Volk's Electric Railway, opened on the seafront in 1883, is the world's oldest electric railway still running.
Its boom began in the 1700s, when doctor Richard Russell sent patients to bathe in, and even drink, its seawater as a cure.
Officially it was 'Brighthelmstone' until 1810; 'Brighton' began as a casual shortening.

Bristol.text: Engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel left his mark here, with the Clifton Suspension Bridge and the pioneering steamship SS Great Britain.
Its name comes from Old English 'Brycgstow', meaning 'site of the bridge'.
Wallace & Gromit and Chicken Run were made here by Aardman Animations.
The British Concorde prototype made its first flight from Bristol's Filton airfield in 1969.

Brooklyn Bridge.text: When it opened in 1883, its main span made it the longest suspension bridge in the world.
The first fixed crossing of the East River, linking Manhattan and Brooklyn.
Engineer Emily Warren Roebling helped her husband, the chief engineer, with the bridge's design work.
Elevated trains rattled across it until 1944, and streetcars until 1950.

Brunei.text: The only country lying entirely on the island of Borneo, which it shares with Malaysia and Indonesia.
It comes in two separate pieces, split apart by Brunei Bay and a slice of Malaysia.
"Darussalam" in its full name means "Abode of Peace".

Brussels.text: The de facto capital of the European Union, hosting many of its main institutions, such as the European Commission.
The Atomium, built for the 1958 World's Fair, is a model of an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times.
Hailed as a capital of the comic strip, its walls are painted with giant murals of comic-book characters.
Its name probably comes from Old Dutch words meaning 'settlement in the marsh', according to the most popular theory.

Bucharest.text: Its giant Palace of the Parliament is listed by Guinness World Records as the heaviest building in the world.
Its grand, eclectic architecture earned it the nickname "Paris of the East".
Tradition links its founding to a man named Bucur; legends variously make him a prince, outlaw, fisherman, shepherd or hunter.
Right inside the city, the wild wetland around Lake Văcărești shelters nearly 100 kinds of birds.

Buckingham Palace.text: The royal family traditionally waves to crowds from the balcony on its East Front.
Boasts 775 rooms, and its garden is the largest private garden in London.
Inside there's a cinema, a swimming pool, a doctor's surgery and even a post office.
Long before the palace, King James I planted a mulberry garden on part of the site to produce silk.

Budapest.text: Opened mainland Europe's first electric underground railway in 1896, and that line is still running today.
People have bathed in its hot springs since Roman times, when huge baths were built at Aquincum, now part of the city.
Only became one city in 1873, when Buda, Óbuda and Pest on either side of the Danube were merged.
One theory says the name "Pest" comes from a Slavic word for cave.

Buenos Aires.text: Its name comes from "Saint Mary of the Fair Winds", whom Spanish sailors thanked for a good voyage.
Avenida 9 de Julio is the world's widest avenue, about 110 metres across, according to Guinness World Records.
Its Teatro Colón became one of the world's top opera houses.
One study found the local accent's melody is closer to the Neapolitan speech of Italy than to any other language.

Bulgaria.text: The Cyrillic alphabet was developed here, at the Preslav Literary School of the First Bulgarian Empire.
Some of the world's oldest known gold jewellery, over 6,000 years old, was found in the Varna Necropolis.
A world-leading producer of rose oil and lavender oil, both prized in perfumes.
In Nestinarstvo, a fire-dancing ritual on UNESCO's heritage list, dancers walk barefoot across glowing coals.

Burj Khalifa.text: At 828 metres, it became the world's tallest building when it opened in Dubai in 2010.
When it opened in 2010, its 163 floors were more than any building had ever had.
Some of its steel was recycled from a demolished palace in East Berlin.
Water dripping from its air conditioning is collected and used to water the park at its feet.

Burkina Faso.text: Its capital, Ouagadougou, hosts FESPACO every two years, a festival of African films that the BBC called Africa's largest film festival.
Until 1984 it was called Upper Volta, after the upper stretches of the Volta River that flow through it.
Its name mixes two local languages: "Burkina" means "upright" in Mooré, and "Faso" means "fatherland", literally "father's house", in Dyula.
Dancing in masks has long been part of traditional ceremonies among its many ethnic groups.

Burundi.text: One of the farthest sources of the mighty Nile rises in its southern mountains.
Famous for its Royal Drummers, who play huge drums carved from hollowed tree trunks and covered with animal skins.
Its Royal Drummers inspired a co-founder of WOMAD, the world-music festival, and played at its very first event in 1982.
It has two capitals: Gitega for government, and Bujumbura, the largest city, for business.

Cairo.text: Greater Cairo is one of the biggest metropolitan areas on Earth, home to well over 20 million people.
Nicknamed 'the city of a thousand minarets' for its wealth of historic Islamic architecture.
Its Arabic name means 'the Vanquisher', and one story links it to the planet Mars rising when the city was founded.
Egyptians often call the city Masr, which is also their everyday name for the whole country of Egypt.

California.text: The most populous US state, home to more than 39 million people.
Death Valley holds North America's lowest point, Badwater Basin, 86 metres below sea level, and is famously scorching hot.
Home to the bulkiest trees on Earth (giant sequoias), the tallest (coast redwoods) and the oldest known single trees (bristlecone pines).
Its name most likely comes from a mythical island in a 1510 Spanish story featuring Queen Calafia.

Cambodia.text: Heartland of the old Khmer Empire, whose kings built Angkor Wat, the largest religious complex in the world.
Home to the Tonlé Sap, Southeast Asia's largest lake by area, which swells to about six times its dry-season size.
A 2007 satellite study found ancient Angkor was the world's largest pre-industrial city by area.
Its Water Festival boat races are held as the rainy season ends and the Tonlé Sap River reverses its flow.

Cambridge.text: Home of the University of Cambridge, founded in 1209 by students who had left Oxford.
University students here wrote some of football's earliest rules, the Cambridge Rules, which helped shape the modern game.
Its cluster of high-tech companies is nicknamed 'Silicon Fen', after California's Silicon Valley.
At the 2001 census, about a quarter of working residents cycled to their jobs.

Cameroon.text: Nicknamed "Africa in miniature" because it packs in coast, desert, mountains, rainforest and savanna.
Around 250 local languages are spoken here, alongside the official languages of English and French.
Portuguese sailors named its Wouri River the "river of shrimps", Rio dos Camarões, which gave the country its name.
Despite its tropical heat, it sent a skier to the 2002 Winter Olympics.

Canada.text: The world's second-largest country by total area, with the longest coastline of any country.
Its border with the United States, counting the Alaska stretch, is the longest international border in the world.
Its name probably comes from "kanata", a St. Lawrence Iroquoian word meaning "village" or "settlement".
Its official maple leaf tartan shows the leaf's colours through the year: green, gold, red, then brown.

Canberra.text: Built as a compromise capital because Sydney and Melbourne each wanted the title.
A fully planned city, designed by American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin.
When the public was asked to suggest a name for the new capital, almost 750 names came in.
Its designers planned to carpet three hills in flowers, each a single colour, but it never happened.

Cancún.text: Purpose-built as a planned city in the 1970s, created by Mexico's government to boost tourism.
Its name comes from the Maya language, in which 'kàan' means snake.
Offshore lies an underwater art museum, MUSA, with around 500 sculptures for divers and snorkellers to explore.
Older English documents sometimes spelled it 'Cancoon', to show how it sounds.

Cape Town.text: South Africa's oldest city and the home of its Parliament.
A thin layer of cloud that sometimes spreads over flat-topped Table Mountain is nicknamed the "tablecloth".
Sits in the unique Cape Floristic Region, giving it one of the highest levels of biodiversity of any similar-sized area on Earth.
Hours after his release in 1990, Nelson Mandela gave his first public speech from the balcony of Cape Town City Hall.

Cape Verde.text: Portuguese settlers founded Cidade Velha here in 1462, one of the first European towns in the tropics.
Despite the green in its name, the islands are so dry and mountainous that under 2% of the land can be farmed.
In January 1832 this was the first place Charles Darwin stepped ashore on HMS Beagle's famous voyage.
Home of singer Cesária Évora, nicknamed the "barefoot diva" because she performed on stage without shoes.

Caracas.text: Its modernist University City campus, designed by Carlos Raúl Villanueva, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Its valley sits close to the Caribbean but is walled off from the shore by El Ávila, a steep mountain range about 2,200 m high.
Locals call the cool fog and chilly nights of December and January the "Pacheco".
Its full official name is Santiago de León de Caracas, given when it was founded in 1567.

Carcassonne.text: This hilltop citadel is famous for its 3 km of double walls studded with 52 towers.
In 1849 the government planned to tear down its walls, but local protests saved them and restoration began in 1853.
Legend says Lady Carcas tricked a besieging army into leaving, and the joyful bells gave the city its name: "Carcas sonne!"
In 2018 an artist temporarily covered its walls with giant yellow circles that only lined up perfectly from one viewpoint.

Cardiff.text: A small town until the 1800s, it boomed as a port shipping coal from the Welsh valleys.
Became a city in 1905 but was only proclaimed the capital of Wales in 1955.
The world's first million-pound business deal is said to have been struck at its Coal Exchange in the early 1900s.
The BBC built its Roath Lock studios in Cardiff Bay in 2011 to film dramas such as Doctor Who.

Casablanca.text: Morocco's largest city and its economic and business centre.
Its name is Spanish for "White House", from the Portuguese "Casa Branca", and its Arabic name means the same.
The famous 1942 film Casablanca was shot almost entirely at a Warner Bros. studio in California, not in Morocco.
The seaside Hassan II Mosque's 210-metre minaret was the tallest in the world when completed in 1993.

Caspian Sea.text: The world's largest inland body of water, so big it's often called the world's largest lake.
Holds about three and a half times as much water as all five Great Lakes of North America combined.
Despite the name "sea", its water is only about a third as salty as the ocean.
Its own seal, the Caspian seal, is one of very few seals that live in inland waters.

Central African Republic.text: Its southwestern rainforests, around Dzanga-Sangha, are noted for forest elephants and western lowland gorillas.
Its national language, Sango, grew up as a creole that let different ethnic groups talk to each other.
The capital, Bangui, sits at the focus of one of the largest magnetic anomalies on Earth.
Groups of standing stones near Bouar may have been raised around 5,000 years ago, late in the Stone Age.

Chad.text: Named after Lake Chad, the shrunken remains of a vast ancient lake that filled this basin thousands of years ago.
Emi Koussi, a giant volcano in its Tibesti Mountains, is the highest peak in the whole Sahara.
"Chad" comes from the Kanuri word for "lake", so Lake Chad is really "Lake Lake".
A small group of crocodiles survives in the Ennedi Plateau, one of the last known colonies in the Sahara.

Charles Bridge.text: Until 1841 it was the only way to cross the Vltava river in Prague.
A 516-metre medieval stone bridge lined with 30 statues, mostly baroque.
Legend says its first stone was laid at 5:31am on 9 July 1357, making the palindrome 1357 9/7 5:31.
Its statues today are all copies; the surviving originals have been moved to a museum to protect them.

Château Frontenac.text: Often billed as the most photographed hotel in the world, it crowns the Upper Town of Old Quebec.
Opened in 1893, it was one of the first of Canada's grand railway hotels, built by the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Rooftop hives house tens of thousands of honey bees, and their honey ends up in the hotel's restaurants.

Chefchaouen.text: Nicknamed the "Blue City" for its buildings painted in shades of blue, tucked into Morocco's Rif Mountains.
Nobody agrees why it's blue: theories range from keeping mosquitoes away to a 1970s push to attract tourists.
It began in 1471 as just a small fortress, which survives today as the town's Kasbah.
Muslim and Jewish refugees from Spain helped settle the young town, building their homes in the Andalusian style.

Chennai.text: Nicknamed the 'Detroit of India' because so many of the country's cars and car parts are made here.
Marina Beach, stretching kilometres along the Bay of Bengal, is one of the longest city beaches in the world.
Joined UNESCO's Creative Cities Network in 2017 for its long musical tradition.
Fort St. George, begun here in 1639, was the first English fortress in India.

Chicago.text: Its name comes from a Native American word for wild onion or wild garlic.
In 1900 engineers reversed the Chicago River so it flowed away from Lake Michigan.
Often called the world's first skyscraper, the ten-storey Home Insurance Building rose here in 1885.
Deep-dish pizza is said to have been invented here, at Pizzeria Uno.

Chichen Itza.text: One of the largest cities of the ancient Maya; its pyramid, El Castillo, was voted one of the New Seven Wonders in 2007.
Home to the largest and best-preserved ball court in ancient Mesoamerica, about 168 metres long.
At the spring equinox, shadows make a feathered serpent seem to slither down the pyramid's steps.
Clap your hands in front of the pyramid's staircase and the echo sounds like a chirping bird.

Chile.text: Stretches over 4,300 km from north to south, yet is only 350 km across at its widest point.
Home to the Atacama, the driest non-polar desert in the world.
Mines nearly a quarter of the world's copper, more than any other country, partly at Escondida, the biggest copper mine on Earth.
Faraway Easter Island, one of the easternmost islands of Polynesia, belongs to this South American country.

Chillon Castle.text: Perched on a little rocky island in Lake Geneva, it's among the most visited medieval castles in Europe.
Lord Byron's 1816 poem The Prisoner of Chillon made it famous, and he supposedly carved his name on a dungeon pillar.
Its distinctive windows are credited to Master James of Saint George, who is believed to have added similar ones to Harlech Castle in Wales.
Its name is thought to mean "flat stone" or "platform", fitting a castle built on a rock.

Chongqing.text: Unlike China's other three direct-controlled municipalities, all in the east, it lies deep inland in the southwest, far up the Yangtze.
The municipality covers an area roughly the size of Austria.
At Liziba station, a Line 2 train glides straight through a residential building.
Called one of the Yangtze's "Three Furnaces", it has some of China's hottest, most humid summers.

Christ the Redeemer (statue).text: The largest Art Deco-style sculpture in the world, gazing over Rio from the top of Corcovado mountain.
Its outstretched arms span 28 metres, and the figure stands 30 metres tall on top of an 8-metre pedestal.
At its 1931 opening, radio pioneer Guglielmo Marconi was meant to switch on the floodlights from Rome, but bad weather foiled the plan.
Though it stands in Brazil, its face was sculpted by a Romanian artist, Gheorghe Leonida.

Church of Saint George, Lalibela.text: Carved downwards into volcanic rock around 800 years ago, it is one of Lalibela's eleven rock-hewn churches.
Seen from above, the whole church is shaped like a cross sunk into the ground.
Visitors reach it through a narrow man-made canyon that spirals down and turns into a tunnel.
A Portuguese priest who saw Lalibela's churches in the 1520s swore an oath his descriptions were true, fearing nobody would believe him.

Church of the Assumption of the Blessed.text: Every hour, day and night, a trumpeter plays a call called the Hejnał from its taller tower.
The tune stops mid-note; legend says a medieval trumpeter was struck by an arrow while sounding the alarm.
Its giant carved altarpiece by Veit Stoss has figures 2.7 metres tall, each carved from a lime tree trunk.
Since 1927, Polish Radio has broadcast the noon trumpet call live from the tower every day.

Cliffs of Moher.text: Running about 14 km along the Atlantic, they reach 214 metres high just north of O'Brien's Tower.
Named after Mothar, an old promontory fort that once stood on Hag's Head.
Atlantic puffins nest in large colonies on remote parts of the cliffs and on little Goat Island.
They starred as the 'Cliffs of Insanity' in the 1987 film The Princess Bride.

Clifton Suspension Bridge.text: Based on Isambard Kingdom Brunel's design, it was finished in 1864, five years after his death.
A toll bridge ever since it opened in 1864, its tolls pay for its upkeep.
Its iron chains are second-hand, bought from Brunel's demolished Hungerford footbridge over the Thames in London.
Look closely: its two towers look alike but are not identical.

CN Tower.text: For 32 years it was the world's tallest free-standing structure, until Dubai's Burj Khalifa overtook it in 2007.
A giant helicopter nicknamed "Olga" flew the antenna to the top in 36 separate pieces.
Feeling energetic? A metal staircase of 1,776 steps climbs to the main deck.
Since 2011, harnessed thrill-seekers on the EdgeWalk can stroll around the outside of the tower's main pod, 356 metres up.

Cologne Cathedral.text: Finished in 1880, 632 years after building began, it was briefly the tallest building in the world.
Built to house a shrine said to hold the bones of the Three Kings, the Wise Men of the Christmas story.
A huge medieval crane sat on its unfinished south tower for about 400 years, part of Cologne's skyline.
Its 24-tonne bell, nicknamed 'Dicker Pitter', was the world's largest free-swinging bell until 2016.

Colombia.text: More bird species have been recorded here than in any other country.
Famous for its emeralds, it has long been the world's biggest source of these green gems.
Named after Christopher Columbus, its name was first dreamed up as a name for the whole New World.
Its national flower is an orchid found naturally nowhere else, named after Colombian botanist José Jerónimo Triana.

Colorado.text: Mount Elbert is the highest point not just in the state but in the whole of North America's Rocky Mountains.
More than 50 of its peaks reach 14,000 feet (4,267 m) or higher, nicknamed "fourteeners".
Denver was picked to host the 1976 Winter Olympics, but in 1972 Colorado voters refused to pay for them.
Its borders were drawn in 1861 using nothing but lines of latitude and longitude.

Colosseum.text: The largest amphitheatre ever built in ancient times, completed in AD 80.
Tens of thousands of Romans, perhaps 50,000 to 80,000, could pack in to watch the shows.
Its name probably comes from a giant bronze statue of Emperor Nero that once stood next to it.
A huge retractable awning once shaded the crowds from sun and rain.

Comoros.text: Its name comes from Arabic words meaning "Islands of the Moon".
The only Arab League member lying entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.
Mount Karthala, its highest peak, is a very active volcano that has erupted more than 20 times since the 1800s.
Coelacanths, ancient fish once thought to have died out millions of years ago, live in the seas around its islands.

Connecticut.text: Called the Constitution State after its 1639 Fundamental Orders, which some consider the first written constitution in Western history.
Yale, America's third-oldest college, was founded here in 1701 as the Collegiate School.
Its name comes from a Mohegan-Pequot word that has been translated as "long tidal river".
Its 1662 royal charter granted it land stretching west all the way to the Pacific Ocean.

Contiguous United States.text: The 48 adjoining states plus Washington, D.C., leaving out Alaska and Hawaii.
Were it a country, it would rank fifth in the world by area, behind Russia, Canada, China and Brazil.
Alaskans have long called it the "Lower 48", and some simply call it "Outside".
Point Roberts, Washington, is cut off from the rest of the country: you can only drive there through Canada.

Conwy Castle.text: King Edward I had this mighty castle built in just four years, between 1283 and 1287.
Part of a World Heritage Site with other castles and town walls that Edward I built in north Wales.
Thanks to a royal charter of 1284, the town's mayor is still also the castle's constable today.
Since 2019 it has been twinned with Japan's Himeji Castle.

Copenhagen.text: One of the world's most bicycle-friendly cities, where some cycle lanes even have their own traffic lights.
Since 2000 the Øresund Bridge has linked it by road and rail to Malmö, across the water in Sweden.
Its old Norse name meant "merchants' harbour" — in old-fashioned English, "chapmen's haven".
The city harbour has been cleaned up so well that people now go swimming in it.

Costa Rica.text: One of the few countries with no standing army, which it abolished in 1948.
In recent years well over 90% of its electricity has come from renewable sources, mostly hydropower.
Its name means "rich coast" in Spanish, and some accounts say Christopher Columbus first used it.
Ancient stone balls carved by the Diquís people reach over 2 metres across and weigh up to 15 tons.

Crete.text: Greece's largest island, and the fifth largest in the Mediterranean Sea.
Home of the Minoans, often called Europe's first advanced civilization, who built grand palaces here over 4,000 years ago.
In Greek myth, the labyrinth at Knossos is where Theseus slew the Minotaur.
Myth also says Daedalus and Icarus escaped King Minos of Crete on wings they made themselves.

Croatia.text: Its coast is scattered with over a thousand islands and islets, though fewer than fifty have people living on them.
Plitvice Lakes, its oldest national park, is a chain of 16 lakes linked by waterfalls over limestone cascades.
The necktie comes from the cravat, a neck scarf worn by Croatian soldiers serving in 17th-century France.
Roman emperor Diocletian built a huge palace in Split and retired there in AD 305.

Cuba.text: The biggest country in the Caribbean by area, though only third by population, after Haiti and the Dominican Republic.
Home of the bee hummingbird, the world's smallest known bird at about 5.5 centimetres long.
Its son music is the root of many other styles, including mambo, cha-cha-chá and salsa.

Cyprus.text: The third-largest island in the Mediterranean, after Sicily and Sardinia.
Cuprum, the Latin word for copper, comes from "metal of Cyprus", thanks to the island's ancient copper mines.
Archaeologists found a Stone Age grave where a person was buried with an eight-month-old cat.
There are no trains here today: the island's government railway ran from 1905 until it closed in 1951.

Czech Republic.text: Has the densest railway network in the European Union, with more track per square kilometre than any other member.
The word "robot" was introduced to the world by a Czech play, Karel Čapek's R.U.R.
Gregor Mendel, the founder of genetics, spent most of his life in the Czech city of Brno.
Czech and Slovak puppetry were added together to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage lists in 2016.

Dakar.text: The westernmost city on the African mainland, sitting on the Cap-Vert peninsula.
Host of the 2026 Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic event ever held in Africa.
From 1978 to 2007 it was often the finish line of the gruelling Dakar Rally, which still bears its name.
Twin hills called the Deux Mamelles are the only high ground in the city, one topped by a lighthouse.

Damascus.text: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
The patterned fabric called damask is named after the city, a trading stop at the western end of the Silk Road.
Canals dug by ancient Aramaeans, later improved by Romans, still form the basis of the old city's water system.
Its grand Umayyad Mosque was begun in 706, more than 1,300 years ago.

Deadvlei.text: Its blackened camel thorn trees are thought to have died 600 to 700 years ago.
The dead trees have never rotted away, because the air here is simply too dry.
The name means "dead marsh", not "dead valley" as many websites claim.
Creeping sand dunes cut the pan off from the river that once flooded it, leaving the trees to die.

Delaware.text: Nicknamed "The First State" because on 7 December 1787 it was the first to ratify the US Constitution.
Over half of all companies listed on the New York Stock Exchange are legally incorporated here, drawn by its business laws.
Most of its border with Pennsylvania is a curve: an arc 12 miles from the cupola of New Castle's courthouse.
No US state has a lower average height above sea level.

Democratic Republic of the Congo.text: The most populous country in the world with French as an official language.
Wild bonobos live in just one country on Earth: this one.
Its namesake, the Congo River, is the deepest river ever recorded, with depths of around 220 metres.
The okapi, nicknamed the "forest giraffe", lives naturally nowhere else on Earth.

Denmark.text: Besides the Jutland peninsula, it is made up of hundreds of islands, more than 400 of them named.
Its royal line goes back more than a thousand years, to the Viking king Gorm the Old in the 900s.
Bluetooth is named after King Harald Bluetooth, because it would unite devices the way he united Denmark's tribes.
Lego, maker of the famous plastic bricks, has its headquarters in the Danish town of Billund.

Dhaka.text: Its colourful cycle rickshaws and their painted art were added to UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list in 2023.
Its fine muslin cloth was so famous that traders as far away as Central Asia simply called muslin 'Daka'.
Bangladesh's National Parliament House sits in a modernist capital complex designed by American architect Louis Kahn.
Every Bengali New Year, a dawn parade of giant birds, fish and animals winds through the city, a tradition recognised by UNESCO.

Djibouti.text: Sits beside some of the world's busiest shipping lanes, at the gateway to the Red Sea.
Nearly all of landlocked Ethiopia's imports and exports pass through Djibouti's ports.
Lake Assal, a salt lake 155 metres below sea level, is the lowest point in Africa.
Steaming limestone chimneys up to 50 metres tall rise around Lake Abbe, on the Ethiopian border.

Dodoma.text: Picked in 1974 to replace coastal Dar es Salaam as capital, being far more central.
Its name means "it has sunk" in the local Gogo language.
Planners pictured it as "the chief village in a nation of villages", built to be explored on foot.
Germany's colonial rulers were already eyeing the area as a possible capital as early as 1915.

Dome of the Rock.text: Built around 691–692 CE, it is the world's oldest surviving work of Islamic architecture.
With its gleaming golden dome, it has been called Jerusalem's most recognisable landmark.
One traditional story says leftover gold coins from the building fund were turned into golden plates to adorn the dome.
Its colourful outer tiles were added in the 1500s under Suleiman the Magnificent, replacing the original mosaics.

Dominican Republic.text: Shares Hispaniola with Haiti, one of only two Caribbean islands split between two countries.
Home to both the Caribbean's tallest peak, Pico Duarte, and its lowest point, salty Lake Enriquillo.
Santo Domingo's cathedral, begun in the early 1500s, is the oldest cathedral still standing in the Americas.
Merengue and bachata, two hugely popular music styles, both come from here.

Douglas, Isle of Man.text: The famous Isle of Man TT motorcycle races start and finish here every year.
Horse-drawn trams still clip-clop along the seafront promenade from spring to early autumn.
A little castle on a rock in the bay, the Tower of Refuge, was built in 1832 as a shelter for shipwrecked sailors.
Barry, Robin and Maurice Gibb of the Bee Gees were all born here.

Dubai.text: The Burj Khalifa became the world's tallest building when it opened here in 2010.
In 2024 its airport was the world's busiest for international passengers, handling over 92 million.
The Burj Khalifa's three-lobed footprint is based on a desert flower native to the region.
Though famous for oil wealth, by 2018 oil made up less than 1% of the emirate's economy.

Dublin.text: Home city of three Nobel-winning writers: W. B. Yeats, George Bernard Shaw and Samuel Beckett.
Its name means 'black pool', after a dark pool where ships moored, now the garden of Dublin Castle.
Handel's famous oratorio Messiah was performed for the very first time here, in April 1742.
Once a royal deer-hunting ground, Phoenix Park is one of the largest enclosed public parks in any European capital.

Dundee.text: Once the world centre of the jute industry, famed for "jute, jam and journalism".
The Beano comic is published here by DC Thomson, which also created The Dandy.
Captain Scott's Antarctic ship RRS Discovery was built here, and is now moored back on the waterfront.
Home to V&A Dundee, the first branch of London's V&A museum to open outside the capital.

Durdle Door.text: A natural limestone arch carved by the sea on Dorset's Jurassic Coast.
'Durdle' comes from an Old English word meaning to pierce or drill, fitting for a rock with a hole.
Rocky islets offshore are called The Bull, The Blind Cow, The Cow and The Calf.
In a 2022 Doctor Who episode, the Thirteenth Doctor regenerated into the Fourteenth here.

Dushanbe.text: Its name means "Monday", after a big bazaar that was held there every Monday.
From 1929 to 1961 the city was called Stalinabad.
When it went up in 2011, its 165-metre flagpole was the tallest in the world.
In 1990 the city sent a Tajik teahouse as a gift to its sister city, Boulder in Colorado.

Ecuador.text: The first country to write the rights of nature into its constitution.
Chimborazo's summit is the farthest point on Earth's surface from its centre, because the planet bulges around the middle.
Owns the famous Galápagos Islands, about 1,000 kilometres out in the Pacific.
Its name is simply Spanish for "equator", the line that runs across the country.

Edinburgh.text: Every August it hosts the Fringe, which has grown into the world's largest performing arts festival.
Called the "Athens of the North" for its Greek-style buildings and its great thinkers of the 1700s.
Its castle sits on top of a rocky crag that is the remains of an extinct volcano.
Legend says a little terrier, Greyfriars Bobby, faithfully guarded his master's grave here for 14 years.

Edinburgh Castle.text: Perched on the plug of an extinct volcano that rose about 350 million years ago.
St Margaret's Chapel, from the early 1100s, is regarded as the oldest building in all of Edinburgh.
Home of the Honours of Scotland: the Scottish crown, sceptre and sword of state.
A gun fires at exactly 1 p.m. every day except Sunday, Good Friday and Christmas Day, first set up so ships could check the time.

Egypt.text: Its Great Pyramid of Giza is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.
Spans two continents, reaching from Africa's northeast corner into Asia across the Sinai Peninsula.
One ancient name, often written Kemet, comes from the word for "black", probably after the rich dark soil left by Nile floods.
Its hieroglyphs are among the world's oldest writing: the earliest known examples are more than 5,000 years old.

Eiffel Tower.text: For about 40 years it was the world's tallest human-made structure, until New York's Chrysler Building overtook it.
Built as a temporary structure for the 1889 World's Fair, it was meant to be taken down in 1909.
On sunny days the top of the tower sways several centimetres away from the sun as the warmed iron expands.
At the very top is a private apartment built for Gustave Eiffel, where he welcomed guests like Thomas Edison.

Eilean Donan.text: Perched on a small tidal island where three sea lochs meet in the western Scottish Highlands.
Regularly called one of Scotland's most photographed monuments, it pops up on shortbread and whisky packaging.
Left in ruins for about two centuries, the castle you see today was rebuilt between 1919 and 1932.
Old survey drawings of the castle only resurfaced when its rebuilding was almost finished, so restorers partly guessed.

El Salvador.text: The smallest country by area on the American mainland, fondly nicknamed "Pulgarcito de América", the Tom Thumb of the Americas.
The only Central American country with no Caribbean coastline; its shores face the Pacific.
Izalco volcano erupted so often, for nearly two centuries, that it earned the nickname "Lighthouse of the Pacific".
Joya de Cerén, a village buried by volcanic ash around AD 600, is often called the "Pompeii of the Americas".

Ellesmere Island.text: Canada's northernmost island, and the tenth-largest island in the world by area.
Alert, at its northern end, is the northernmost continuously inhabited settlement in the world.
Scientists found Tiktaalik here, a 375-million-year-old "fishapod" showing how fish began evolving into four-legged land animals.
Its Inuktitut name, Umingmak Nuna, means "land of muskoxen".

Empire State Building.text: Opened in 1931 after just 13 and a half months of building, it was the world's tallest building until 1970.
A movie star in its own right, it has appeared in more than 250 films and TV series since King Kong in 1933.
Its spire was first meant as a mooring mast for airships, until planners realised high winds made docking impossible.
One of a few dozen New York buildings with a ZIP code all to itself, which it was given in 1980.

Equatorial Guinea.text: The only sovereign country in Africa where Spanish is an official language, a legacy of its days as Spanish Guinea.
Despite its name, none of its land lies on the equator; only the island of Annobón sits south of it.
In January 2026 its capital moved from Malabo, on Bioko island, to Ciudad de la Paz, a planned city on the mainland.
Portuguese explorer Fernão do Pó, the first European to see Bioko in 1472, named the island Formosa, meaning 'beautiful'.

Eritrea.text: Its capital, Asmara, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017 for its remarkably well-preserved early modernist buildings.
Its name comes from the ancient Greek name for the Red Sea, built on the word erythros, meaning 'red'.
Cycling, first introduced in colonial times, is one of its two most popular sports, alongside football.
Its Danakil Depression, around 125 metres below sea level, is a rift where the Earth's crust is slowly being pulled apart.

Estonia.text: In 2005 it became the first country to hold nationwide binding internet voting, in its local elections.
The software behind Skype was written by developers based here.
Its Song Festival, held since 1869, is one of the world's biggest choral events, with a joint choir of over 30,000 singers.
Bogs and mires cover almost a quarter of the country's land.

Eswatini.text: Mainland Africa's second-smallest country by area, stretching no more than about 200 km from north to south.
Renamed from Swaziland in 2018, partly to stop people mixing it up with Switzerland.
By tradition the king, whose title means 'lion', reigns alongside his mother, whose title means 'she-elephant'.
Its most important cultural event, the Incwala or 'Kingship Ceremony', is timed by the full moon nearest the December solstice.

Ethiopia.text: Africa's second most populous country, home to well over 100 million people.
The famous 3.2-million-year-old fossil 'Lucy', known locally as Dinkinesh, was discovered here in 1974.
Its traditional calendar has 13 months: twelve of 30 days, plus a short month of five or six days.
Africa's biggest coffee grower, and the homeland of the arabica coffee plant.

Federated States of Micronesia.text: Its four states – Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae – include around 607 islands stretched across nearly 2,700 km of ocean.
Nan Madol, a UNESCO-listed ruin of artificial islets linked by canals, is often called the "Venice of the Pacific".
On Yap, huge stone discs up to 3.6 metres wide served as money, and often stayed put when they changed owners.

Fiji.text: Made up of more than 330 islands, about 110 of which are permanently lived on.
The 180° meridian runs right across Taveuni island, but the International Date Line bends so all of Fiji shares one time.
Its rugby sevens team won the nation's first ever Olympic medal, a gold, in 2016.
Polished sperm-whale teeth called tabua are treasured gifts in Fiji, still exchanged at weddings, birthdays and funerals.

Finland.text: Covered mostly by forest and dotted with over 180,000 recorded lakes.
In 1906 it became the first place where all adult citizens, women included, could both vote and stand for parliament.
Freed from heavy Ice Age glaciers, land by the Gulf of Bothnia is still rising about a centimetre a year.
At its northernmost tip, the summer sun doesn't set for more than two months.

Flag of Afghanistan.text: Afghanistan's national flag has changed several times since the start of the 20th century.
Black, red and green tricolours were used for most of the 20th century, starting in 1928.
The tricolour's central emblem, ringed with wheat, contains two tiny Afghan flags of its own.

Flag of Albania.text: A black double-headed eagle on a red field; the eagle has long been a symbol of Albanians.
The design echoes the coat of arms of the family of Skanderbeg, a famous medieval Albanian hero.
Researchers say no trace survives of the original flag raised in Vlorë on 28 November 1912, when Albania declared independence.
A star was added to the flag in 1946 and removed again in 1992.

Flag of Algeria.text: Algeria's official description defines the flag's exact green and red by wavelengths of light, not paint codes.
Émilie Busquant, wife of nationalist leader Messali Hadj, is generally credited with sewing an early version of the flag in 1934.
Navy ships fly their own version, with two white crossed anchors in the top corner.

Flag of Andorra.text: One of only two national flags showing cattle: two red cows here, and an aurochs head on look-alike Moldova's.
The yellow middle stripe is slightly wider than the blue and red ones, in a ratio of 8:9:8.
The motto on its shield, "Virtus Unita Fortior", means "Virtue United is Stronger".
An early version is said to have been designed by France's Napoleon III, though a local reformer may be the real creator.

Flag of Angola.text: Its yellow emblem shows a machete for farmers, half a cogwheel for industrial workers and a star for progress.
First adopted on 11 November 1975, the day Angola became independent from Portugal.
A 2003 contest picked a new design with a sun inspired by ancient rock paintings, but it was never adopted.

Flag of Antigua and Barbuda.text: Read from the sun down, its black, yellow, blue and white stand for soil, sun, sea and sand.
The rising sun symbolises the dawn of a new era.
Artist Reginald Samuel's design beat entries from more than 600 local people in the competition for the 1967 flag.
The big V shape holding its stripes and sun is a symbol of victory.

Flag of Argentina.text: Manuel Belgrano first raised it on 27 February 1812, where the city of Rosario stands today.
The golden Sun of May in the middle copies an engraving on Argentina's first coin, approved in 1813.
It also became the model for the flag of the United Provinces of Central America.
Argentina's Flag Day, 20 June, marks the anniversary of creator Manuel Belgrano's death in 1820.

Flag of Armenia.text: First flown by the First Republic of Armenia in 1918, the red, blue and orange tricolour returned in 1990.
By law, orange stands for the creative talent and hard-working nature of the Armenian people.
In 1885 a priest designed an Armenian flag after students in Paris asked for one for writer Victor Hugo's funeral.

Flag of Australia.text: The 1901 design competition drew 32,823 entries, and five almost identical designs shared the prize.
One of those five winning designers, Ivor Evans, was a fourteen-year-old schoolboy from Melbourne.
The big Commonwealth Star first had six points for the six colonies; a seventh was added in 1908 for the territories.
Its Southern Cross stars are named after the first five Greek letters, from brightest to faintest.

Flag of Austria.text: Considered one of the oldest national symbols still in use, it was first recorded on a seal in 1230.
Legend says Duke Leopold V's white tunic was soaked red in battle, except for a white band under his belt.
Unlike the Habsburgs' black-and-yellow banner, red-white-red stood for the country itself rather than a ruling family.

Flag of Azerbaijan.text: Blue stands for Azerbaijan's Turkic identity, red for progress and green for Islam.
One explanation for the eight-pointed star links its points to the eight letters of "Azerbaijan" in Arabic script.
When raised in 2010, Baku's 162-metre flagpole was the world's tallest, until Tajikistan's beat it in 2011.
Azerbaijan's national anthem wishes the country happiness under its "three-coloured flag".

Flag of Bahrain.text: Its five white points stand for the Five Pillars of Islam.
The earliest flags were plain red; a white stripe was added after an 1820 maritime treaty with Britain.
The zigzag edge arrived in 1932, to tell Bahrain's flag apart from its neighbours'.
Sometimes mistaken for Qatar's flag, which is maroon rather than red and has nine points.

Flag of Bangladesh.text: The red disc sits slightly toward the pole, so it looks perfectly centred when the flag flutters.
Nicknamed Lal–Sobuj, meaning "the Red–Green", after its red circle on a dark green field.
An early version had a yellow map inside the disc, dropped in 1972 partly because it was hard to draw correctly on both sides.
The very first one, made by students in 1970, was sewn from cloth donated by a Dhaka tailor's shop.

Flag of Barbados.text: The trident in the middle is snapped off at the handle, marking the break from colonial rule.
Blue stripes stand for the sea and sky, and the gold stripe between them for the sand.
Designed by art teacher Grantley Prescod, whose entry won a nationwide contest that drew over a thousand designs.
Officially adopted at midnight on 30 November 1966, the very moment Barbados became independent.

Flag of Belarus.text: Down the side nearest the pole runs a red-and-white pattern like a traditional embroidered towel.
That folk pattern was designed back in 1917 by a woman named Matrona Markevich.
Red fills the top two-thirds and green the bottom third, so the stripes are deliberately unequal.
Official rules even set the pole's colour: it should be gold, or ochre.

Flag of Belgium.text: Officially it's an unusual, almost square 13:15 shape, though it's rarely seen that way.
Its black, yellow and red come from the coat of arms of the medieval Duchy of Brabant.
Revolutionaries first flew it with horizontal stripes in 1830; they turned vertical in January 1831.
Flags over the royal palaces usually fly only while the monarch is in Belgium, a handy clue to the king's whereabouts.

Flag of Belize.text: Two men holding the coat of arms make people a main feature, something almost no other national flag can claim.
Its Latin motto, Sub Umbra Floreo, means "Under the Shade I Flourish", written beneath a towering mahogany tree.
Known as the "Flag of Unity", it was designed by two government officials for a 1981 independence competition.
Until 2019 there was no official standard, so colours, proportions and even the men's shading varied.

Flag of Benin.text: Its green, yellow and red are the Pan-African colours, the same trio found on Ethiopia's flag.
Its national anthem explains the colours: green for hope, red for the ancestors' courage, yellow for the nation's treasures.
Chosen in 1959, it was swapped for a green flag with a red star in 1975, then brought back in 1990.

Flag of Bhutan.text: The dragon is the Druk, or Thunder Dragon, which gives Bhutan its local name: Druk Yul, 'The Thunder Dragon Kingdom'.
The dragon holds a jewel in each claw, standing for the country's wealth and the safety of its people.
The dragon started out green and was changed to white in 1956.
Early versions were squarish, until the king reportedly noticed they didn't flutter as nicely as India's rectangular flag.

Flag of Bolivia.text: Landlocked Bolivia still has a naval ensign, flown by navy boats on its rivers and lakes.
Since 2009 the rainbow-chequered Wiphala has been a national symbol too, flown beside the tricolour.
Its shape went undefined for over 150 years, until a 2004 decree fixed an unusual 15:22 ratio.
The civil flag is plain stripes; only the state version carries the coat of arms in the centre.

Flag of Bosnia and Herzegovina.text: The yellow triangle roughly echoes the shape of the country itself.
Its stars are meant to go on forever, which is why half-stars are cut off at the top and bottom.
