Adopted in 1998, its blue was made a little darker than first proposed to echo the European Union's flag.

Flag of Botswana.text: Its sky-blue background stands for water and rain, precious in such a dry country.
The black stripe framed in white stands for racial harmony.
Its designer ran a contest, judged every entry "hopeless", and drew the flag himself.
One of only a few African flags with none of the Pan-African red, yellow or green.

Flag of Brazil.text: The starry globe shows the sky over Rio de Janeiro on 15 November 1889, the day the republic was proclaimed.
Each star stands for a state or the Federal District; there were 21 in 1889 and there are 27 today.
The motto "Ordem e Progresso", Order and Progress, comes from the French thinker Auguste Comte.
Green and yellow come from the old imperial flag, where they stood for the emperor's and empress's royal families.

Flag of Brunei.text: A yellow background stands for the monarchy, since yellow is traditionally the colour of royalty in Southeast Asia.
Its white and black diagonal stripes honour two of the sultan's chief ministers, and the white one is slightly wider.
On the red emblem's crescent, yellow Arabic letters spell the national motto, "Always Render Service with God's Guidance".
Apart from the central emblem, added in 1959, this design has flown since 1906.

Flag of Bulgaria.text: Bulgaria's 1879 Tarnovo Constitution already described a flag of white, green and red horizontal bands.
Hung vertically, Bulgarian law says the colours must read white, green, red from left to right.
From 1971 to 1990 the flag's emblem carried the year 681, when the First Bulgarian Empire was founded.
In 866, a pope advised Bulgaria's ruler to swap his horse-tail banner for the Holy Cross.

Flag of Burkina Faso.text: Red, green and yellow are the Pan-African colours of Ethiopia, chosen to show unity with other former African colonies.
A yellow star sits where the red and green bands meet, standing for a guiding light.
Back when the country was Upper Volta, black, white and red stripes stood for three branches of the Volta River.
That old Upper Volta flag was virtually identical to the flag of the German Empire.

Flag of Burundi.text: A white diagonal cross splits it into red and green sections around a white disc holding three stars.
Under the monarchy, one version showed the karyenda, a royal drum said to have divine power.
When the royal drum was removed in 1966, the sorghum plant beside it, an important local crop, stayed on its own for a while.

Flag of Cambodia.text: A white picture of the temple Angkor Wat sits in the middle of a double-width red band.
Red and blue are Cambodia's traditional colours, standing for the nation and the king.
First adopted in 1948, it came back in 1993 when the monarchy was restored.
Almost every Cambodian flag used between 1970 and 1993 also showed the temple of Angkor Wat in some form.

Flag of Cameroon.text: Began in 1957 as a plain green, red and yellow tricolour; today's single star arrived in 1975.
From 1961 to 1975 it carried two stars, one each for East and West Cameroon in a federation.
In 1975 the two stars made way for one large central star, a symbol of national unity.

Flag of Canada.text: The maple leaf's 11 points were picked after wind-tunnel tests showed that design blurred least in strong winds.
Its extra-wide white centre band is called a "Canadian pale", named after this very flag.
First raised on February 15, 1965, a date now celebrated every year as National Flag of Canada Day.
Historian George Stanley based the winning design on the flag of Canada's Royal Military College.

Flag of Cape Verde.text: Ten yellow stars in a circle stand for the ten islands that make up the country.
Its stripes are unequal, in a 6:1:1:1:3 ratio, so the top blue band is twice as tall as the bottom one.
Its 1992 designer, chosen through a contest, wanted a flag nobody would mistake for another country's.
Blue stands for the sky and sea surrounding the archipelago.

Flag of Chad.text: Almost identical to Romania's flag, though Chad's colours may vary more than Romania's official shades.
The two flags only matched after 1989, when Romania removed the emblem from its tricolour.
A first proposal had a green stripe, swapped for blue to avoid confusion with Mali's flag.
Officially, blue stands for the sky and hope, yellow for the sun and the desert, and red for progress, unity and sacrifice.

Flag of Chile.text: Nicknamed La Estrella Solitaria, “The Lone Star”, after the single white star in its blue square.
Its star is said to stand for Venus, the morning star, which mattered to Chile's Indigenous Mapuche people.
Every building, homes included, must fly it on Navy Day, National Day and Army Day each year.
The original 1817 design was laid out using the golden ratio, with its star tilted slightly towards the pole.

Flag of China.text: Called the “Five-star Red Flag” in China, it was first raised over Beijing's Tiananmen Square on 1 October 1949.
Look closely: each of the four small stars is turned so one point aims at the centre of the big star.
Around 3,000 designs were sent in when the new flag was being chosen in 1949.
In 2020 the Chang'e 5 lander unfurled a real one on the Moon, making China the second country after the US to do so.

Flag of Colombia.text: Unlike most tricolours, its stripes aren't equal: yellow fills the top half, with blue and red sharing the rest.
Ecuador and Venezuela fly similar yellow, blue and red flags, because all three come from the flag of Gran Colombia.

Flag of Costa Rica.text: Its red middle stripe is twice as wide as each of the blue and white stripes around it.
The red stripe was suggested in 1848 by Pacífica Fernández, the president's wife, who admired revolutionary France.
Almost a twin of Thailand's flag: both have five red, white and blue stripes, but in reversed colour order.
On the government's version, seven stars in the coat of arms stand for the country's seven provinces.

Flag of Croatia.text: Atop its red-and-white checkerboard shield sits a crown made of five small shields for historic regions.
Also known in Croatian as Trobojnica, meaning “the Tricolour”.
Red, white and blue stripes have been used as the Croatian flag since 1848.

Flag of Cuba.text: Known as the “Lone Star” flag, it was designed in 1849, more than 50 years before Cuba became independent.
Its three blue stripes stood for the three departments Cuba was divided into at the time.
The poet Miguel Teurbe Tolón helped design it, and his wife Emilia sewed the very first one.
Puerto Rico's flag, first raised by independence campaigners in 1895, was modelled on it.

Flag of Cyprus.text: Its copper-orange map honours the island's rich copper ore; the word “copper” itself comes from Latin for “metal of Cyprus”.
Cyprus's constitution asked for a flag of “neutral design and colour”, so it shows neither Greece's blue nor Turkey's red.
The two olive branches under the map are symbols of peace.
An early proposal from the British colonial government was just a rust-brown letter K on white.

Flag of Denmark.text: Guinness World Records names it the oldest national flag in continuous use, counting from 1625.
Its name, Dannebrog, probably means "red cloth".
Legend says it fell from the sky during a battle in 1219, though that story was first written down centuries later.
Sweden, Norway, Finland and Iceland later took up its off-centre Nordic cross for their own flags.

Flag of Djibouti.text: Raised for the very first time on independence day, 27 June 1977.
The red star in the white triangle stands for national unity.
The design began life in the 1960s as the party flag of a movement campaigning for independence.
Djibouti lies on the Afar Triangle, where three tectonic plates, the African, Somali and Arabian, are slowly pulling apart.

Flag of Dominica.text: One of only a handful of national flags with purple, among the least used flag colours.
Its parrot is the sisserou, an endangered bird found nowhere else but Dominica.
Ten green stars circle the parrot, one for each of the island's ten parishes.
A playwright, Alwin Bully, designed it in 1978 as the island prepared for independence.

Flag of Ecuador.text: Its coat of arms shows Chimborazo, Ecuador's highest mountain, with a steamboat on the river below.
A condor perches on top of the shield, its wings spread wide.
Francisco de Miranda, who devised its colours, credited a late-night chat about colour with the German writer Goethe.
Take away its coat of arms and it looks just like Colombia's flag.

Flag of Egypt.text: A gold-coloured eagle, the Eagle of Saladin, sits in the middle of the white band.
Its red, white and black stripes inspired the flags of several other Arab countries, such as Iraq, Sudan and Yemen.
From 1922 Egypt's flag was green, with a white crescent and three white stars.

Flag of El Salvador.text: Its grandest version, with the coat of arms, is officially called the Bandera Magna, Spanish for "Great Flag".
The blue stripes stand for the Pacific and the Atlantic, even though El Salvador has no Atlantic coast.
From 1865 to 1912 it looked like the US flag, with a star for each department.
The first blue-white-blue flag, in 1822, was made by the wife and sister of General Manuel José Arce.

Flag of Equatorial Guinea.text: Six stars on the coat of arms stand for the country's five islands and its mainland.
A silk-cotton tree takes centre stage; local legend says an early treaty with Europeans was signed beneath one.
The blue triangle stands for the sea linking the country's scattered parts.
At independence in 1968 the flag was raised without its coat of arms, which was added later.

Flag of Eritrea.text: The big red triangle roughly copies the shape of the country itself.
Green stands for farming and livestock, and blue for the riches of the sea.
Its golden olive branch and wreath come from Eritrea's earlier flag of 1952.
In 1995 it was stretched from 2:3 into a long 1:2 shape, twice as wide as it is tall.

Flag of Estonia.text: Its blue, black and white began as the colours of an Estonian student society, whose first tricolour was made in 1884.
By law it rises over Tallinn's Pikk Hermann tower every day at sunrise, but never before 7 a.m., and comes down at sunset.
In a popular reading, blue is the sky, black the soil of the homeland, and white purity and hard work.
Some Estonians have proposed swapping the stripes for a Nordic cross in the same colours, but the idea never caught on.

Flag of Eswatini.text: Designed by King Sobhuza II, it shows a Nguni ox-hide shield lying across two spears and a staff.
The tassels hanging from the staff are widowbird and lourie feathers, which only the king may use.
The shield's black and white are meant to show black and white people living together in peace.

Flag of Ethiopia.text: In 1897 Emperor Menelik II joined three pennants into one striped flag, with the first letter of his name in the middle.
The colour order was later flipped to put green on top, and nobody knows exactly why.
Many African nations adopted its green, yellow and red at independence to honour Ethiopia's resistance to colonial rule: the Pan-African colours.
The golden star's evenly spaced rays are said to stand for the equality of all Ethiopians.

Flag of Fiji.text: A British lion holding a cocoa pod tops the shield, above sugar cane, a coconut palm, a dove and bananas.
Fiji is the only republic whose national flag still carries the British Union Jack.
Over 2,000 designs were sent in to replace it in 2015, but the plan was dropped in 2016.
Its popularity soared after Fiji won its first-ever Olympic gold medal under it, at the 2016 Games.

Flag of Finland.text: In Finland, the blue cross on white was first flown by a Helsinki yacht club founded in 1861.
At Midsummer it stays up all night, because darkness never comes to any part of Finland on Midsummer's Night.
Blue is said to stand for the country's thousands of lakes and the sky, and white for the winter snow.
Flag etiquette says it must never touch the ground, and after washing it must be dried indoors.

Flag of France.text: When adopted in 1790 it had red nearest the pole; the order was flipped to today's blue-white-red in 1794.
French Navy flags have unequal stripes, red widest, because flapping makes the far end look smaller.
Behind the president on TV, a flag with a narrower white stripe is often used so all three colours fit in shot.
According to the French government, white was the king's colour, while blue and red were the colours of Paris.

Flag of Gabon.text: Its yellow stripe stands for the Equator, which cuts right across Gabon, and for the sun.
Green stands for Gabon's great forests and blue for the sea along its long Atlantic coast.
Its unusual 3:4 shape is set down in law, and only a handful of other national flags share it.
The 1959 version had a little French flag in the corner, removed just over a week before independence in 1960.

Flag of Georgia (country).text: Nicknamed the Five-Cross Flag, it has a big red cross touching all four edges plus a smaller cross in each corner.
A map drawn in 1367 already shows Tbilisi's flag as a large cross with smaller crosses in each quarter.
Georgia's heraldry council says a coin found in 2021, minted under King David IV, shows a five-cross design.
Georgians mark Flag Day every 14 January, the date Parliament adopted it in 2004.

Flag of Germany.text: In 1832, tens of thousands rallied for freedom and unity at the Hambach Festival, waving black, red and gold flags en masse.
One theory traces the colours to the Lützow Free Corps, whose uniforms were mainly black with red facings and gold buttons.
When Germany hosted the 2006 football World Cup, public flag-waving across the country rose dramatically.
A giant Unity Flag was hoisted outside Berlin's Reichstag at the stroke of midnight as Germany reunited on 3 October 1990, and still flies there.

Flag of Ghana.text: Designed in 1957 by Theodosia Okoh, a Ghanaian artist and teacher, for the country's independence.
Its black star was borrowed from the flag of the Black Star Line, a shipping company founded by Marcus Garvey.
After Ethiopia's, it was the second African flag to use red, gold and green, colours that spread to many other flags.
Ghana's national football team takes its nickname, the Black Stars, from the star on the flag.

Flag of Greece.text: Greeks call it the Galanólefki, the "Blue-and-White", after its nine stripes of alternating blue and white.
A popular interpretation says the nine stripes stand for the nine syllables of the motto "Freedom or Death" in Greek.
Its blue has ranged from light to dark over the years, with darker shades increasingly used since the late 1960s.
The striped design first flew in 1822 as Greece's naval flag, but only became the country's sole national flag in 1978.

Flag of Grenada.text: Look closely by the hoist and you'll spot a nutmeg, a nod to one of the islands' main exports.
Its six border stars stand for the parishes, and the central star for Carriacou and Petite Martinique, counted as a seventh parish.
Designed by Grenadian Anthony C. George, it was hoisted at midnight on 7 February 1974, the day of independence.
Nutmeg and mace are so important here that Grenada is nicknamed the "Isle of Spice".

Flag of Guatemala.text: At its centre perches the resplendent quetzal, Guatemala's national bird and a symbol of liberty.
A scroll in the coat of arms bears 15 September 1821, the date Central America gained independence from Spain.
Nicknamed the "Blue-and-White", its colours come from the old Federal Republic of Central America, like several neighbours' flags.

Flag of Guinea.text: Red, yellow and green from left to right, it is the exact reverse of neighbouring Mali's flag.
Rwanda's flag from 1961 to 2001 carried a large black R to tell it apart from Guinea's near-identical flag.
Its colours partly nod to Ghana, whose first president was a close associate of Guinea's first president, Sékou Touré.

Flag of Guinea-Bissau.text: It is almost identical to the flag of the independence party PAIGC, minus the party's initials under the star.
The red bar sits on the hoist side to represent the country's position on the west coast of Africa.
Its yellow stripe stands for the northern savannas and its green stripe for the southern forests.

Flag of Guyana.text: Its nickname is the "Golden Arrowhead", after the gold arrow shape pointing across it.
American Whitney Smith, who coined the word "vexillology" for the study of flags, designed it while a student at Harvard.
Smith's proposal was modified, with black and white added, before it was adopted at independence in 1966.

Flag of Haiti.text: Haitian lore says Dessalines ripped the white out of a French tricolour, and his god-daughter Catherine Flon sewed the rest together.
At the 1936 Olympics it emerged that Liechtenstein's flag was the same plain blue and red, so Liechtenstein added a golden crown.
One of a handful of national flags that show a picture of themselves, flying within the coat of arms at the centre.
A royal palm topped by a cap of liberty stands above the motto "L'Union fait la Force" – Unity is strength.

Flag of Honduras.text: The two blue bands represent the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea, with the white land between them.
Its five stars stand for the five nations of the old Federal Republic of Central America and hope for their reunion.
The national anthem's chorus sings of "five pale blue stars", the stars on the flag's white stripe.

Flag of Hungary.text: Since 2012, Hungary's constitution officially reads its colours as strength (red), fidelity (white) and hope (green).
Its red, white and green come from the historic Hungarian coat of arms.
A law of 1848 first made the red-white-green tricolour an official national symbol.

Flag of Iceland.text: Icelandic law describes it as sky-blue with a snow-white cross and a fiery-red cross inside.
Its colours are often read as volcanic fire, ice and snow, and Iceland's mountains and sea.
The red cross was added in 1915, partly because the plain blue-and-white version looked too much like Greece's flag.
By the rules, it may not be raised before 7 a.m. and must never stay up past midnight.

Flag of India.text: Nicknamed Tiranga, "the tricolour", it carries a navy-blue wheel with 24 spokes at its centre.
Until 2021, the law said it could only be made of khadi, a hand-spun cloth championed by Gandhi.
An earlier version had a spinning wheel in the middle, swapped for the Ashoka wheel in 1947.
Until 2002, ordinary Indians could fly it only on national days; one businessman's court battle helped change the rules.

Flag of Indonesia.text: Its name, Sang Saka Merah Putih, means "the Heirloom Red-White".
Almost a twin of Monaco's flag, differing only slightly in its shade of red and its shape.
Its red and white colours come from the banner of the 13th-century Majapahit Empire.
Singapore's flag has exactly the same proportions, but adds a crescent moon and five stars.

Flag of Iran.text: An Arabic phrase is written in Kufic script 11 times along the green band and 11 along the red, 22 in all.
Green, white and red were already laid down as the flag's colours in Iran's laws of 1907.
A 1910 decree on the old lion-and-sun emblem even fixed the exact shape of the lion's tail.
The modern design, with its red emblem in the middle, was adopted in July 1980.

Flag of Iraq.text: Its red, white and black stripes come from the Arab Liberation Flag, first flown in Egypt in 1952.
Green Arabic lettering in Kufic script sits in the middle of the white stripe.
From 1924 to 1959, Iraq's flag carried two seven-pointed white stars standing for the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.
The basic red-white-black tricolour has flown since 1963, with only the central symbols changing.

Flag of Ireland.text: In 1848 its white centre was explained as "a lasting truce between Orange and Green".
The third stripe is orange, not gold: the government says yellowish versions "should be actively discouraged".
Green ribbons have been worn on St Patrick's Day since at least the 1680s.

Flag of Israel.text: Its two blue stripes echo a tallit, the Jewish prayer shawl, framing a Star of David.
In 1885, the village of Rishon LeZion paraded a blue-and-white Star of David flag to celebrate its third birthday.
A white flag with blue stripes and a Star of David was unveiled in Boston, USA, back in 1891.
Its official size is 160 by 220 centimetres, an unusual 8:11 shape.

Flag of Italy.text: Every 7 January, Italy celebrates Tricolour Day, recalling when Reggio Emilia's Cispadane Republic first made it a state's national flag in 1797.
The earliest record of Italy's green, white and red is a ribbon badge called a cockade, worn in Genoa in 1789.
Italians call it simply il Tricolore, "the Tricolour".
The air force's display team, the Frecce Tricolori, paints the sky with green, white and red smoke trails.

Flag of Ivory Coast.text: Looks like Ireland's flag flipped round, with orange at the pole and a less stretched shape.
After winning a 2018 world sprint title, Murielle Ahouré borrowed an Irish flag from a fan and waved it reversed.
As officially explained, white stands for peace and green for hope and a better future.
In 1960 a lawmaker proposed turning the orange stripe red, but other lawmakers opposed it and the orange stayed.

Flag of Jamaica.text: Since Mauritania added red stripes in 2017, it's widely called the only national flag with no red, white or blue.
First drawn with horizontal stripes, it was switched to a diagonal cross because it looked too like Tanganyika's flag.
A contest drew over 360 designs but found no winner, so a cross-party committee of MPs designed it instead.
Raised on 6 August 1962, the very day Jamaica became independent from the United Kingdom.

Flag of Japan.text: Officially it's the 'flag of the sun', but most people in Japan call it Hinomaru, the 'circle of the sun'.
The earliest recorded sun flag in Japan was used at Emperor Monmu's court in the year 701.
Merchant ships were legally required to fly it from 1870, yet no law named it Japan's national flag until 1999.
Before the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, the red disc was resized so it would stand out beside other countries' flags.

Flag of Jordan.text: Its design grew out of the 1916 flag of the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire.
The white star's seven points stand for the seven verses of Al-Fatiha, the opening chapter of the Quran.
Neat geometry: the red triangle's sides line up exactly with the flag's diagonals.

Flag of Kazakhstan.text: A golden steppe eagle soars beneath a 32-rayed sun on a turquoise field.
Down the hoist runs a gold pattern called koshkar-muiz, meaning 'the horns of the ram'.
The sun's rays are shaped like grains, a sign of abundance and prosperity.
Its designer, Shaken Niyazbekov, first coloured the ornament red; it was changed to gold in July 1992.

Flag of Kenya.text: At its centre sits a red, white and black Maasai shield with two crossed spears.
A compromise design, it blended the flags of two rival independence-era parties, adding white edges for peace and unity.
Kenya's constitution fixes the flag's exact colours, using shades from a British Standard colour chart.

Flag of Kiribati.text: A golden frigatebird flies over a rising sun, above blue and white waves for the Pacific.
The sun's 17 rays stand for the 16 Gilbert Islands plus Banaba.
Three wavy white stripes represent the country's three island groups: the Gilbert, Phoenix and Line Islands.
London heralds wanted a bigger bird and sun, but locals insisted on their original design, first raised in 1979.

Flag of Kuwait.text: Kuwaiti law sets it at twice as long as it is wide, with a black trapezium beside the pole.
A giant kite shaped like this flag, made in New Zealand, became the world's largest kite in 2005.
Adopted in 1961, it replaced a red flag decorated with white Arabic writing.

Flag of Kyrgyzstan.text: The sun's 40 rays stand for the 40 tribes that the folk hero Manas united, according to tradition.
Inside the sun is a tündük, the round roof opening of a yurt, seen from inside the tent.
In 2023 the sun's wavy rays were straightened, partly because they looked like a sunflower.

Flag of Laos.text: Nicknamed the 'Moon flag': its white disc is said to be a full moon over the Mekong River.
The blue middle stripe, twice as tall as each red one, stands for the Mekong River.
Designed in 1945 by the scholar Maha Sila Viravong, it flew briefly then and returned as the national flag in 1975.
The royal flag it replaced showed a white three-headed elephant under a nine-tiered umbrella.

Flag of Latvia.text: A medieval chronicle mentions a 'red flag with a white stripe' around 1279, making it among the world's oldest flags.
Its red is an unusually dark shade, so distinctive it's sometimes called 'Latvian red'.
One legend says a wounded chief's white sheet became the first flag, leaving only its middle stripe unstained.
The white stripe in the middle is only half as wide as each red stripe.

Flag of Lebanon.text: A green cedar of Lebanon sits in the middle, so tall its tip and base touch the red stripes.
Until 1990 the cedar was usually drawn with a brown trunk; now the whole tree must be green.
By one account, seven members of parliament finished the design with coloured pencils in November 1943, just days before independence.
The cedar is such a beloved symbol that Lebanon is nicknamed the "Land of the Cedars".

Flag of Lesotho.text: At its centre is a black mokorotlo, the traditional Basotho hat.
Today's design was adopted in 2006, on the 40th anniversary of independence.
Lesotho's very first flag in 1966 also showed the mokorotlo hat, but in white.
Lesotho has just one neighbour: South Africa.

Flag of Liberia.text: Nicknamed the "Lone Star", it closely resembles the US flag, reflecting Liberia's founding by settlers from the United States and the Caribbean.
Its eleven red and white stripes stand for the signatories of Liberia's Declaration of Independence.
In 1847 a committee of seven women, led by Susannah Lewis, hand-stitched Liberia's newly redesigned flag.
Many foreign-owned ships fly Liberia's flag, because Liberia lets them register there to avoid other countries' taxes and rules.

Flag of Libya.text: Red, black and green stripes carry a white crescent and star, with the black band twice as wide as the others.
From 1977 to 2011 Libya flew a plain all-green flag, with no design at all.
First adopted in 1951, today's flag was brought back in 2011.
The design grew from the Senussi banner: a black field with a star and crescent.

Flag of Liechtenstein.text: At the 1936 Olympics, Liechtenstein discovered its plain blue-and-red flag was identical to Haiti's.
To tell the two apart, a golden princely crown was added in the corner in 1937.
Hung vertically, the crown is turned so it always stays upright.
Its blue and red were first used as livery colours by Prince Joseph Wenzel I in 1764.

Flag of Lithuania.text: Yellow stands for the sun, green for forests and countryside, and red for bravery.
Delegates in 1917 found a red-and-green design too gloomy, so a yellow stripe for the rising sun was added.
Lithuania's state flag shows the Vytis, a white knight charging across a red banner that was already recorded in 1410.
Government offices must fly the flag around the clock, not just from sunrise to sunset.

Flag of Luxembourg.text: Almost a twin of the Dutch flag, but longer, with a lighter blue and red.
Its red, white and blue were in use from the 1840s, yet only became official by law in 1993.
Luxembourg's ships fly the "Red Lion" instead, so they aren't mistaken for Dutch vessels.

Flag of Madagascar.text: In 1958 the radio station Radio Tananarive invited people to send in designs for the new flag.
Through many changes of government, the flag has stayed exactly the same since 1958.
At first its colours had no special meaning at all.
Officially, the white recalls rice, a staple food, and the red the clay bricks of most houses.

Flag of Malawi.text: A red rising sun with 31 rays sits on the black stripe.
The rising sun stands for the dawn of hope and freedom for Africa.
From 2010 to 2012 a different flag with a full white sun flew, before the original came back.

Flag of Malaysia.text: Called Jalur Gemilang, "Stripes of Glory", a name picked in 1997.
Its 14 equal stripes stand for the 13 states and the federal territories.
The original design came from Mohamed Hamzah, a 29-year-old architect.
A 1949 flag contest drew 373 entries, and the public voted on three finalists.

Flag of Mali.text: Green, gold and red stripes in the pan-African colours, shared by many flags across Africa.
The first flag had a black kanaga figure with arms raised to the sky on its gold stripe; it was removed in 1961.
Flip it left to right and you get neighbouring Guinea's flag, which runs red, yellow, green.

Flag of Malta.text: The little cross in the corner is the George Cross, a bravery award King George VI gave to the whole island in 1942.
Legend says Count Roger of Sicily gave Malta its red and white in 1091, but historians have debunked the tale as a myth.
The cross once sat on a blue square; at independence in 1964 that was swapped for a thin red edge to make it less prominent.
Maltese merchant ships fly a different flag: red with a white border and a white eight-pointed Maltese cross.

Flag of Mauritania.text: The red stripes top and bottom were only added in 2017; before that the flag was green with a golden star and crescent.
The new flag was first raised on 28 November 2017, the anniversary of independence from France.
Official guidelines say each red stripe must be exactly one-fifth of the flag's height.
Drawing it really small? The rules set a minimum size of just 5.5 by 7.8 millimetres.

Flag of Mauritius.text: Nicknamed "The Four Bands", it has four equal stripes of red, blue, yellow and green.
Blue stands for the Indian Ocean around the island, and green for farmland that stays green all twelve months of the year.
Its designer, retired schoolteacher Gurudutt Moher, was honoured with a national title only in 2018, after his death.

Flag of Mexico.text: The eagle on a cactus eating a snake recalls the Aztec legend of the sign that showed where to found Tenochtitlan, today's Mexico City.
Without its emblem it looks a lot like Italy's flag, but Mexico's greens and reds are darker and the flag is longer.
Since 1999, giant "monumental flags", many of them 14.3 by 25 metres on 50-metre poles, have flown over Mexican cities.
Mexico celebrates Flag Day every 24 February.

Flag of Moldova.text: Its blue, yellow and red stripes are based on Romania's flag, reflecting the two countries' close cultural ties.
The eagle in the middle holds an olive branch for peace, and its shield shows the head of an aurochs, a wild ox.
Its designers picked an emerald-tinted blue from the wall paintings of Voronet monastery, rather than Romania's ultramarine.

Flag of Monaco.text: Red and white have been the colours of Monaco's ruling Grimaldi family since at least 1339.
Nearly identical to Indonesia's flag, but squarer: Monaco's is 4:5 while Indonesia's is 2:3.
Poland's flag uses the same two colours, just flipped, with white on top.
A separate princely flag, the coat of arms on white, flies at the Prince's Palace and on the Prince's yacht.

Flag of Mongolia.text: The blue middle stripe stands for the eternal blue sky.
The Soyombo symbol includes two fish because, in Mongol mythology, fish never sleep, like the watchful spirit of the Mongol people.
Until 1992 a star sat above the Soyombo symbol; it was removed when the current flag was adopted.
Mongolia's 1911 flag was a yellow banner with prayer text and red silk tails streaming from it.

Flag of Montenegro.text: A red field framed by a golden border, with the national coat of arms right in the middle.
Comes in two versions: a horizontal one mostly flown outdoors and a vertical one mostly hung indoors.
Adopted in 2004, its design is based on an old royal banner.
In socialist Yugoslavia, Montenegro's red-starred tricolour was exactly the same as Serbia's flag.

Flag of Morocco.text: A green five-pointed star sits on a bright red field, and by law one of its points must point upwards.
Its red recalls the ruling Alawi dynasty, whose old flag was simply a red field.
Under French and Spanish control it could fly only on land; only after independence in 1956 could it fly at sea too.
The star must be woven into the cloth so that it can be seen from both sides of the flag.

Flag of Mozambique.text: The only national flag with an AK-47 rifle, crossed here with a hoe on top of an open book.
The book, hoe and rifle stand for education, production and defence.
Green stands for the country's soil, and golden-yellow for the riches of the subsoil beneath it.
Today's design dates from 1 May 1983; from 1975 until shortly before then, the flag had diagonal stripes.

Flag of Myanmar.text: Its yellow, green and red stripes with a big white star were first raised at 3 p.m. on 21 October 2010.
The three stripes honour the yellow-green-red tricolours flown during the struggle for independence.
An early version of the tricolour, from 1935, had a peacock in the centre.
Hung vertically, the yellow stripe must be on the left and the star must point left.

Flag of Namibia.text: One of the few national flags built around a diagonal band, here red edged with white.
The golden sun has twelve rays, one for each of twelve Namibian ethnic groups.
A national competition for the flag drew 870 design entries.
Its blue triangle stands for the clear Namibian sky and the Atlantic Ocean.

Flag of Nauru.text: A map in a flag: the thin gold stripe is the Equator, and the star marks Nauru one degree south of it.
The star has twelve points, one for each of the island's twelve original tribes.
White in the star stands for phosphate, once Nauru's major natural resource.
A shape in maths, the Nauru graph, is named for its resemblance to the flag's 12-pointed star.

Flag of Nepal.text: The only national flag in the world that isn't a rectangle or a square.
The only national flag that is taller than it is wide, shaped like two stacked pennants.
Until 1962, the sun and moon on the flag had human faces.
Nepal's constitution includes step-by-step geometric instructions for drawing the flag's exact shape.

Flag of New Zealand.text: Four red stars edged in white show the Southern Cross, a constellation of the southern sky.
Designed in 1869 for the colony's ships, it was quickly taken up as the national flag.
In a 2016 referendum, voters chose to keep it over a silver fern design, by 57% to 43%.
Often mistaken for Australia's flag, whose Southern Cross is drawn with five all-white stars instead.

Flag of Nicaragua.text: One of only a handful of national flags with purple in it, thanks to a rainbow in the coat of arms.
Its blue-white-blue stripes come from the flag of the old Federal Republic of Central America.
The emblem's triangle, volcanoes, rising sun and rainbow all appeared on the original Central American emblem.
First adopted in 1908, it wasn't made official until 1971.

Flag of Niger.text: Orange, white and green stripes with an orange disc in the middle, which is thought to stand for the sun.
A common reading: orange for the Sahara in the north, white for the Sahel, green for the fertile south.
Traditionally drawn in an unusual, almost square 6:7 shape, for reasons nobody knows.
Adopted in 1959, a year before independence, and kept unchanged ever since.

Flag of Nigeria.text: Chosen from around 3,000 entries in a nationwide competition held before independence.
The winning design first had a red sun with rays on the white stripe, but the committee removed it.
Green stands for agriculture, while the white stripe stands for peace and unity.
Designer Taiwo Akinkunmi came up with it while studying electrical engineering in London.

Flag of North Korea.text: A wide red stripe edged in thin white and broad blue, with a red star inside a white disc near the pole.
Adopted on 8 September 1948, when the country passed its first constitution.
In 1948 one delegate worried such a long flag would fold up when hoisted, but his call for a shorter one was waved away.
For diplomatic ceremonies, gold tassels may be attached to its outer edge.

Flag of North Macedonia.text: A yellow sun on red whose eight rays widen as they stretch all the way to the flag's edges.
Its sun is the "new sun of Liberty" sung about in the national anthem, "Today over Macedonia".
Designer Miroslav Grčev drew 12 sun designs; his last, with rays covering the whole flag, was chosen in 1995.
In Yugoslav times, Macedonia was the only republic whose flag didn't use the Pan-Slavic colours.

Flag of Norway.text: Designed in 1821 by Fredrik Meltzer, a member of Norway's parliament.
Meltzer recommended red, white and blue as "three colours that now denote freedom", as in the French, Dutch, American and British flags.
A union badge shared with Sweden once filled its corner, mockingly nicknamed "the herring salad" after the colourful, decorated dish.

Flag of Oman.text: Its emblem shows a curved khanjar dagger fastened over two crossed swords, traditional Omani weapons.
Until 1970 the country flew a plain red banner; white and green bands were then added.
Green recalls the Jebel Akhdar, or "Green Mountains", in the north and the fertility of the land.

Flag of Pakistan.text: Approved by Pakistan's Constituent Assembly on 11 August 1947, just three days before independence.
The white stripe by the pole stands for the country's religious minorities.
In the emblem, the crescent stands for progress and the five-pointed star for light and knowledge.
It grew out of the Muslim League's green crescent-and-star banner, with a white strip added at the pole.

Flag of Palau.text: That golden disc is a full moon, not a sun, set slightly off-centre towards the pole.
Palauans consider the full moon the best time for fishing, sowing, harvesting and carving canoes.
The light blue stands for the Pacific Ocean and the move from foreign rule to self-government.

Flag of Panama.text: Panama's first First Lady, María de la Ossa de Amador, secretly sewed the country's very first flags in 1903.
The blue and red are said to stand for rival Conservative and Liberal parties, with white for the peace between them.
The very first version had blue in the top-left quarter; the quarters were later shifted to put white there.

Flag of Papua New Guinea.text: A 15-year-old schoolgirl, Susan Karike, redesigned it in 1971 on a page torn from her exercise book.
Karike swapped a proposed blue, yellow and green design for a bold diagonal in red, black and yellow.
A golden bird-of-paradise flies on the red half, while the Southern Cross shines in white stars on black.

Flag of Paraguay.text: The only national flag with a different design on each side: the national seal on the front, the treasury seal on the back.
Turn it over and you'll find a yellow lion beneath a red cap on a pole, with the words "Peace and Justice".
Its red, white and blue stripes are often said to echo the French Tricolour, a symbol of liberty.
Paraguay's very first flag, raised in 1811, was plain blue with a white six-pointed star in the corner.

Flag of Peru.text: Peru's first flag, decreed in 1820, was quartered diagonally in red and white.
One story says General San Martín took its colours from red-and-white flamingos he saw on Peru's coast.
Its red-white-red vertical stripes are written into Article 49 of Peru's constitution.

Flag of Poland.text: White and red come from two old coats of arms: Poland's White Eagle and Lithuania's white knight, both on red shields.
White goes on top because the eagle's colour ranks above the red of its shield in Polish heraldry.
Indonesia and Monaco use the same two colours, but with the red stripe above the white.
Since 2004, Poles have celebrated a special Flag Day every 2 May.

Flag of Portugal.text: Its green and red were the colours of the Republican Party, adopted after the monarchy fell in 1910.
The golden globe-like device is an armillary sphere, a navigation tool of Portugal's sailors in the Age of Discovery.
Count them: seven yellow castles line the red border of the shield.
Inside the shield, five little blue shields each carry five white dots.

Flag of Qatar.text: No other national flag is more than twice as wide as it is tall.
Its zigzag edge has nine points, said to mark Qatar as the ninth "reconciled emirate".
British letters from the 1930s say its locally dyed red faded to a chocolate colour under the hot desert sun.
Since 2012, the law has fixed its exact shade as Pantone 1955 C, a deep maroon.

Flag of Romania.text: Chad's flag is almost identical, though the two designs came about completely independently of each other.
Blue, yellow and red appear on flags and coats of arms from Romanian lands as far back as the 1300s.
Until 2023 the law named its colours after paint pigments: cobalt blue, chrome yellow and vermilion.
Every 26 June is Romania's National Flag Day, set by a law in 1998.

Flag of Russia.text: The oldest surviving white, blue and red Russian flag was flown by Tsar Peter the Great on the White Sea in 1693.
One story says Peter modelled it on a Dutch ship's red, white and blue flag, reordering the colours.
Its colours inspired the Pan-Slavic colours seen on the flags of Slovakia, Slovenia and Serbia.
From 1858 until 1896, the national flag was a black, yellow and white tricolour instead.

Flag of Rwanda.text: Its golden sun has 24 rays that don't quite touch the sun itself.
Rwandan artist and engineer Alphonse Kirimobenecyo designed it, showing the sun lighting up the country's lush greenery.
The sky-blue stripe fills the whole top half, twice as tall as the yellow or green.
By law, official flags are 100% polyester, sewn so the stitching between stripes can't be seen.

Flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis.text: A student, Edrice Lewis, designed it, beating 257 other entries in a national competition.
It was first raised one minute after midnight on 19 September 1983, the day of independence.
Its two white stars stand for the two islands, as well as hope and liberty.
The yellow stripes represent the sunshine the islands enjoy all year round.

Flag of Saint Lucia.text: Its two central triangles stand for the Pitons, twin volcanic peaks rising from the island's southwest coast.
Local artist Dunstan St Omer designed it, and it first flew in 1967, twelve years before full independence.
Yellow stands for sunshine and prosperity, while the blue is the sky and the surrounding seas.
At independence in 1979 the design stayed, though the blue's shade and the triangles' sizes were nudged slightly.

Flag of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.text: Sometimes called "The Gems", its three green diamonds are arranged in a V for Vincent.
The 1979 original showed the coat of arms on a breadfruit leaf, which was hard to recognise from afar.
When a national contest found no winning design, a Swiss graphic artist was asked to modernise the old flag.
Gold stands for the islands' sand and sunshine; green for their plentiful vegetation.

Flag of Samoa.text: Its five white stars form the Southern Cross which, as one prime minister put it, tells the world where Samoa is.
Two paramount chiefs designed it in 1948 with four stars; a smaller fifth star joined in 1949.
By law, people in public must stand still while the flag is raised or lowered, and drivers must stop.
Samoa's first national flag, from 1873, was red with a white cross and a white star.

Flag of San Marino.text: White stands for peace and light blue for liberty, and a scroll on the arms reads LIBERTAS, meaning freedom.
The coat of arms in the middle shows three towers standing on three peaks.
Officially it is 3 units tall by 4 long, though a 2:3 version may be used abroad.
Each of San Marino's municipalities, called castelli, flies the same white and blue with its own coat of arms.

Flag of São Tomé and Príncipe.text: According to the president's office, its two black stars stand for the country's two islands, São Tomé and Príncipe.
Designed by Manuel Pinto da Costa, who became the country's first president.
The yellow middle band is one-and-a-half times as wide as each green band.
It shares its colours and a black star with the first flags of Cape Verde and Guinea-Bissau, also former Portuguese colonies.

Flag of Saudi Arabia.text: Made with two matching sides so the Arabic writing reads correctly, right to left, from either side.
Out of respect for the sacred creed written on it, the flag is never lowered to half-mast.
The white sword beneath the writing stands for safety and justice.
Similar flags flew from the 1930s, but the exact design only became official on 15 March 1973.

Flag of Senegal.text: Its green star replaced a little human figure, the kanaga, from the flag of the short-lived Mali Federation.
Its three vertical stripes were inspired by the French tricolour, which flew over Senegal until 1960.
Senegal's government calls yellow "the colour of arts, literature, and intellect".

Flag of Serbia.text: Legend says that when copying Russia's flag caused offence, Prince Miloš asked: "Could we simply turn it upside down?"
A red, blue and white tricolour, in changing versions, has flown for Serbia since 1839.
A 1281 treasury list mentioning "a flag of red and blue fabric" is the oldest known record of Serbian flag colours.
Four fire-steels sit around the cross on its coat of arms, a design dating back to medieval Serbia.

Flag of Sierra Leone.text: The blue stripe recalls the natural harbour of Freetown, the capital.
It was first hoisted at midnight on 27 April 1961, the day Sierra Leone became independent.
Its green, white and blue were borrowed from the new coat of arms, which was designed first.
Its early colonial badge showed an elephant, an oil palm and mountains, the same as the Gold Coast's but marked S.L.

Flag of Singapore.text: The crescent moon stands for a young nation on the rise; the five stars for democracy, peace, progress, justice and equality.
A National Day tradition since 1970: a giant flag carried across Singapore's sky beneath a helicopter.
In 2007, 8,667 volunteers holding red and white umbrellas formed a giant living Singapore flag.
Adopted in 1959, when Singapore became self-governing, it stayed on after full independence in 1965.

Flag of Slovakia.text: Without its shield, the white, blue and red stripes would look almost exactly like Russia's flag; only the shades differ.
Adopted without any emblem in 1990, the flag only gained its coat of arms in 1992.
Its designers based the shield on a 14th-century coat of arms, enlarging its three hills to make them a national symbol.

Flag of Slovenia.text: The shield shows Mount Triglav, Slovenia's highest peak, in white against a blue sky.
Two wavy blue lines under the mountain stand for the Adriatic Sea and Slovenia's rivers.
Its three golden stars were borrowed from the Counts of Celje, a powerful medieval noble family.
Students led by a poet first raised the white-blue-red tricolour in Ljubljana on 7 April 1848.

Flag of Somalia.text: Somali scholar Mohammed Awale Liban designed it himself, and it was approved in 1954, six years before independence.
Its light blue was chosen as a thank-you to the United Nations, which helped steer Somalia to independence.
The white five-pointed Star of Unity stands for five regions of the Horn of Africa where Somali people live.

Flag of South Africa.text: When adopted in 1994, it was the only national flag with six colours in its main design, not counting coats of arms.
The green Y shape is meant to show different parts of society coming together and taking the road ahead in unity.
Intended only as a temporary flag, it was officially announced just seven days before it first flew, sending flag makers into a frantic rush.
Its official red isn't plain red but "chilli red", as named in the country's constitution.

Flag of South Korea.text: Called the Taegukgi, its red and blue circle shows yin and yang, the balance of opposite energies.
Each of the four black bar patterns in the corners stands for heaven, earth, water or fire.
Korea had no national flag at all before 1876, only a royal standard for the king.
Even the flagpole is specified: white, silver or green, topped with a cap shaped like a mugunghwa flower bud.

Flag of South Sudan.text: The flag is older than the country: it was adopted in 2005, six years before South Sudan became independent.
Its blue triangle represents the waters of the Nile, described as a source of life.
For years versions differed, with tilted or upright stars and dark or sky-blue triangles, until the government picked one in 2023.

Flag of Spain.text: The yellow stripe is twice as tall as each red one, a layout now known as the "Spanish fess".
It began in 1785 as a navy flag, picked by King Charles III from 12 different designs.
Spain's old white navy flags were too easily confused with other nations', so the new one had to stand out against sky and sea.
Its nickname, la Rojigualda, comes from gualda, or weld, a plant once used to make yellow dye.

Flag of Sri Lanka.text: Known as the Lion Flag, it shows a golden lion gripping a kastane sword in its right front paw.
Since 1972, four bo-tree leaves have filled its corners, replacing the spearheads used before.
The last Kandyan king's lion standard was taken to England in 1815, and campaigners later rediscovered it in Chelsea.

Flag of Sudan.text: Several Arab flags share red, white and black stripes; Sudan's stands out with a green triangle at the hoist.
Sudan's first national flag, raised at independence in 1956, was blue, yellow and green for the Nile, the Sahara and farmland.
Before independence the territory had no flag of its own, so Egypt's and Britain's flags flew side by side.
At a 1955 conference, Sudan was represented by a simple white flag with SUDAN written in red capitals.

Flag of Suriname.text: Five stripes of green, white and red carry a big yellow star standing for unity and a golden future.
Art teacher Jack Pinas won the national contest to design it in 1975, though his entry was tweaked.
Before independence, Suriname's flag showed five coloured stars linked by a black oval, one star for each of its main peoples.

Flag of Sweden.text: Its colours and cross were probably inspired by Sweden's coat of arms of 1442, which splits blue with a gold cross.
A royal letter of 1562 gave the first legal description: "yellow in a cross fashioned on blue".
Sweden's navy flies a version with three pointed tails, called the "three-tongued flag" in Swedish.

Flag of Switzerland.text: Swiss law makes the national flag square, a shape shared only by Vatican City's flag.
The Red Cross symbol is this flag with its colours swapped, honouring Switzerland, where the first Geneva Convention was held.
Each arm of the white cross is exactly one-sixth longer than it is wide.
In Switzerland's standard German it's a "Fahne", while Germany calls national flags a "Flagge".

Flag of Syria.text: Three equal stripes of green, white and black, with three red stars in the middle.
Every flag Syria has flown since independence in 1946 has used the pan-Arab colours green, black, white and red.

Flag of Tajikistan.text: Its golden crown sits under seven stars, because seven stands for perfection and happiness in Persian mythology.
The crown nods to a popular belief that the name "Tajik" comes from "taj", Persian for crown.
The wide white stripe stands for purity, mountain snow and ice, and cotton.

Flag of Tanzania.text: When Tanganyika and Zanzibar united in 1964, their flags merged: green and black from one, blue from the other.
One of a fairly small number of national flags crossed by a diagonal band.
Its blue stands for the Indian Ocean and the country's many lakes and rivers.
The thin stripes edging its black band stand for the country's mineral wealth.

Flag of Thailand.text: Adopted on 28 September 1917; since 2016 that date has been a national day celebrating the flag.
From 1855, Siam's flag showed a white elephant on a red background.
Legend says King Vajiravudh wanted a symmetrical flag after seeing the old elephant flag flown upside down.
Costa Rica's flag is almost a twin, with the same stripes but the red and blue swapped.

Flag of the Bahamas.text: Aquamarine stripes stand for the surrounding sea, gold for the sun, and a black triangle for the people's strength.
Rather than pick one winner, organisers blended ideas from many entries in a national design contest.
First raised at midnight on 10 July 1973, the moment The Bahamas became independent.
The old colonial badge showed a ship chasing pirates, with the motto "Pirates expelled, commerce restored".

Flag of the Central African Republic.text: Four horizontal stripes are crossed by a single vertical red band, with a yellow star in the corner.
Designer Barthélemy Boganda first meant it for a proposed "United States of Latin Africa".
Boganda told lawmakers its colours, standing for four territories and France, "came out of my heart".
Unchanged since 1958, it even stayed in use when the country briefly became an empire in the 1970s.

Flag of the Comoros.text: Its four coloured stripes and four stars stand for the four main islands of the archipelago.
Today's design arrived with a new constitution approved by referendum in 2001, after five earlier flags since 1963.
The first Comorian flag was designed in 1963 by Suzanne Gauthier, twelve years before independence.

Flag of the Czech Republic.text: It's Czechoslovakia's old flag, kept by the Czech Republic when the country split in two at the end of 1992.
The blue triangle was added in 1920, partly because the plain white-over-red flag looked almost exactly like Poland's.
By law, its blue triangle reaches exactly halfway across the flag, its tip landing at the very centre.
Its designer, Jaroslav Kursa, was an archivist at the Czechoslovak Ministry of the Interior.

Flag of the Democratic Republic of the C.text: One of the few national flags with a diagonal line: a red stripe edged in yellow cuts across its sky blue.
Red stands for the blood of the country's martyrs, yellow for its wealth, and the star for the future.
From 1971 to 1997, when the country was called Zaire, its flag was green with an arm holding a flaming torch.
Adopted in 2006, today's flag brought back a 1960s design but swapped royal blue for sky blue.

Flag of the Dominican Republic.text: Designed by Juan Pablo Duarte, the "Father of the Nation", it was first hoisted in February 1844.
The first flags were sewn by women of the independence movement, among them Concepción Bona and María Trinidad Sánchez.
Its coat of arms shows an open Bible and the motto "Dios, Patria, Libertad": God, Fatherland, Liberty.
Take away the coat of arms and you get the merchant flag flown by ships.

Flag of the Federated States of Micrones.text: Its four white stars stand for the states of Chuuk, Pohnpei, Kosrae and Yap, set like the points of a compass.
It grew from a six-star trust territory flag; three of those districts, including Palau, went their own way.
The blue field stands for the Pacific Ocean, and its shade was first borrowed from the United Nations flag.
Kosrae earned the fourth star after it was split off from Pohnpei.

Flag of the Gambia.text: Its blue band is the Gambia River, the country's key feature and the source of its name.
The winning design came from Louis Thomasi, who worked as an accountant.
It was first raised at midnight on 18 February 1965, the day The Gambia became independent.
Red stands for the sun and savanna, green for forests and farming, and the thin white stripes for unity and peace.

Flag of the Maldives.text: The earliest Maldivian flag was plain red; a black-and-white striped strip called the Dhandimathi was later added by the pole.
In 1965, the year of independence, the black-and-white stripes were dropped, leaving today's red-bordered green flag with its white crescent.
Its red border honours the nation's heroes, while the green centre stands for peace and prosperity.
A version of the Sultan's old flag, with a star beside the crescent, still serves as the President's standard.

Flag of the Marshall Islands.text: Its star has 24 points, one for each electoral district, and four extra-long points for the main centres Majuro, Jaluit, Wotje and Ebeye.
The rising diagonal band is the equator, with the star sitting above it because the islands lie in the Northern Hemisphere.
The white and orange halves of the band stand for the two island chains, Ratak ("sunrise") and Ralik ("sunset").
Designed by Emlain Kabua, who became the country's first First Lady, it was adopted in 1979.

Flag of the Netherlands.text: Often called the oldest tricolour flag still in use, it dates back to the Dutch Republic of the 1600s.
It started out orange, white and blue; red gradually replaced the orange between about 1630 and 1660.
In 1937 a royal decree just one sentence long settled it: the colours are red, white and blue.
When students graduate, families often fly the flag with the graduate's school bag hung from the top of the pole.

Flag of the Philippines.text: Flown upside down, with the red stripe on top, it signals that the country is at war.
Its three stars stand for the main island groups: Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao.
The sun's eight rays honour eight provinces that rose up against Spanish rule in 1896.
The very first one was hand-sewn in Hong Kong by Marcela Agoncillo and two helpers.

Flag of the Republic of the Congo.text: Among flags in the Pan-African green, yellow and red, it's the only one with a diagonal design.
Green stands for farms and forests and yellow for friendship, but the red's meaning was never officially explained.
Replaced by a red flag in 1970, the original 1959 design came back in 1991.
Under French rule, the colony was not allowed a flag of its own.

Flag of the Seychelles.text: Five bands fan out across it from one side, symbolising a dynamic new country moving into the future.
Adopted in 1996, it is the country's third flag since independence in 1976.
Blue is the sky and sea, yellow the sun, red the people, white social justice, and green the land.
The 1976 flag looked very like that of a steamship company whose ships often called at the islands.

Flag of the Solomon Islands.text: Its five stars stood for the country's five provinces; more provinces have been created since, but the stars stayed at five.
Blue is for water, green for land, and the thin yellow stripe is the sun's rays dividing them.
Unlike the flags of nearby Australia and New Zealand, its stars are not the Southern Cross.
Adopted in November 1977, the flag flew eight months before the country actually became independent.

Flag of the United Arab Emirates.text: Designed in 1971 by Abdullah Mohammed Al Maainah, aged just 19, who won a nationwide design contest.
Made from the four pan-Arab colours: red, green, white and black.
All seven emirates use it as their own flag, and every emirate except Fujairah also has a separate one.
Dubai and Ajman have identical emirate flags: red with a white bar next to the pole.

Flag of the United Kingdom.text: Three crosses layered as one: St George for England, St Andrew for Scotland and St Patrick for Northern Ireland.
Wales isn't represented, because the earlier flag of Great Britain was designed while Wales was part of England.
It has a right way up, yet it's often flown upside down by accident, even on shop-made hand flags.
In Chinese it's nicknamed the "Rice-Character Flag" because it looks like the character for rice, 米.

Flag of the United States.text: Today's 50-star design is the 27th version, as a star is added whenever a new state joins.
In 2007 the 50-star flag became the longest-used version, overtaking the 48-star flag of 1912 to 1959.
The tale of Betsy Ross sewing the first flag is a legend: neither Washington's diaries nor Congress's records mention it.
When it first reached China in 1784, people called it the "Flower Flag", a name still heard in some words today.

Flag of Timor-Leste.text: Its white star is called "the light that guides" and stands for peace.
Officially its white star is tilted, with one tip pointing towards the flag's left edge, though many flags show it upright.
In East Timorese culture, flags are treated as sacred objects with real symbolic power.

Flag of Togo.text: Designed in 1960 by Togolese artist Paul Ahyi, the year Togo became independent.
Its five green and yellow stripes stand for Togo's five regions.
The white star stands for peace, intelligence and light.
Nobody's quite sure of its proportions: one flag expert says about 3:5, another 2:3.

Flag of Tonga.text: Tonga has flown the same flag since 1875.
An earlier red-cross-on-white design looked almost exactly like the Red Cross emblem, so the cross moved into a corner.
Like Britain's Red Ensign, it is mostly red with a special design in the top corner.

Flag of Trinidad and Tobago.text: One of the few national flags with a diagonal stripe, designed by Carlisle Chang for independence in 1962.
Red stands for fire and the sun, black for the earth, and white for water.
Before 1962, the colonial flag carried a badge of a ship arriving in front of a mountain.

Flag of Tunisia.text: Ruler Hussein II created it in the 1830s so that Tunisia's warships could be told apart from other fleets.
Its red crescent and star are symbols linked to the Ottoman Empire, which once ruled the region.
Its exact geometry was only written into law in 1999, with the white disc spanning one-third of the flag's length.
According to Tunisia's embassy in France, the white disc stands for the nation shining like the sun.

Flag of Turkey.text: Based on the Ottoman Empire's flag, whose white crescent and star on red was introduced in 1844.
Often called al bayrak, "the red flag", while the national anthem calls it "the red banner".
Its exact proportions and shade of red were fixed by the Turkish Flag Law of 1936.

Flag of Turkmenistan.text: A red stripe packed with five intricate carpet patterns celebrates the country's famous carpet-making.
Each of its five carpet guls stands for one of Turkmenistan's five major tribes.
Olive branches were added in 1997 to mark the UN recognising Turkmenistan's permanent neutrality.
In 2008 it was raised on a 133-metre pole in Ashgabat, the world's tallest free-standing flagpole until 2010.

Flag of Tuvalu.text: Its nine yellow stars are laid out like a map of the country's nine islands.
Chosen from 40 proposals when Tuvalu became independent in 1978.
Replaced in 1995 by a design without the Union Jack, the original flag came back in 1997.
In 1995 one star was briefly removed, leaving eight to echo the name Tuvalu, meaning "eight standing together".

Flag of Uganda.text: At its centre stands a crested crane, a symbol of good fortune, long life and wealth among the Baganda people.
According to flag expert Whitney Smith, black stands for the people, yellow for sunshine and red for brotherhood.
By one account, an earlier green-and-blue design was dropped partly because its green faded quickly in the sun.
Adopted on 9 October 1962, the very day Uganda became independent.

Flag of Ukraine.text: Blue-and-yellow banners flew over Lviv's town hall during the revolutions of 1848, an early forerunner of today's flag.
Dark blue was picked over sky blue in 1992 for a practical reason: sky-blue flags fade quickly in the sun.
Ukraine has held a Day of the National Flag every 23 August since 2004.
The constitution describes it simply as two equally sized horizontal bands of blue and yellow.

Flag of Uruguay.text: Nine blue and white stripes stand for Uruguay's nine original departments, an idea borrowed from the stripes of the US flag.
When first adopted in 1828 it had 19 stripes, until a law cut them to nine in 1830.
The golden Sun of May in the corner marks the May Revolution of 1810 and also shines on Argentina's flag.
Uruguay has three official flags: this one plus the Artigas flag and the flag of the Treinta y Tres.

Flag of Uzbekistan.text: Twelve white stars sit beside a crescent moon, in rows of three, four and five.
Thin red lines between the blue, white and green stripes are said to stand for the power of life.
Chosen in 1991 from more than 200 contest entries, soon after independence.
Since 2010, Uzbek law has banned using the flag in advertisements.

Flag of Vanuatu.text: A curled boar's tusk, a symbol of prosperity, wraps around two crossed namele leaves.
The namele leaves have 39 leaflets, one for each member of Vanuatu's first parliament.
The yellow Y-shape echoes the way Vanuatu's islands are laid out on the map.
Its colours came from the flag of the party that led the New Hebrides to independence in 1980.

Flag of Vatican City.text: One of only two national flags drawn as a perfect square, along with Switzerland's.
Its white half carries a papal crown, the tiara, above the crossed keys of Saint Peter.
Before 1808, the Papal States commonly flew a yellow and red flag instead.
Adopted in 1929, the year a treaty with Italy created the independent state of Vatican City.

Flag of Venezuela.text: Its yellow, blue and red stripes were designed by Francisco de Miranda for an 1806 expedition to free Venezuela.
Miranda's tricolour also inspired the flags of neighbours Colombia and Ecuador.
Miranda named a yellow, blue and red banner of a citizens' guard in Hamburg, Germany, as one inspiration.

Flag of Vietnam.text: Known as the 'red flag with the golden star', it is the only flag in ASEAN with no white in it.
The star's five points are said to stand for groups in society, such as farmers, workers, intellectuals and soldiers.
In 1955 the star was redrawn with straighter points, giving the design used today.
In Vietnamese, 'golden' and 'yellow' are the same word: vàng.

Flag of Yemen.text: Raised on 22 May 1990, the very day North and South Yemen joined into one country.
Officially, red stands for unity and sacrifice, white for a bright future and black for the dark past.
It looks exactly like the flag Libya used from 1969 to 1972.

Flag of Zambia.text: An orange African fish eagle soars above it, showing the people's ability to rise above problems.
Unusually, its emblem sits at the far end from the flagpole rather than in the centre or near the pole.
The orange stripe stands for Zambia's mineral wealth, mainly copper.
First raised on independence day in 1964, it replaced the Blue Ensign of British-ruled Northern Rhodesia.

Flag of Zimbabwe.text: The golden Zimbabwe Bird copies a carved soapstone bird found at the ancient ruins of Great Zimbabwe.
The first draft had no bird; it was added after a designer pointed out its uniqueness and history.
Its white triangle is officially a symbol of peace.
The bird first appeared as an emblem in 1924, on Southern Rhodesia's coat of arms.

Florence.text: Many academics consider it the birthplace of the Renaissance.
Standard Italian grew from the local Florentine dialect, made prestigious by writers such as Dante.
For six years, from 1865 to 1871, it was the capital of the Kingdom of Italy.
Its historic centre, packed with Renaissance art and architecture, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.

Florence Cathedral.text: Its dome, finished in 1436, is still the largest masonry dome in the world.
Brunelleschi invented new hoisting machines to lift its materials, including over 4 million bricks.
A young apprentice named Leonardo da Vinci sketched the dome's lifting machines, so he is often credited with inventing them.
Above the main door, a one-handed clock counts 24 hours in old 'Italian time', with the day ending at sunset.

Florida.text: The only US state that borders both the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean.
St. Augustine, founded by the Spanish in 1565, is the oldest continuously occupied European settlement in the continental US.
Ponce de León named it in 1513 for its lush greenery and because it was Easter, called Pascua Florida in Spanish.
Britton Hill, its highest point at just 105 metres, is the lowest high point of any US state.

Forbidden City.text: Home to 24 Ming and Qing emperors, it was the centre of power in China from 1420 to 1924.
UNESCO recognises it as the world's largest collection of preserved ancient wooden structures.
A popular myth says it has 9,999 rooms; experts count 8,886 "bays" of rooms.
Its gates are studded with nine-by-nine rows of golden door nails, except one gate, which has only eight rows.

Forth Bridge.text: When it opened in 1890 it had the world's longest cantilever span, a record it held until Canada's Quebec Bridge opened in 1917.
The first major structure in Britain built of steel.
'Painting the Forth Bridge' is an expression for a never-ending job, though nonstop repainting never actually happened.
In an 1887 demonstration, Japanese engineer Kaichi Watanabe was held up between its two seated designers to show how it works.

France.text: The world's most visited country, welcoming a record number of foreign visitors in 2025.
Mont Blanc, on its border with Italy, is the highest point in Western Europe.
Its longest land border isn't in Europe at all: it's with Brazil, through French Guiana in South America.
In 1895 the Lumière brothers held a paid film screening in Paris, traditionally regarded as the birth of cinema.

Fushimi Inari-taisha.text: Head shrine of Inari, the Shinto spirit of rice, said to have as many as 32,000 branch shrines across Japan.
Businesses donated its roughly 10,000 torii gates, and about 800 stand in rows forming a tunnel.
Stone foxes, seen as Inari's messengers, guard the shrine, some holding the key to a rice store in their mouths.
Nintendo's Shigeru Miyamoto said the shrine helped inspire Star Fox, where pilots fly through rings.

Gabon.text: Straddling the equator, it has forest covering nearly 90% of its land.
Home to more than half of all African forest elephants.
At Oklo, uranium ore ran natural nuclear chain reactions about 1.7 billion years ago, the only place this is known to have happened.
In 2002 it set aside about a tenth of its territory as 13 new national parks.

Gaborone.text: Built almost from scratch, founded in 1964 as the capital for a soon-to-be independent Botswana.
Locals call it "GC", short for Government Camp, the old colonial headquarters.
Once spelled Gaberones, short for "Gaborone's Village", after Chief Gaborone of the Tlokwa people.
Headquarters of the Southern African Development Community, a regional bloc of nations.

Gateway Arch.text: At 630 feet (192 m), this stainless-steel curve is the world's tallest arch.
Visitors ride to the top in tiny five-seat pods that swivel to stay level, like Ferris wheel cars, as they climb.
A time capsule holding 762,000 signatures, many from students, was welded into its top piece.
Architect Eero Saarinen's winning design faced 171 rival entries, including one from his own father.

Gateway of India.text: Completed in 1924, this 26-metre basalt arch on the waterfront has become synonymous with Mumbai.
Built to mark King George V's 1911 visit, yet the king only saw a cardboard model, as building began in 1915.
In 1948 the last British troops to leave independent India marched out through this arch.
Ferries from its jetties carry visitors to the Elephanta Caves, about fifty minutes away by boat.

Geneva.text: Home to dozens of international organisations, including the Red Cross and many United Nations agencies.
Nearby CERN, founded in 1954, is the world's largest particle physics laboratory.
Its giant lakeside fountain, the Jet d'Eau, began life in 1886 as a safety valve for a water-power network.
Each December's Escalade festival features chocolate cauldrons filled with vegetable-shaped marzipan.

Georgia (country).text: Archaeologists found the world's oldest known traces of grape wine here, in clay jars about 8,000 years old.
Fossils found at Dmanisi, about 1.8 million years old, are the oldest known remains of early humans in Eurasia.
In Greek legend, the Golden Fleece sought by the Argonauts lay in Colchis, in what is now western Georgia.
At a traditional feast called a supra, a toastmaster known as the tamada leads long, thoughtful toasts.

Georgia (U.S. state).text: The last and southernmost of the original Thirteen Colonies that became the United States.
Civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. was born in Atlanta, its largest city.
Its official state vegetable is the Vidalia onion.
Raises more chickens for meat than any other US state.

Germany.text: The most populous country in the European Union, with well over 80 million people.
Johannes Gutenberg introduced moveable-type printing to Europe here, helping books and knowledge spread far and wide.
German bakeries make hundreds of kinds of bread, plus over a thousand kinds of pastries and rolls.
Its famous Autobahn motorways have no general national speed limit for some kinds of vehicles.

Ghana.text: Lake Volta, created by the Akosombo Dam, is the world's largest artificial lake by surface area.
One of the world's top cocoa producers, growing the beans that end up as chocolate.
No country lies closer to 0° latitude, 0° longitude, an empty patch of ocean about 570 km off its coast.
Kofi Annan, who led the United Nations as Secretary-General from 1997 to 2006, was a Ghanaian diplomat.

Giant's Causeway.text: About 40,000 interlocking basalt columns, left behind by an ancient volcanic eruption.
Declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
Most of the stepping-stone columns are six-sided, but some have anywhere from four to eight sides.
In one popular legend, giant Finn McCool built it, then hid from a bigger Scottish giant by dressing up as a baby.

Glasgow.text: Scotland's most populous city, set on the banks of the River Clyde.
Opened in 1896, its Subway is the world's third-oldest underground metro, after London's and Budapest's.
The first official international football match, Scotland against England, was played here in 1872 and ended 0-0.
Its name is often said to mean "dear green place", still a fond nickname for the city.

Glenfinnan Viaduct.text: Scotland's longest concrete railway bridge, striding across 21 arches about 100 feet above the River Finnan.
Appearing in four Harry Potter films earned it the nickname "The Harry Potter Bridge".
Legend said a horse fell into one of its piers; scans found a horse and cart, but inside a different viaduct.
Look closely at a Bank of Scotland £10 note from the 2007 series and you'll find this viaduct.

Golden Gate Bridge.text: When it opened in 1937, it had the longest main span and the tallest towers of any suspension bridge in the world.
A famous travel guide called it "possibly the most beautiful, certainly the most photographed, bridge in the world".
The US Navy wanted it painted in black and yellow stripes; the architect picked "International Orange" instead.
On foggy days, two horns on the south tower sound a 2-second blast, then pause for 18 seconds, over and over.

Golden Temple.text: Sikhism's holiest site, a gurdwara rising from a sacred pool in the heart of Amritsar.
Its free community kitchen, run by volunteers, serves around 100,000 vegetarian meals a day to anyone who comes.
Its four entrances, one on each side, symbolise that people of every background are welcome.
Its "golden" nickname came after Maharaja Ranjit Singh had the sanctum covered in gold leaf in 1830.

Göreme.text: Famous for 'fairy chimneys', rock towers that people hollowed out into churches and houses in the Middle Ages.
Little visited until the 1970s, by 2000 it had become the tourist capital of Cappadocia.
Cave homes here had animal mangers and grape-treading presses carved straight out of the rock.
Almost all of the village's old cave houses have now been turned into hotels.

Grand Canyon.text: Carved by the Colorado River, it runs about 277 miles and plunges more than a mile deep.
Its rock walls lay bare nearly two billion years of Earth's geological history, layer upon layer.
Surprisingly, it isn't the world's deepest canyon: gorges in the Himalayas, in Nepal and Tibet, are far deeper.
The North Rim sits over 1,000 feet higher than the South Rim, and gets more rain and snow.

Grand-Place.text: Considered one of the world's most beautiful squares, it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998.
Every two years in August, nearly a million begonias or dahlias are laid out here as a giant flower carpet.
Its Gothic Town Hall, built between 1401 and 1455, is the square's only surviving medieval building.
The writer Victor Hugo stayed in one of its guildhalls, called Le Pigeon, in 1852.

Great Bear Lake.text: The largest lake lying entirely inside Canada, and the eighth-largest in the world by area.
Sits right on the Arctic Circle, and its surface usually stays frozen from November until July.
In 1995 an angler pulled out a 32.65 kg lake trout here, the biggest ever caught by angling.
So clear that in 1828 explorer John Franklin could still see a white rag lowered to about 15 fathoms (27 m).

Great Mosque of Djenné.text: The largest mud-brick building in the world; the current mosque was completed in 1907.
Palm sticks poking out of its walls double as built-in scaffolding for the yearly replastering.
Ostrich eggs sit on top of the spires of its three tall towers.
It stands on a platform raised 3 metres above the market, keeping it safe when the Bani River floods.

Great Pyramid of Giza.text: The oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and the only one still largely standing.
For more than 3,700 years it was the tallest structure humans had ever built.
Builders used an estimated 2.3 million stone blocks, weighing about 6 million tonnes altogether.
It once gleamed with smooth white limestone casing; most was later stripped away, making it about 8 metres shorter.

Great Slave Lake.text: North America's deepest lake, plunging to 614 metres.
The tenth-largest lake in the world by area, stretching 469 km across Canada's Northwest Territories.
Gold found on its North Arm in the 1930s led to the founding of Yellowknife, now the territory's capital.
In winter a 6.5 km road across the ice links Yellowknife to Dettah, a trip of 27 km by land in summer.

Great Sphinx of Giza.text: The oldest known monumental sculpture in Egypt, carved straight out of the rock of the Giza Plateau.
A lion with a human head, measuring 73 metres from paw to tail.
Despite a popular myth, Napoleon's soldiers did not shoot off its nose with a cannon.
Drifting sand once buried it up to its shoulders, until the young Thutmose IV had its front paws dug out around 1400 BC.

Greece.text: Thanks to its thousands of islands, it has the longest coastline of any country on the Mediterranean.
Ancient Athens became the world's most famous early democracy after reforms by Cleisthenes in 508 BC.
By tradition, the very first Olympic Games were held here in 776 BC.
About 80% of the land is mountains or hills, topped by Mount Olympus, mythical home of the Greek gods.

Greenland.text: The world's largest island, if you don't count continents like Australia.
The least densely populated country or territory in the world.
According to Icelandic sagas, Erik the Red named this icy land "Greenland", supposedly hoping the pleasant name would attract settlers.
Tiny Kaffeklubben Island, off its north coast, is the world's northernmost undisputed point of land.

Guangzhou.text: From 1757 to 1842, its Thirteen Factories were the only legal place for foreign trade with China.
Also called Canton, it has over 2,200 years of history and was a major Silk Road terminus.
Nicknamed "City of Rams": one legend tells of five immortals riding in on rams and bringing rice farming.
