Its Canton Fair, first held in 1957, is China's oldest and largest trade fair.

Guatemala.text: The most populous country in Central America.
The heartland of the ancient Maya civilization, whose great city of Tikal can still be explored today.
Its name comes from a Nahuatl word meaning "place of many trees".
Dozens of volcanoes rise across the land, and a few, including Fuego and Pacaya, still erupt.

Guatemala City.text: Its metropolitan area is the largest in Central America.
In 1821 the Act of Independence of Central America, declaring the region free from Spain, was signed here.
Sits on the site of Kaminaljuyu, a Maya city mostly occupied from about 1500 BCE to 1200 CE.
Its city zones are numbered 1 to 25, yet there is no Zone 20, 22 or 23.

Guggenheim Museum Bilbao.text: Frank Gehry's shimmering museum, opened in 1997, revived Bilbao so dramatically that the change became known as the "Bilbao effect".
In a 2010 survey, architecture experts named it more often than any other building as one of the most important since 1980.
One critic called it a "fantastic dream ship" wrapped in titanium, its shiny panels reminiscent of fish scales.
Despite its wild curves, it was finished on time and on budget, which is rare for such daring architecture.

Guinea.text: Three great West African rivers, the Niger, the Gambia and the Senegal, all begin in its highlands.
One of the world's biggest producers of bauxite, the ore that aluminium is made from.
Sometimes called Guinea-Conakry, after its capital, to tell it apart from Guinea-Bissau and Equatorial Guinea.
Its national football team is nicknamed Syli nationale, the National Elephants.

Guinea-Bissau.text: Its Bijagós archipelago, scattered off the coast, was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2025.
Cashew nuts are among its major exports, alongside fish and ground nuts.
Very low-lying: its highest point, Monte Torin, is only about 260 metres above sea level.
Its best-known music, gumbe, is a lively, drum-driven style that blends several of the country's folk traditions.

Gullfoss.text: The "Golden Falls" are one of Iceland's most popular sights and a highlight of the Golden Circle tour.
The Hvítá river tumbles down a three-step "staircase", then plunges in two drops into a crevice 32 m deep.
Farmer's daughter Sigríður Tómasdóttir is widely credited with saving the falls from a dam, and is often called Iceland's first environmentalist.
An animated version of the falls appears in the third season of Avatar: The Last Airbender.

Guyana.text: The only country in mainland South America with English as its official language.
Kaieteur Falls, deep in its rainforest, is one of the world's most powerful waterfalls.
Its name comes from an Indigenous word meaning "land of many waters".
Mount Roraima and other flat-topped tepui mountains here are said to have inspired Arthur Conan Doyle's 1912 novel The Lost World.

Hạ Long Bay.text: Some 1,600 limestone islands, each crowned with thick jungle, rise steeply out of the sea.
UNESCO listed it as World Heritage in 1994 for its beauty, and again in 2000 for its geology.
Hạ Long means "descending dragon"; one legend says it is where a mother dragon came down to live.
For generations, fishing families lived out on the bay in floating houses, though many have since moved ashore.

Hadrian's Wall.text: Begun by the Romans in AD 122, it stretched about 73 miles right across Britain, coast to coast.
Though sometimes loosely called the border, it lies entirely within England and has never divided England from Scotland.
Bronze cups engraved with the names of its forts have turned up far away, probably treasured as Roman souvenirs.
A World Heritage Site since 1987, now shared with Germany as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire.

Hagia Sophia.text: Completed in AD 537, it held the world's largest interior space.
For over five hundred years it was the largest church in the world.
Graffiti in runes, thought to be left by Viking-era Scandinavian guards, is scratched into an upstairs gallery.
Ottoman builders copied its style for great mosques built about a thousand years later.

Haiti.text: The first country in the Americas to fully abolish slavery, founded in 1804 by people who had freed themselves.
The mountaintop Citadelle Laferrière, completed in 1820, is one of the largest fortresses in the Americas.
Its name comes from the Indigenous Taíno language and means "land of high mountains".
On the night of Christmas Eve 1492, Columbus's flagship, the Santa María, ran aground near today's Cap-Haïtien.

Half Dome.text: Sheer on one side and rounded on the others, it looks like a giant granite dome sliced in half.
Once called 'perfectly inaccessible', it was first climbed in 1875 by drilling iron bolts into the rock.
Hikers haul themselves up the final 400 feet gripping two steel cables as handrails.
Ansel Adams took his famous photo Monolith, the Face of Half Dome from a ledge here in 1927.

Hallgrímskirkja.text: Its 74.5-metre tower makes it Iceland's tallest church and one of the tallest structures in the country.
Its architect is said to have shaped it like Iceland's 'organ pipe' columns of basalt rock.
Building it took 41 years, from 1945 to 1986.
The Leif Erikson statue out front, a gift from the United States, is older than the church itself.

Hallstatt.text: This lakeside village gave its name to the Hallstatt culture, an Iron Age world linked to the early Celts.
Salt has been mined in the mountain here since prehistoric times, and was already a busy, organised industry in the Bronze Age.
A local chapel displays decorated skulls inscribed with each person's name, job and date of death.
A Chinese mining company built a full-size copy of the whole village in Huizhou, Guangdong, unveiled in 2012.

Hamburg.text: Germany's second-largest city, and one of its three city-states alongside Berlin and Bremen.
Around 2,500 bridges cross its rivers and canals, far more than in Venice or Amsterdam.
Before they were famous, the Beatles honed their act in its clubs between 1960 and 1962.
Home to Miniatur Wunderland, the world's largest model railway according to Guinness World Records, built inside an old warehouse.

Hanoi.text: Founded as a royal capital in 1010 and named Thăng Long, meaning "ascending dragon".
Its Temple of Literature was the site of Vietnam's oldest university.
Its old name Đông Kinh, "eastern capital", gave Europeans the name Tonkin for all of northern Vietnam.
The One Pillar Pagoda, first built in 1049, was inspired by a king's dream of a lotus flower.

Harare.text: Founded in 1890 as Fort Salisbury, it took the name Harare in 1982, two years after independence.
Named after the village of a Shona chief, Neharawa, nicknamed "he who does not sleep".
In late August, new leaves on the local msasa trees paint the countryside wine red.
Sitting on a plateau about 1,483 m high, it enjoys a mild subtropical highland climate.

Havana.text: Its old town and ring of Spanish forts became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982.
In the mid-1700s it was bigger than both Boston and New York City.
Its coat of arms shows three castles, standing for the three forts that once defended the city.

Hawaii.text: The only US state made entirely of islands, and the only one not on the North American mainland.
Measured from its base on the ocean floor, its volcano Mauna Kea is taller than Mount Everest.
The only state never to have recorded a temperature below zero Fahrenheit.
Any respected elder may be called "aunty" or "uncle", whether related or not.

Helsinki.text: The world's northernmost urban area with over a million people, and the northernmost capital in the EU.
Founded in 1550 by King Gustav I of Sweden as a trading town to rival Tallinn across the gulf.
Until about 1930, English speakers knew it by its Swedish name, Helsingfors.
Its 19th-century neoclassical buildings around Senate Square earned it the nickname "The White City of the North".

Hiroshima Peace Memorial.text: A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996, its skeletal dome is preserved as a ruin and a symbol of peace.
It began life in 1915 as an exhibition hall, designed by Czech architect Jan Letzel.
To fund its preservation, Hiroshima's first popularly elected mayor even collected donations on the streets of Tokyo.

Hispaniola.text: The most populous island in the West Indies, shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic.
Pico Duarte, at 3,101 metres, is the highest peak in the Antilles.
Santo Domingo, founded in the 1490s, is the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the Americas.
Salty Lake Enriquillo lies 46 metres below sea level, the lowest point on the whole island.

Ho Chi Minh City.text: Vietnam's most populous city, home to well over 10 million people.
Under French rule it was nicknamed the 'Pearl of the Orient'.
The first newspaper in the Vietnamese language, Gia Định Báo, was launched here in 1865.
Renamed in 1976, yet people still call it Saigon in everyday conversation.

Hobbiton Movie Set.text: The hobbits' home village in both The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit film trilogies.
Director Peter Jackson spotted this family sheep farm from the air in 1998 while hunting for locations.
The big oak above Bag End was a real tree, cut down nearby and rebuilt on set with artificial leaves.
Since 2012 the Green Dragon Inn from the films has been a working inn, serving drinks to visitors.

Hokkaido.text: The northernmost and second-largest of Japan's four main islands.
Its only land link to the rest of Japan is the Seikan railway tunnel beneath the Tsugaru Strait.
Hokkaido has more brown bears than anywhere else in eastern Asia outside Russia.
In winter, big floes of drift ice often clog the Sea of Okhotsk off its northern coast.

Hollywood Sign.text: One of America's best-known landmarks, often shown in films to tell viewers a story is set in Los Angeles.
Put up in 1923 as a temporary advert for a housing estate, it read HOLLYWOODLAND until LAND came down in 1949.
The original sign had around 4,000 light bulbs, flashing HOLLY, WOOD and LAND in turn.
When the sign was rebuilt in 1978, rock star Alice Cooper paid for one of the O's, in memory of Groucho Marx.

Honduras.text: In its far west lie the ruins of Copán, the best-known ancient Maya city-state in the country.
Part of the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef lies offshore, where dolphins, manta rays and whale sharks swim around the Bay Islands.
In Spanish, "honduras" means "depths"; one story links the name to Columbus giving thanks for escaping deep waters.
In 2012, laser scanning revealed long-hidden settlements in the Mosquitia jungle, linked to the legend of the "White City".

Hong Kong.text: No city in the world has more skyscrapers.
Over 90% of residents' daily trips are made by public transport, the highest share in the world.
The name means "fragrant harbour", perhaps from incense factories that once lined the coast.
Commuters glide uphill on the Mid-Levels escalators, a covered chain of moving stairs and walkways stretching over 800 metres.

Honolulu.text: The most remote major US city, and one of the most isolated big cities in the world.
The westernmost and southernmost major US city and state capital.
Its name is Hawaiian for "sheltered harbor".
King Kamehameha III made it the Hawaiian Kingdom's capital in 1845, and later kings built ʻIolani Palace here.

Honshu.text: The largest of Japan's four main islands and the seventh-largest island on Earth.
The second-most populous island in the world, after Indonesia's Java.
An old name for it was Akitsushima, meaning "dragonfly island".
Its highest peak is the volcano Mount Fuji, and its Shinano River is Japan's longest.

Houston.text: The largest US city with no formal zoning rules separating homes from businesses.
Officially nicknamed 'Space City' since 1967, as home of NASA's Johnson Space Center.
Its Texas Medical Center is the largest medical center in the world.
Named in 1836 after Sam Houston, who became President of the Republic of Texas that year.

Hudson Bay.text: At about 1.23 million square kilometres, it's the world's second-largest body of water called a bay, after the Bay of Bengal.
Its low-lying western shore, the Hudson Bay Lowlands, is Canada's largest continuous peatland.
Its water is less salty than the ocean, so it freezes more readily and is largely iced over from mid-December to mid-June.
A 1668 voyage that traded here for beaver furs led to the founding of the Hudson's Bay Company in 1670.

Hungarian Parliament Building.text: One of the world's biggest parliament buildings, it stretches 268 metres along the bank of the Danube.
Builders used about 40 million bricks, half a million precious stones and 40 kilograms of gold.
Its 96-metre height is said to honour 896, traditionally counted as the year Hungary was founded.
The Holy Crown of Hungary has been on display in its sixteen-sided central hall since 2000.

Hungary.text: Home to Lake Balaton, the largest lake in Central Europe by surface area.
Hungarian is unrelated to its neighbours' languages, but is a distant cousin of Finnish and Estonian.
The Rubik's Cube was invented here, by the Hungarian Ernő Rubik.
Its footballers have won three Olympic titles.

Iceland.text: Sits right on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the Eurasian and North American plates are pulling apart.
Its parliament, the Althing, began in 930 and is one of the world's oldest functioning legislative assemblies.
Most Icelanders have no inherited family name: their surname comes from a parent's first name, as in Jónsdóttir, 'Jón's daughter'.

Idaho.text: Best known for potatoes, it grows around a third of the nation's crop.
Nicknamed the Gem State, it has the star garnet as its official state gem.
The world's first ski chairlifts were built in 1936 at its Sun Valley resort.
In 1865 an official broke into Lewiston's capitol and rode off with the territorial seal, carrying the capital to Boise.

Iguazu Falls.text: Spread along a 2.7-kilometre edge, these falls form one of the biggest waterfall systems on Earth.
Islands split the edge into anywhere from 150 to 300 separate waterfalls, depending on the water level.
In one Guaraní legend, a furious serpent god split the river to make the falls when a young woman fled by canoe with her lover.

Illinois.text: Three US presidents were elected while living here: Abraham Lincoln, Ulysses S. Grant and Barack Obama.
Cahokia, the largest urban center of the ancient Mississippian culture, stood here and is now a World Heritage Site.
Floods shifted the Mississippi River, leaving Kaskaskia, its first capital, on the river's west side.
Its first planned border would have given it no Lake Michigan shore; a delegate lobbied to move it north.

Indiana.text: Home of the Indianapolis 500, often billed as the world's largest single-day sporting event.
Its motto, Crossroads of America, comes from its many highways, railroads and old canals.
Its highest point, Hoosier Hill, is only about 1,250 feet above sea level, in a patch of woods on a farm.
US Steel created the city of Gary in 1906 and named it after the company's founding chairman.

Indonesia.text: The world's largest archipelagic state, made up of somewhere between 13,000 and 17,000 islands.
Its island of Java is the most heavily populated island in the world.
The name comes from India plus the Greek word nesos, meaning 'Indian islands'.
More than 700 languages are spoken across its islands.

Inverness.text: The northernmost city in the United Kingdom, given city status as a Millennium City in 2000.
Often called the Capital of the Highlands.
Its river, the Ness, flows from Loch Ness through the city to the sea at the Moray Firth.
Shakespeare set Macbeth and Lady Macbeth's castle in Inverness, where much of the play's drama unfolds.

Iowa.text: In the heart of the Corn Belt, it is the nation's largest producer of corn.
Its blue, white and red striped flag resembles France's, a nod to its days as part of French Louisiana.
Its nickname, the Hawkeye State, comes from James Fenimore Cooper's novel The Last of the Mohicans.
The baseball diamond built for the 1989 film Field of Dreams is in a cornfield near Dyersville.

Iran.text: Home to one of the world's oldest continuous major civilizations, long known in the West as Persia.
Mount Damavand, about 5,600 metres high, is the tallest volcano in all of Asia.
In the 1600s, Isfahan's vast Naqsh-e Jahan Square hosted royal polo matches, watched by the shah from his palace balcony.

Iraq.text: Covers most of ancient Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates often called the cradle of civilisation.
Ancient Sumer, in its south, saw some of the very first cities, writing and monumental buildings.
The Epic of Gilgamesh, regarded as the earliest surviving great work of literature, comes from here.
Several tales in One Thousand and One Nights feature famous figures from Baghdad's Abbasid era.

Islamabad.text: Built from scratch as a planned city in the 1960s, it replaced the port of Karachi as Pakistan's capital.
A Greek architect, Constantinos Doxiadis, drew up the city's master plan, dividing it into eight zones.
Its striking Faisal Mosque, completed in 1986, was designed by Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay, with a modern take on Islamic architecture.
Right next door is the older city of Rawalpindi; the pair form one metropolitan area of well over five million people.

Istanbul.text: A city on two continents: about two-thirds of its people live in Europe and the rest in Asia.
Over nearly 16 centuries it was the capital of four empires, including the Roman and Ottoman Empires.
Its name is commonly thought to come from a Greek phrase meaning 'to the city'.
Legend says it sits on seven hills, but there are actually more than 50 within the city limits.

Italy.text: Two whole countries, Vatican City and San Marino, sit entirely inside it.
Sicily's Mount Etna, often called Europe's largest active volcano, is in an almost constant state of eruption.
Both the piano and the violin were invented here.
Known as the birthplace of opera.

Ivory Coast.text: As of 2023, the world's biggest exporter of cocoa beans, the main ingredient of chocolate.
Its capital, Yamoussoukro, has the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace, often named the largest church building in the world.
Old European traders also called this shore the 'Coast of Teeth', after the ivory traded there.
Since 1986 its government has asked that its official name, Côte d'Ivoire, not be translated.

Jakarta.text: Indonesia's independence was proclaimed here in 1945.
Under Dutch rule it was called Batavia, after the Batavi, an ancient Germanic people the Dutch saw as their ancestors.
Its territory covers about ten times more sea than land, taking in the waters around the Thousand Islands.
Home to the secretariat of ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

Jamaica.text: Reggae, ska, rocksteady and dub were all born in its recording studios.
The third-largest island in the Caribbean by area, after Cuba and Hispaniola.
The film Cool Runnings is loosely based on its first Olympic bobsled team.

Japan.text: Its name, Nihon or Nippon, means 'sun origin', which is why it's called the Land of the Rising Sun.
Made up of more than 14,000 islands strung along Asia's Pacific coast.
Its 1947 constitution has never been changed, making it the oldest unamended constitution in the world.
The Tale of Genji, written by Murasaki Shikibu a thousand years ago, is often called the world's first novel.

Java.text: The world's most populous island, home to more than half of all Indonesians.
Almost entirely volcanic in origin, it has 112 volcanoes, 35 of them still active.
Fossils of an ancient human relative, Homo erectus, found here are nicknamed "Java Man".
The Javan rhino, one of the rarest large mammals on Earth, survives only in Java's Ujung Kulon National Park.

Johannesburg.text: Founded in 1886 after gold was discovered nearby, it grew to over 100,000 people within a decade.
Its nickname eGoli means "Place of Gold".
Its FNB Stadium, the largest stadium in Africa, hosted the 2010 FIFA World Cup final.

Jordan.text: Its Dead Sea shore, more than 400 metres below sea level, is the lowest dry land on Earth.
Petra, the stone-carved capital of the ancient Nabataeans, is its most popular sight.
The Dead Sea holds about ten times more salt than the ocean, so swimmers simply bob on top.
Apart from 26 kilometres of Red Sea coast at Aqaba, it is completely landlocked.

Kabul.text: At about 1,790 metres up in a Hindu Kush valley, it is one of the highest capital cities in the world.
Thought to be over 3,500 years old, it was a key stop on the ancient Silk Road.
Babur, founder of India's Mughal Empire, loved Kabul so much that he wished to rest there; his remains were later moved from Agra.
It sits roughly halfway between Istanbul in the west and Hanoi in the east.

Kampala.text: Its name comes from "Hill of the Impala", a royal hunting ground of the Kabaka, Buganda's king.
Originally built on seven hills, though it has long since spread beyond them.
By one estimate, in 2015 its metropolitan area produced more than half of everything Uganda's economy made.
Kikaya Hill holds the Bahá'í House of Worship known as the Mother Temple of Africa, opened in 1961.

Kansas.text: The geographic center of the 48 contiguous US states lies here, near the town of Lebanon.
Home of Dorothy Gale, the heroine of The Wonderful Wizard of Oz.
Until 1989, a ranch survey point here was the central reference point for all maps of North America.
A joke study called it "flatter than a pancake", but by maximum relief it's only the 23rd-flattest state.

Karachi.text: Pakistan's first capital, until the government moved north at the end of the 1950s.
Its two big seaports handle the vast majority of Pakistan's trade with the rest of the world.
Said to be named after Mai Kolachi, whose son, the story goes, slew a man-eating crocodile.
Muhammad Ali Jinnah, Pakistan's founder, was born here, and his birthplace is now a museum.

Kathmandu.text: Durbar Square, Swayambhu and Pashupatinath are all part of the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Named after the Kasthamandap, a wooden temple said to be built from the timber of a single tree.
An ancient legend says the valley was once a huge, deep lake home to mythical serpents.

Kazakhstan.text: The world's largest landlocked country, and the ninth-largest of all by land area.
Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, and Yuri Gagarin's first human orbit both blasted off from the Baikonur Cosmodrome here.
The wild apple that gave rise to today's eating apples still grows in the Ili valley of southern Kazakhstan.

Kentucky.text: Mammoth Cave National Park holds the world's longest known cave system.
Hosts the Kentucky Derby, first run in 1875 and nicknamed "the most exciting two minutes in sports".
A surveying error created the Kentucky Bend, a piece of the state cut off by Missouri and Tennessee.
Officially a Commonwealth, one of only four states to use the term, with Massachusetts, Virginia and Pennsylvania.

Kenya.text: Named after Mount Kenya, whose local names liken its black rock and white snow to a male ostrich's feathers.
Each year more than a million wildebeest and 200,000 zebras surge across the Mara River on their great migration.
Famous for its long-distance runners, who keep winning Olympic gold in races from 800 metres to the marathon.
Since 2007, the M-Pesa service has let people send money and pay for things using just a mobile phone.

Khartoum.text: Built where the White Nile and the Blue Nile meet.
Really three cities in one: Khartoum, Khartoum North and Omdurman, split by the two Niles and joined by bridges.
The spot where the two rivers meet is called al-Mogran, meaning simply 'The Confluence'.
One folk explanation says its name comes from the Arabic for 'trunk', after the narrow strip of land between the Niles.

Kinderdijk windmills.text: Its 19 windmills, most built in 1738 and 1740 to drain the land, are the largest group of old windmills in the Netherlands.
When pumping stations replaced some of the mills, the millers and their families were allowed to carry on living inside them.
Kinderdijk means "children dike"; legend says a cat kept a baby's cradle afloat here during a great flood in 1421.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997, officially called the Mill Network at Kinderdijk-Elshout.

Kinkaku-ji.text: Kyoto's famous Golden Pavilion has its top two storeys covered in pure gold leaf, shimmering in the pond below.
Each of its three floors is built in a different architectural style: palace, samurai house and Zen temple.
Before becoming a Zen temple, it was a retirement villa bought in 1397 by the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu.
When it was regilded in the 1980s, about 20 kilograms of gold leaf went onto the pavilion.

Kinshasa.text: The largest city in the world where French is an official language.
One of the world's fastest-growing megacities, now home to well over 10 million people.
Brazzaville, capital of the neighbouring Republic of the Congo, sits just across the river, about 4 km away.
In 1974 it hosted the "Rumble in the Jungle", where Muhammad Ali beat George Foreman to regain boxing's heavyweight title.

Kiribati.text: Its islands are scattered over about 3.4 million square kilometres of ocean, straddling both the equator and the 180th meridian.
Its easternmost islands sit in UTC+14, the most advanced time zone on Earth.
Caroline Island was renamed Millennium Island in 1997, as the Line Islands would be the first area to enter the year 2000.
Kiritimati, once called Christmas Island, has more land than any other atoll with a lagoon.

Ko Phi Phi Le.text: Maya Bay shot to worldwide fame as a filming location for the 2000 movie The Beach.
Its island is a ring of steep limestone hills wrapped around two shallow bays.
Closed in 2018 so its coral could recover, the bay reopened in 2022 with boats and swimming banned.
While the tourists were away, blacktip reef sharks came back and began breeding in the bay again.

Kolkata.text: Its spectacular Durga Puja festival is recognised by UNESCO for its importance to the world's cultural heritage.
Home to India's oldest port still in operation.
Four Nobel Prize winners, including the poet Rabindranath Tagore, are linked with the city.

Kosovo.text: Uses the euro as its official currency, even though it isn't formally a member of the eurozone.
Prizren, a cultural centre in Ottoman times, is recognised as Kosovo's historic capital.
The name comes from the Serbian word for blackbird, by way of a plain called Blackbird Field.
Near Pristina lie the ruins of Ulpiana, an important Roman city named after Emperor Trajan.

Kraków.text: Its Old Town and the nearby Wieliczka Salt Mine were Poland's first UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
Many historic Polish kings are buried in Wawel Cathedral, on the hill where the city began.
Every hour a trumpet call rings out from St Mary's Basilica, and it breaks off suddenly mid-tune.
The earliest known written mention of bagels comes from Kraków, in Jewish community rules from 1610.

Kremlin.text: Italian master builders raised its great walls, and many of its towers, between 1485 and 1495.
Tucked inside the Grand Kremlin Palace is the lower floor of a church from 1393, among the oldest buildings left in Moscow.
The Tsar Bell here, the heaviest bell in the world, cracked in a fire before it was ever rung.
Voltaire is said to have joked that the Kremlin's greatest treasures were a bell never rung and a cannon never fired.

Kuala Lumpur.text: Its name means "muddy confluence" in Malay, after the spot where two rivers meet.
Home to the Petronas Towers, the tallest twin buildings in the world.
The official story credits a Malay chief who sent Chinese miners to open tin mines here in 1857.
Still Malaysia's capital, where Parliament meets, though most federal government offices moved to the new city of Putrajaya.

Kuwait.text: Its name comes from a word meaning "fortress built near water".
In 2026 its dinar was the world's most valuable currency unit, with one dinar worth more than three US dollars.
The famous Kuwait Towers aren't just for show: two of the three also work as water towers.
A pioneer of Gulf theatre, its plays and TV dramas have long been enjoyed in neighbouring countries.

Kyiv.text: Ukraine's capital straddles both banks of the mighty Dnieper River.
St. Sophia Cathedral and the Monastery of the Caves here are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
One legend says three brothers and their sister founded the city, naming it after the eldest brother, Kyi.
The city grew up on the Dnieper's western bank and only spread across to the east in the 20th century.

Kyoto.text: Japan's imperial capital for more than a thousand years, from 794 until the emperor moved to Tokyo in 1869.
Its name means 'capital city', while Tokyo's means 'eastern capital'.
The original city was laid out on the model of Chang'an, the ancient Chinese capital.
The Kyoto Protocol on greenhouse gases takes its name from the 1997 conference held here.

Kyrgyzstan.text: The Tian Shan mountains cover over 80% of the land, so it is sometimes nicknamed "the Switzerland of Central Asia".
Its vast mountain lake Issyk-Kul, whose name means "Hot Lake", rarely freezes despite bitterly cold winters.
One theory says "Kyrgyz" means "forty tribes", which the 40-rayed sun on the national flag recalls.
Storytellers here keep alive the Epic of Manas, a hero tale on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

La Paz.text: At roughly 3,650 metres, it is the world's highest administrative capital; Bolivia's constitutional capital is Sucre.
Home to the world's largest urban cable car network, Mi Teleférico, which opened in 2014.
The presidential palace is nicknamed the "Burnt Palace" because it has caught fire several times.
Its Witches' Market sells herbs, remedies and other ingredients used in Aymara traditions.

Lagos.text: Rivals Cairo as Africa's biggest city, with an estimated population of well over 15 million.
Its name comes from the Portuguese word for "lakes"; in Yoruba the city is called Èkó.
Heart of Nollywood, Nigeria's huge film industry, and a hotspot for Afrobeats music.
The city's Yoruba motto, "Èkó ò ní bàjẹ́!", means "Lagos will not spoil!"

Lahore.text: Its Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens are both UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
A UNESCO City of Literature and a major centre of Pakistan's book publishing.
Pakistan's Basant festival, welcoming spring, is centred here, with the Lahore Canal decorated with floating lanterns.
Home to 'Lollywood', Pakistan's Punjabi-language film industry, and a major centre of qawwali music.

Lake Baikal.text: The deepest lake in the world, plunging 1,642 metres at its deepest point.
The largest freshwater lake by volume, holding more water than all of North America's Great Lakes combined.
At an estimated 25 to 30 million years old, it's considered the oldest lake in the world.
Home to the nerpa, a freshwater seal found nowhere else on Earth.

Lake Balkhash.text: A lake of two halves: its western part is fresh water, while its deeper eastern half is salty.
The largest lake lying wholly within Kazakhstan, curving like a sickle for about 600 km.
Its two halves meet at the Uzynaral Strait, just 3.5 km wide and about 6 metres deep.
Mountain rivers pour into it but none flows out again, so its water escapes by evaporation instead.

Lake Bled.text: Rowers know it well: the World Rowing Championships have been held here four times, most recently in 2011.
Gold ornaments left as offerings over 3,000 years ago show it was an important Bronze Age sacred site.
Bled's famous cream cake is a protected local speciality, and millions have been baked at one hotel's patisserie alone.
Visitors reach the island by pletna, a wooden boat whose name comes from a Bavarian German word for a flat-bottomed boat.

Lake Como.text: Over 400 metres deep, it is one of Europe's deepest lakes, with a bed far below sea level.
Glaciers carved it into the shape of an upside-down letter Y.
Scenes from Star Wars: Attack of the Clones and the James Bond film Casino Royale were shot on its shores.
Wealthy Romans holidayed here too: Pliny the Younger named his two lakeside villas Comedy and Tragedy.

Lake Erie.text: The southernmost, shallowest and smallest by volume of North America's five Great Lakes.
Point Pelee, the southernmost point of mainland Canada, juts into its waters on a peninsula.
When it freezes over, islanders in the western basin race iceboats, which look like sailboats on skates.
Local folklore tells of "Bessie", a Loch Ness-style monster, with unconfirmed sightings going back to the 1800s.

Lake Huron.text: Home to Manitoulin Island, the largest island in any freshwater lake on Earth.
Joined to Lake Michigan by the Straits of Mackinac at the same water level, so hydrologists treat the pair as one lake.
About 9,000 years ago, a ridge now sunk beneath the lake was a land bridge crossed by herds of caribou.
French explorers, the first Europeans to visit, often called it La Mer Douce, "the fresh-water sea".

Lake Ladoga.text: The largest lake lying entirely in Europe by area, found near St Petersburg in Russia.
Has a seal all of its own: the Ladoga ringed seal, a freshwater subspecies living only in this lake.
A methane lake on Saturn's moon Titan, Ladoga Lacus, is named after it.
Around 660 islands are scattered across its waters, including Valaam.

Lake Malawi.text: Home to more species of fish than any other lake in the world, including at least 700 kinds of cichlid.
Bordered by Malawi, Mozambique and Tanzania, it is the world's fourth-largest freshwater lake by volume.
David Livingstone nicknamed it the Lake of Stars, because fishermen's lanterns on the water looked like stars from afar.
Its layers of water never mix, so the deep water stays permanently apart from the surface.

Lake Michigan.text: The only one of the five Great Lakes lying wholly within the United States.
The world's largest lake by area that sits entirely inside a single country.
Some of its beaches have "singing sands" that squeak underfoot, thanks to their high quartz content.
Together with the other Great Lakes, its shores are sometimes called America's "Third Coast", after the Atlantic and Pacific.

Lake Onega.text: Europe's second-largest lake by area, after nearby Lake Ladoga, and only slightly smaller than the whole of Lebanon.
About 1,200 Stone Age rock carvings of animals, people and boats, made thousands of years ago, decorate its eastern shore.
On its Kizhi island stands a 22-domed wooden church built without nails, except for its domes and roof shingles.
One rocky cape with ancient carvings on its shore is called Besov Nos, meaning "Devil's nose".

Lake Ontario.text: The smallest Great Lake by surface area – yet it holds more than three times as much water as Lake Erie.
Last in the Great Lakes chain, it empties into the St. Lawrence River and on to the Atlantic Ocean.
Its name probably comes from an Iroquoian word meaning "lake of shining waters" or "beautiful lake".
In 1954, 16-year-old Marilyn Bell became the first person to swim across it; a Toronto park is named after her.

Lake Superior.text: The largest freshwater lake on Earth by surface area, unless you count Lakes Michigan and Huron, joined by a strait, as one.
It holds enough water to cover all of North and South America about 30 cm (a foot) deep.
Its Ojibwe name, gichi-gami, means "great sea" – Longfellow spelled it "Gitche Gumee" in a famous poem.
Isle Royale, its biggest island, has lakes of its own – and some of those lakes have islands too.

Lake Tanganyika.text: Second only to Siberia's Lake Baikal in both depth and volume of fresh water.
Roughly 98% of the cichlid fish species living here are found nowhere else on Earth.
Sneaky "cuckoo catfish" slip their eggs in with cichlids' eggs, so cichlid parents carry them in their mouths as their own.
An ancient lake: its central basin began forming around 9 to 12 million years ago.

Lake Victoria.text: Africa's largest lake by area and the biggest tropical lake in the world.
Its only outflow is the Nile, which leaves the lake near Jinja in Uganda.
Three countries share it: Tanzania has almost half, Uganda 45% and Kenya just 6%.
Known locally by names such as Nam Lolwe and Nyanza, it was renamed after Queen Victoria by explorer John Hanning Speke.

Lake Winnipeg.text: Rain falling in four Canadian provinces and four US states can end up here; its watershed covers almost a million square kilometres.
Forests and rivers on its east side became part of Pimachiowin Aki, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, in 2018.
Huge but shallow: its average depth is only about 12 metres.
In 1998 about 3.7% of all the world's American white pelicans were counted nesting on its Pipestone Rocks.

Laos.text: The only landlocked country in Southeast Asia.
Its Plain of Jars holds thousands of ancient stone jars, which archaeologists link to burials.
One local legend says a giant king made the Plain of Jars' huge jars to brew rice wine for a victory party.
Its great medieval kingdom was called Lan Xang, meaning "a million elephants".

Las Vegas.text: Calls itself the Entertainment Capital of the World, famous for its huge casino-hotels.
Its name is Spanish for "The Meadows", after grassy land fed by desert springs.
The famous Las Vegas Strip actually lies outside the city limits.

Las Vegas Strip.text: Many of the world's largest hotel resorts line this famous stretch of road.
Surprise: the Strip lies just outside the Las Vegas city limits, in the towns of Paradise and Winchester.
Most of it is officially an All-American Road, one of America's designated scenic routes.
Its first resort, El Rancho Vegas, opened in 1941 with only about 65 rooms in little cottage bungalows.

Latvia.text: Its huge song festival, held since 1873 and normally every five years, gathers tens of thousands of singers and dancers.
More than half of the country is covered by forest.
In the 1600s its capital, Riga, was one of the biggest cities in the whole Swedish Empire.
Alongside a national bird and flower, it even has a national insect: the two-spot ladybird.

Leaning Tower of Pisa.text: Its nearly four-degree lean comes from soft ground that couldn't hold its weight.
It started leaning while still being built in the 12th century, and construction took 199 years.
Galileo is said to have dropped two cannonballs of different weights from the top to test how things fall.
Engineers added 870 tonnes of lead weights from 1993 to tug it slightly straighter.

Lebanon.text: The city of Byblos is considered one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
Its name comes from a Phoenician word meaning "white", apparently after the snowy peaks of Mount Lebanon.
Lebanon's name turns up in three of the twelve tablets of the ancient Epic of Gilgamesh.
Mountains close to the coast mean you can ski in the morning and swim in the Mediterranean in the afternoon.

Leeds.text: Kirkgate Market here is one of the largest indoor markets in Europe.
Roundhay Garden Scene, believed to be the oldest surviving film, was shot here in 1888.
In 1767 Joseph Priestley worked out how to make fizzy soda water here, using gas from a brewery's beer vat.
People from here are known locally as "Loiners", a word nobody can quite explain.

Lesotho.text: The only independent country lying entirely above 1,000 metres; even its lowest point is about 1,400 metres up.
One of just three countries entirely surrounded by another; the other two, Vatican City and San Marino, sit inside Italy.
The director of Black Panther said his fictional kingdom of Wakanda was inspired by Lesotho.
Its national dress centres on the Basotho blanket, a covering originally made of wool.

Liberia.text: Declared independent in 1847, it is the oldest republic in Africa today.
Holds about forty percent of what remains of West Africa's Upper Guinean rainforest.
Its capital, Monrovia, and Washington, D.C. are the only two world capitals named after an American president.
The national motto is "The Love of Liberty Brought Us Here".

Library of Celsus.text: Built by a Roman consul in the 2nd century as a monument to his father, Celsus.
A library and a tomb in one: Celsus himself lies in a marble coffin in a crypt beneath it.
Statues on its front stand for Wisdom, Knowledge, Intelligence and Excellence.
Its famous front lay in ruins for centuries until archaeologists stood it back up between 1970 and 1978.

Libya.text: Its Great Man-Made River, named by Guinness World Records as the largest irrigation project, pipes ancient underground water from the desert to coastal cities.
The name "Libya" first appears in an inscription of the Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II.
The ruins of Leptis Magna, hometown of Roman emperor Septimius Severus, are among the best-preserved Roman sites in the Mediterranean.
In parts of its desert, decades can pass without a single drop of rain.

Liechtenstein.text: One of only two doubly landlocked countries, surrounded entirely by landlocked neighbours; the other is Uzbekistan.
The world's smallest country to border two countries, squeezed between Austria and Switzerland.
No member of its ruling family set foot in the country bearing their name until 1818.
Has had no army since 1868, after its parliament refused to pay for one.

Lima.text: Around a third of all Peruvians live in its metropolitan area.
Its historic centre, full of colonial-era buildings, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988.
Founded in 1535, it was first called Ciudad de los Reyes, the "City of Kings".
Cold ocean waters offshore mean this desert city gets hardly any rain, just misty winter drizzle.

Lisbon.text: Sitting at the mouth of the River Tagus, it is the westernmost capital of a mainland European country.
Belém Tower and Jerónimos Monastery, both in the ornate Manueline style, together make up one UNESCO World Heritage Site.
One old legend says the hero Ulysses founded the city while sailing west to the ends of the known world.
Its little yellow trams are sized to squeeze up the steep hills and narrow streets of the old centre.

Lithuania.text: In 1990 it became the first Soviet republic to break away, declaring its independence restored a year before the Soviet Union dissolved.
In the 1400s the Grand Duchy of Lithuania was Europe's largest state by area, stretching from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea.
By one French scientist's 1989 calculation, the geographic centre of Europe lies here, about 26 km north of Vilnius.
Basketball is the most popular sport, and the men's national team has won the EuroBasket championship three times.

Liverpool.text: Home of the Beatles, it was named the "City of Pop" by Guinness World Records in 2001 for its many No. 1 hits.
Locals are called Scousers after scouse, a stew made popular by sailors.
Its Chinatown is home to what is often called Europe's oldest Chinese community.
In 1830 it and Manchester became the first cities linked by an intercity railway.

Ljubljana.text: Crowned European Green Capital for 2016 for its environmental achievements.
A dragon is the city's symbol, perched on its coat of arms and standing guard on the Dragon Bridge.
The oldest wooden wheel ever found, over 5,000 years old, was dug out of marshes about 20 km south of the city.
Grew up on the site of Emona, a Roman settlement that began as a military camp around 50 BC.

Los Angeles.text: Founded in 1781 by 44 settlers as the Town of Our Lady the Queen of the Angels.
By the early 1920s, most of the world's film industry had settled here, much of it in Hollywood.
Hosting in 2028 makes it only the third city to stage the Summer Olympics three times.
Wild bobcats live within this enormous city.

Louisiana.text: The only US state divided into parishes instead of counties, reflecting its French heritage.
Over 90% of America's crawfish farms are here, and the crawfish has been its state crustacean since 1983.
Named in 1682 by explorer La Salle to honor King Louis XIV of France.
Unlike every other US state, its private law follows the civil law tradition of France and Spain rather than English common law.

Louvre Pyramid.text: I. M. Pei's glass pyramid, completed in 1989, is the Louvre's main entrance and a famous Paris landmark.
It has 673 glass panes, not the 666 claimed by a long-running rumour.
Its glass sides slope at an angle close to that of the ancient Egyptian pyramids.
An upside-down companion, the Inverted Pyramid, lights the museum's underground passages.

Luanda.text: The most populous Portuguese-speaking national capital in the world.
Founded in 1576 by Portuguese explorer Paulo Dias de Novais, it is one of Africa's oldest colonial cities.
Its first name was a mouthful: São Paulo da Assunção de Loanda.

Lusaka.text: Chosen as capital of Northern Rhodesia in 1929 for its central location, replacing Livingstone.
Began in 1905 as a railway water stop, named after a local Lenje chief called Lusaaka.
Its main street, Cairo Road, was named for its hoped-for place on a road running from the Cape to Cairo.
When it became capital in 1935, a special train carried all the government officials up from Livingstone.

Luxembourg.text: The world's only remaining sovereign grand duchy, headed by a Grand Duke.
In 2020 it became the first country in the world to make public transport free nationwide.
Luxembourgish is the national language, but laws are written only in French, and German is also used in government.
The country grew from a small castle on a rocky outcrop called the Bock, acquired by a count in 963.

Luxor Temple.text: Built around 1400 BC on the Nile's east bank in ancient Thebes, today's Luxor.
A 2.7-kilometre avenue lined with sphinxes links this temple to the great temple of Karnak.
One of the two obelisks from its entrance now stands in the Place de la Concorde in Paris.
A working mosque still sits inside the ancient temple, left in place when the ruins were dug out.

Luzon.text: The largest and most populous island in the Philippines, home to more than half of all Filipinos.
The Philippine capital, Manila, stands on its shores.
Its name is thought to come from lusong, a Tagalog word for a big wooden mortar for pounding rice.
Mayon Volcano here is famous for its beautifully symmetrical cone.

Lyon.text: The Lumière brothers invented the cinematograph here, earning it a key place in cinema history.
Every December, around the 8th, a four-day Festival of Lights fills the city with candlelit windows and dazzling light shows.
Narrow passageways called traboules cut right through buildings to link the streets on either side.
Interpol, the international police organisation, has its worldwide headquarters here.

Machu Picchu.text: This Inca citadel was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007.
Its central buildings are made of precisely shaped stone blocks fitted together without any mortar.
In the Quechua language, its name is often translated as "old mountain" or "old peak".
A Peruvian explorer got there before the famous 1911 expedition, writing "A. Lizárraga 1902" in charcoal on a temple window.

Madagascar.text: The world's fourth-largest island, cut off from every other landmass for about 88 million years.
More than 90% of its wildlife is found nowhere else on Earth.
About half of all the world's chameleon species live here and nowhere else.
Its first settlers probably sailed all the way from present-day Indonesia in outrigger canoes.

Madrid.text: Its 'Golden Triangle of Art' groups three great museums, the Prado, Reina Sofía and Thyssen-Bornemisza, along one boulevard.
A bear and a strawberry tree have been the city's emblem since the Middle Ages.
Retiro Park's glass Palacio de Cristal was inspired by London's Crystal Palace.

Maine.text: The only US state that borders just one other state: New Hampshire.
Called the Pine Tree State, it has the highest share of forest cover of any US state.
Part of Massachusetts until 1820, when it voted to break away and become its own state.
Its official state dessert is blueberry pie, and its official state treat is the whoopie pie.

Málaga.text: The artist Pablo Picasso was born here in 1881.
Founded by the Phoenicians around 770 BC, it is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Western Europe.
Walls of the ancient Phoenician city can still be seen in the cellar of the Picasso Museum.
It sits on the Costa del Sol, whose name means "Coast of the Sun".

Malawi.text: Its name means "flames" in the Chichewa and Chitumbuka languages.
Nicknamed "the Warm Heart of Africa" for the friendly, welcoming nature of its people.
Lake Malawi, along its eastern edge, is said to have one of the richest collections of lake fish in the world.
Before independence in 1964 it was a British protectorate called Nyasaland.

Malaysia.text: Its king is chosen every five years from among the rulers of nine Malay states.
Split in two by the South China Sea: one half on the Asian mainland, the other on the island of Borneo.
Rainforests in East Malaysia hide Rafflesia, giant flowers that can grow up to a metre across.
Kuala Lumpur is the capital, but the government and top courts work from the planned city of Putrajaya.

Maldives.text: The world's lowest-lying country: more than 80% of its coral islands sit less than a metre above sea level.
The smallest country in Asia by area.
Its chain of 26 atolls stretches right across the equator.
One theory says its name comes from Sanskrit words meaning "garland of islands".

Mali.text: In the 1300s the Mali Empire was Africa's wealthiest state, and its emperor Mansa Musa is often called one of history's richest people.
In medieval times its desert city of Timbuktu became a renowned centre of learning.
The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud-brick building in the world.
Palm-wood sticks poking out of Djenné's mosque walls double as built-in scaffolding for its yearly repairs.

Malta.text: Its Ġgantija temples on Gozo are among the world's oldest free-standing structures, built even before Egypt's pyramids.
EU studies count the entire country as a single urban region, which is why it's often described as a city-state.
Maltese is a Semitic language with close ties to both Arabic and Sicilian.
Movie scenes for both Gladiator films were shot on the island.

Managua.text: Was a small fishing village before becoming Nicaragua's capital in 1852.
Stretches along the southern shore of Lake Managua, also called Lake Xolotlán.
Four small crater lakes lie within the city limits, including Tiscapa Lagoon near the centre.
Footprints left in volcanic ash about 2,100 years ago are on show at the Acahualinca museum.

Manarola.text: One of the five Cinque Terre villages, whose coast and hillsides form a national park and UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Paths, trains and boats link the Cinque Terre villages, since cars reach them only with great difficulty.
The clifftop path to Riomaggiore is the Via dell'Amore, or Way of Love, once a handy meeting place for young sweethearts.
Every Christmas since 1961, a nativity scene made of thousands of lights glows on the hill above the village.

Manchester.text: Its booming cotton mills made it what is often called the world's first industrial city.
The Manchester Baby, the world's first electronic stored-program computer, ran its first program here in 1948.
Scientists here first isolated graphene, a wonder material just one atom thick, in 2004.

Manila.text: Packing in about 45,000 people per square kilometre, it is one of the most densely populated cities in the world.
Its name comes from Maynilà, often explained as 'where indigo plants are abundant' or 'where nilad plants are abundant'.
For over two centuries, Spanish galleons sailed from here to Acapulco, trading Mexican silver for Chinese silk and Asian spices.
Its Basilica of San Sebastián, finished in 1891, is often described as the only all-steel church in Asia.

Maputo.text: Known as Lourenço Marques until 1976, after a Portuguese navigator who explored the area in 1544.
Avenues lined with jacaranda and acacia trees earned it the nickname City of Acacias.
Its grand railway station, built 1913 to 1916, is sometimes wrongly credited to Gustave Eiffel.
The city is a province on its own: Mozambique's smallest by area and the most densely populated.

Marina Bay Sands.text: Its three hotel towers are joined at the top by the SkyPark, a 340-metre skyway holding a 150-metre infinity pool.
When it opened in 2010, the SkyPark's 66.5-metre overhang was the world's longest public cantilever.
Its ArtScience Museum is shaped like a lotus flower.
The resort has the world's first floating Apple store, sitting out on the waters of the bay.

Marrakesh.text: One of Morocco's four imperial cities, founded around 1070 as the capital of the Almoravid dynasty.
Many European names for Morocco, such as Maroc and Marruecos, come from the city's own name.
Its red walls and red sandstone buildings earned it the nickname "the Red City".
Storytellers and musicians perform in its great Jemaa el-Fnaa square, especially at night.

Marseille.text: Founded around 600 BC by Greek sailors, it is generally considered the oldest city in France.
The Calanques National Park, with its white cliffs and turquoise coves, reaches right inside the city's limits.
France's national anthem is named after volunteers from Marseille, who sang it as they marched into Paris in 1792.
Its famous fish stew, bouillabaisse, contains at least three kinds of very fresh local fish.

Marshall Islands.text: About 98% of its territory is lagoon water – the largest share of water to land of any sovereign state.
Made of 29 coral atolls, it's one of only four countries built on atolls, with Kiribati, the Maldives and Tuvalu.
Islanders made stick charts mapping ocean swells, but navigators left them at home and studied them before sailing.
European maps named the islands after British captain John Marshall, who explored the area in 1788.

Maryland.text: Wraps around much of Chesapeake Bay, the largest estuary in the United States.
Land it gave up, including the old town of Georgetown, became part of Washington, D.C.
Its official state sport, since 1962, is jousting.
Near the small town of Hancock, the state squeezes to less than 2 miles wide.

Massachusetts.text: Harvard University in Cambridge is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States.
The Pilgrims of the Mayflower founded Plymouth Colony here in 1620.
Both basketball and volleyball were invented here, in the cities of Springfield and Holyoke.
Its official state cookie is the chocolate chip cookie, and its state dessert is Boston cream pie.

Matterhorn.text: Its four steep faces point roughly north, south, east and west, like a giant pyramid.
Some claim it is the most photographed mountain in the world.
Its German name joins 'Matte' (meadow) and 'Horn', often translated as 'the peak of the meadows'.
Since 2023 a cable car has linked its Swiss and Italian sides directly.

Mauritania.text: About 90% of its land lies within the Sahara desert.
Its desert holds the Richat Structure, a giant 40 km ring of rock often called the Eye of Africa.
Iron-ore trains up to 3 km long cross its desert, among the longest and heaviest trains in the world.
Its name comes from Mauretania, the Latin name for an ancient region further north in North Africa.

Mauritius.text: The only known home of the dodo, which died out soon after people settled there.
The only country in Africa where Hinduism is the most practised religion.
Dutch sailors named it in 1598 after Prince Maurice of Nassau.
Portuguese sailors who landed in 1507 found the island completely uninhabited.

Mediterranean Sea.text: At the Strait of Gibraltar, its gateway to the Atlantic, Europe and Africa are only about 14 km apart.
Its name comes from Latin for "in the middle of land".
In Turkish it's Akdeniz, "the White Sea" – a neat contrast with the Black Sea to the north.
About 5.9 million years ago it was cut off from the Atlantic and partly or completely dried out.

Melbourne.text: Its trams run on the largest urban tram network still operating anywhere in the world.
Australian rules football traces its roots to games played in parkland beside the Melbourne Cricket Ground in 1858.
Australia's federal parliament met here from 1901 until it moved to the new capital, Canberra, in 1927.
Its changeable weather gives it a reputation for having "four seasons in one day".

Meteora.text: Its six surviving monasteries, perched on towering rock pillars, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988.
The name means 'lofty' or 'elevated', and is related to the word 'meteor'.
As early as the 800s, hermit monks lived in hollows and cracks high in the rock towers.
Monks once reached one monastery only by a long ladder, which they pulled up whenever they felt threatened.

Mexico.text: Home to more native Spanish speakers than any other country.
With over 200,000 species, it holds an estimated 10 to 12% of the world's biodiversity.
Maize was first domesticated here from a wild grass about 9,000 years ago.
Its ancient Mesoamerican cultures counted in twenties rather than tens, using a base-20 number system.

Mexico City.text: Founded around 1325, it is the oldest capital city in the Americas.
It began as Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, built on an island in a lake.
Built on an old lakebed, parts of the city have sunk as much as nine metres since the early 1900s.
Chapultepec Park was once a retreat for Aztec rulers, and was opened to the public in 1530.

Miami.text: Known as the only major US city founded by a woman, citrus grower Julia Tuttle.
Nicknamed the 'Magic City' because it seemed to spring up overnight.
Alligators from the neighbouring Everglades sometimes wander into town and onto highways.
Its name traces back to Mayaimi, an old name for Lake Okeechobee and the people living around it.

Michigan.text: Bordering four of the five Great Lakes gives it the longest freshwater coastline of any US state.
Made of two peninsulas, joined by the 5-mile-long Mackinac Bridge.
Long known as the centre of the US car industry, home to its Big Three carmakers.
People from the Upper Peninsula are nicknamed "Yoopers", from "U.P.'ers".

Milan.text: Its Gothic cathedral took nearly six centuries to finish and is Italy's largest church; the bigger St Peter's is in Vatican City.
Leonardo da Vinci painted The Last Supper here, on a wall of the monastery of Santa Maria delle Grazie.
Its ancient name, Mediolanum, meant "the settlement in the middle of the plain".
For over a century, until 402, it was the capital of the western half of the Roman Empire.

Milford Sound.text: A fiord carved by glaciers, its sheer rock walls rise 1,200 metres or more straight out of the water.
With over six metres of rain a year, it is known as New Zealand's wettest inhabited place.
A Welsh-born sealer named it after Milford Haven, a harbour back in his homeland.

Mindanao.text: The second-largest island in the Philippines, after Luzon.
Mount Apo, a volcano rising 2,954 metres, is the highest point in the Philippines.
Just offshore lies the Philippine Deep, the third-deepest ocean trench on Earth.
Many of the country's pineapples and bananas come from here: it's the biggest supplier of both.

Minnesota.text: Nicknamed the "Land of 10,000 Lakes", it actually has more than 11,000 lakes over 10 acres.
The mighty Mississippi River begins its journey here, at Lake Itasca.
Its isolated Northwest Angle is the only part of the 48 contiguous states north of the 49th parallel.
Its name comes from Dakota words for cloudy water; Dakota women once explained it to a missionary's wife by dropping milk into water.

Minsk.text: Capital of Belarus, first mentioned in old records way back in 1067.
One of its two rivers, the Nyamiha, now flows hidden underground.
The National Library is shaped like a giant cut gem, a shape called a rhombicuboctahedron.
The only city in Belarus with an underground metro, which opened in 1984.

Mississippi.text: Musicians from its Delta region were key to the development of the blues.
Rock 'n' roll legend Elvis Presley was born in the town of Tupelo.
Named after the Mississippi River, whose name comes from the Ojibwe 'misi-ziibi', meaning 'great river'.
The USA's top producer of farm-raised catfish, a title it has held since the late 1980s.

Missouri.text: St. Louis hosted the 1904 Summer Olympics, the first Games held in the United States.
Borders eight different states, a record shared only with its neighbour Tennessee.
Nicknamed the "Cave State", it has more than 7,300 recorded caves.
Mark Twain modelled Tom Sawyer's riverside town on Hannibal, where he grew up.

Mogadishu.text: One theory says Marco Polo mixed this port up with a big island, garbling its name into "Madagascar".
When the traveller Ibn Battuta arrived in 1331, he described it as "an exceedingly large city" at the height of its wealth.
In the Middle Ages its fine cloth was famous, shipped as far as Egypt.
Summer here, from June to August, is actually the coolest and rainiest time of year.

Moldova.text: Since 2005 its Mileștii Mici winery has held the Guinness World Record for the largest wine cellar by number of bottles.
Underground wine cellars at the Cricova winery stretch for more than 120 km.
At Old Orhei, monks still pray in cave chapels carved into a limestone cliff high above the Răut River.
A small landlocked country tucked between Romania to the west and Ukraine on every other side.

Monaco.text: Only Vatican City is smaller by area, and no country in the world is more densely populated.
Hosts the Monaco Grand Prix, one of the original races of Formula One, on its own streets.
The Grimaldi family, still its rulers, first seized the rock in 1297 by disguising themselves as monks.
Still growing: a whole new neighbourhood, Le Portier, was built on land reclaimed from the sea and opened in 2024.

Mongolia.text: The world's most sparsely populated sovereign state, with about 3.5 million people spread over a vast land.
The second-largest landlocked country by area, after Kazakhstan.
Nicknamed the "Land of the Eternal Blue Sky", Mongolia enjoys about 250 sunny days a year.

Mont-Saint-Michel.text: A tidal island where the sea rises and falls by around 14 metres between highest and lowest tides.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site visited by more than three million people a year.
Legend says the archangel Michael appeared to a local bishop in 708 and told him to build a church on the rock.
In 2015 a rare 'supertide' completely covered the new bridge to the island.

Montana.text: The fourth-largest US state by area, it is slightly bigger than Japan or Germany.
Rivers from Triple Divide Peak, in Glacier National Park, drain to the Pacific, the Gulf of Mexico and Hudson Bay.
Jeannette Rankin of Montana was the first woman to be a member of the US Congress.
Its name comes from the Spanish word "montaña", meaning mountain.

Montenegro.text: Its name means "Black Mountain", often said to describe the dark forests that once cloaked Mount Lovćen.
It uses the euro as its currency, even though it adopted it on its own and isn't in the eurozone.
Its mountains are among the most rugged in Europe, with peaks rising above 2,500 metres.
Kotor's old town walls zigzag up the mountainside for 4.5 km, guarding a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Montevideo.text: Every single match of the very first FIFA World Cup, in 1930, was played here.
Its seaside avenue, the Rambla, runs for over 20 km along the coast, one of the longest esplanades in the world.
Snow has fallen here only four times on record, one flurry landing during the 1930 World Cup's opening match.
A popular story says the name comes from a sailor's cry "Monte vide eu" ("I saw a mount"), though most experts doubt it.

Montreal.text: The largest mainly French-speaking city in the Americas.
The only Canadian city to have hosted the Summer Olympics, in 1976.
Its name comes from Mount Royal, the three-peaked mountain the first settlement was built around.
Every summer it hosts a jazz festival that Guinness World Records has named the largest in the world.

Monument Valley.text: Towering sandstone buttes, the largest rising about 1,000 feet above the valley floor, make it an icon of the American West.
Director John Ford shot classic Westerns here, including Stagecoach (1939) and The Searchers (1956).
Rusty iron oxide paints the valley red, while darker blue-grey rocks get their colour from manganese oxide.
It lies within the Navajo Nation, whose name for it means 'valley of the rocks'.

Moraine Lake.text: Its view was printed on the back of Canada's $20 bill in 1969 and 1979, earning it the nickname "Twenty Dollar View".
That startling azure comes from fine rock flour, washed in by glaciers, scattering blue sunlight back out of the water.
Fed almost entirely by melting snow and glaciers, the lake doesn't fill to the brim until mid to late June.
Since 2023, private cars have been banned from its road, so visitors arrive by shuttle, bus, bike or on foot.

Moscow.text: The northernmost and coldest megacity on Earth.
First written about in 1147, as a meeting place for two medieval princes.
Its metro stations are famous for their murals, mosaics and glittering chandeliers.
Seven Stalin-era skyscrapers, the 'Seven Sisters', stand at roughly equal distances from the Kremlin.

Mosque–Cathedral of Córdoba.text: Begun as a great mosque in 785 and turned into a cathedral in 1236, it has been a World Heritage Site since 1984.
Rows of two-tier arches, horseshoe-shaped below and rounded above, are seen as one of the original mosque's most innovative features.
About 850 columns of jasper, onyx, marble, granite and porphyry fill the hall, which has been likened to a forest of stone.
Traditional accounts say a Byzantine emperor sent a master mosaic-maker and about 1,600 kg of glittering tiles as a gift.

Mount Everest.text: The highest mountain on Earth above sea level, measured in 2020 at 8,848.86 metres.
The China–Nepal border runs right across its summit.
Rocks near the top are marine limestone, holding fragments of trilobites and other sea creatures from an ancient ocean floor.
Named after the British surveyor Sir George Everest, who actually objected to the honour.

Mount Fuji.text: Japan's highest mountain, an active volcano with its summit about 3,776 m above sea level.
Its most recent eruption lasted from late 1707 into 1708.
Many climbers hike through the night to watch sunrise from the top, a moment called goraikō, "arrival of light".
In 1832, Tatsu Takayama became the first woman on record to reach the summit, when women were still banned from climbing.

Mount Kilimanjaro.text: Africa's highest mountain, and the highest free-standing mountain above sea level in the world.
Built from three volcanic cones: Mawenzi and Shira are extinct, but Kibo, the highest, is only dormant.
Once named Kaiser-Wilhelm-Spitze, its summit is now Uhuru Peak, which means "Freedom Peak" in Swahili.
The name of its highest cone, Kibo, is usually explained as meaning "spotted", after its patches of snow.

Mount Rushmore.text: Granite carvings of four presidents' heads, each about 60 feet (18 metres) tall: Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Lincoln.
The presidents were meant to be carved down to the waist, but the money ran out; only Washington goes below the chin.
Named after a New York lawyer whose guide told him the nameless peak would now carry his name.
Behind Lincoln's head is an unfinished Hall of Records, where a time capsule was sealed in 1998.

Mozambique.text: When it joined the Commonwealth in 1995, it was the only member never to have been part of the British Empire.
Cars drive on the left here, like its English-speaking neighbours, although Portugal, not Britain, colonised it.
The country takes its name from the small Island of Mozambique, its colonial capital until 1898.
Between the 7th and 11th centuries, Swahili port towns grew along its coast, shaping a distinct Swahili culture.

Mumbai.text: Heart of Bollywood, one of the world's most prolific film industries.
The city began as seven separate islands, which the British started joining together with a causeway in 1782.
Its name comes from the goddess Mumbadevi plus 'aai', the Marathi word for mother.
Boasts three UNESCO World Heritage Sites, including the grand Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus railway station and the Elephanta Caves.

Munich.text: Home of Oktoberfest, the world's largest Volksfest, or folk festival.
Oktoberfest began in October 1810 as a party celebrating the Bavarian crown prince's wedding.
The city's name means "to the monks", after the tiny monastic settlement it grew from.
Germany's largest city that isn't also a state of its own, unlike Berlin and Hamburg.

Muscat.text: Known since the 1st century AD as a leading port for trade between East and West.
Two forts rebuilt by the Portuguese in the 1580s, Al Jalali and Al-Mirani, still guard the old harbour.
One suggested origin of the name is an Old Persian word meaning "strong-scented".
Low white buildings are a typical feature, set against the rugged Hajar Mountains.

Myanmar.text: The largest country by area in mainland Southeast Asia.
Breakfast here often means mohinga, a fish noodle soup that is also the national dish.
Tea isn't just for drinking: pickled tea leaves, called lahpet, are tossed into salads.
Its capital, Naypyidaw, has a name usually translated as "royal capital" or "abode of kings".

Nairobi.text: Giraffes roam Nairobi National Park, inside the city, with skyscrapers in the background.
The name comes from a Maasai expression meaning "cool waters".
It sprang up in the late 1890s as a depot on a brand-new railway line.
A sanctuary in the city's national park hand-rears orphaned baby elephants and rhinos.

Namibia.text: One of the most sparsely populated countries in the world, with vast open spaces.
Its constitution commits the state to protecting ecosystems and wildlife for Namibians both present and future.
Named after the Namib Desert, a Khoekhoe name often translated as "vast place".
Squeezed between two deserts: the Namib along the coast and the Kalahari to the east.

Naples.text: The art of the Neapolitan pizza maker, the pizzaiolo, is on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage.
Founded by ancient Greeks, it is one of the oldest continuously inhabited urban areas in the world.
Its university, founded in 1224, is regarded as the oldest state-funded secular university in the world.
The BBC described it as "the Italian city with too much history to handle."

Nauru.text: Just 21 square kilometres in area, it's the world's third-smallest country.
There's no official capital at all – Yaren simply serves as the seat of parliament.
A British sea captain in 1798 called it "Pleasant Island" because it looked so attractive.
The favourite sport is Australian rules football, considered the national team sport.

Naypyidaw.text: A purpose-built capital, raised from scratch on an empty site about 320 km north of the old capital, Yangon.
Its name is Burmese for "abode of the king", usually translated as "royal capital".
Reporters have marvelled at its 20-lane boulevard, which, like most of the city's roads, is often almost empty.
When its zoo opened in 2008, the star attraction was a climate-controlled penguin house in the middle of tropical Myanmar.

Nazca lines.text: Ancient Peruvians drew these giant desert pictures by clearing reddish pebbles to expose the paler ground beneath.
Laid end to end, all the lines would stretch more than 1,300 kilometres.
Over 70 animal figures hide among the lines, including a hummingbird, a spider, a monkey and a condor.
Drones have helped archaeologists spot several hundred new figures in the 21st century, and more probably await discovery.

Nebraska.text: The only US state whose legislature has just one house.
The tree-planting holiday Arbor Day was founded in Nebraska City.
Kool-Aid was invented in Hastings in 1927 and is now the official state soft drink.

Nepal.text: Home to eight of the world's ten highest mountains, including Mount Everest.
Lumbini, in southern Nepal, is the Buddha's birthplace according to Buddhist tradition.
Its double-pennant flag is the only national flag that isn't rectangular, and the constitution explains how to draw it.
In Nepali, Mount Everest is called Sagarmāthā.

Netherlands.text: Its name means "lower countries", and about a quarter of the land lies below sea level.
For centuries windmills pumped water off the land, even draining whole lakes to create new farmland called polders.
Though small, it is one of the world's biggest exporters of food and farm products by value.
A dam finished in 1932, the Afsluitdijk, turned an arm of the sea called the Zuiderzee into a lake.

Neuschwanstein Castle.text: This fairytale palace inspired Disneyland's Sleeping Beauty Castle.
Built for King Ludwig II of Bavaria as a mountain retreat and a tribute to his hero, the composer Richard Wagner.
After all that building, King Ludwig II lived there for a total of only 172 days.
Behind the medieval look hid the latest 19th-century gadgets: telephone lines, central heating and toilets that flushed automatically.

Nevada.text: Gets less rain and snow on average than any other US state, about 9.5 inches a year.
Officially the "Silver State", thanks to silver's importance to its history.
Despite being so dry, its name means 'snowy' in Spanish, after its snow-capped mountain ranges.
Its border with California includes a diagonal line over 400 miles long, starting in Lake Tahoe.

New Delhi.text: Built as a brand-new capital, designed by British architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker.
Until December 1911, the capital of British-ruled India was Calcutta, not Delhi.
India Gate, the great memorial arch finished in 1931, was inspired by the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.
Its Jantar Mantar observatory, built in 1724, has 13 giant instruments made to predict the movements of the sun, moon and planets.

New Guinea.text: The world's second-largest island by area, shared between Papua New Guinea and Indonesia.
Around a thousand languages are spoken here, making it the most linguistically diverse place on Earth.
Its outline is often compared to a bird-of-paradise, so its northwestern end is called the Bird's Head Peninsula.
A Spanish explorer named it in 1545, thinking its people resembled those of Guinea in Africa.

New Hampshire.text: Has the shortest ocean coastline of any US coastal state.
Mount Washington holds the record for the fastest wind ever measured at a staffed weather station: 231 mph.
Its rocky face, the Old Man of the Mountain, collapsed in 2003 but still appears on highway signs.
Nicknamed "The Granite State" for its many granite formations and quarries.

New Jersey.text: The most densely populated of all fifty US states.
Its name comes from Jersey, a small island in the English Channel.
Atlantic City built America's first boardwalk in 1870, and the drive-in movie theatre was patented in New Jersey in 1933.

New Mexico.text: Its capital, Santa Fe, founded in 1610, is the oldest and highest state capital in the US, at about 7,000 feet.
Three UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie wholly inside it, more than in any other US state.
Its red Zia sun flag topped a 2001 survey of 72 US and Canadian flags by North American flag experts.
Every year the skies over Albuquerque fill with hot-air balloons at the famous International Balloon Fiesta.

New York (state).text: Long Island, at its south-eastern tip, is the most populous island in the whole United States.
Niagara Falls State Park, created in 1885, is widely recognized as the oldest state park in the United States.
Before England took over in 1664, it was the Dutch colony of New Netherland.
Nobody knows for sure who first called it the "Empire State", but the nickname was already in use by about 1820.

New York City.text: The most populous US city, with more than twice as many people as Los Angeles.
Dutch settlers called it New Amsterdam until the English renamed it for the Duke of York in 1664.
Much of its public transport runs 24 hours a day, carrying about a third of all mass-transit riders in the US.
Around 12 million immigrants passed through nearby Ellis Island, many sailing past the Statue of Liberty on arrival.

New Zealand.text: The last large habitable land on Earth to be settled by humans.
In 1893 it became the first country where all women could vote in national elections.
Aotearoa, its Māori name, is often translated as "land of the long white cloud".
With no mammal predators, birds like the kiwi and kākāpō evolved to be flightless.

Newcastle upon Tyne.text: Famed for its bridges over the Tyne, including the 1849 High Level Bridge, with trains on top and road traffic below.
In 1879 Joseph Swan demonstrated his light bulb here, and it became one of the first cities in the world lit by electricity.
"Taking coals to Newcastle" means doing something pointless, because the city was once a great centre of coal shipping.
It began as Pons Aelius, a Roman fort and bridge named after Emperor Hadrian's family.

Newfoundland (island).text: Vikings built a camp here around the year 1000, the only confirmed Norse site in North America outside Greenland.
Tree rings show Vikings were cutting wood at L'Anse aux Meadows in 1021, nearly 500 years before Columbus.
Cape Spear, near St. John's, is the easternmost point of North America, not counting Greenland.
A piece of France, Saint Pierre and Miquelon, lies just 19 km off its south coast.

Niagara Falls.text: Three waterfalls on the Canada–US border; the biggest, Horseshoe Falls, is North America's most powerful waterfall by flow rate.
During peak tourist hours, more than 168,000 cubic metres of water thunder over the crest every minute.
In 1969 engineers built a temporary dam and switched off the American Falls for several months.
The falls are slowly wearing away upstream; at today's pace they would reach Lake Erie in about 50,000 years.

Nicaragua.text: Lake Nicaragua, Central America's largest freshwater lake, is home to bull sharks that can live in fresh water.
Nicaraguan Sign Language arose among deaf schoolchildren in the 1970s and 1980s, giving linguists a rare look at a brand-new language.
Baseball, not football, is the country's most popular sport.

Niger.text: Most of the country lies in the Sahara Desert, so most people live in the greener south and west.
Africa's second-largest landlocked country by area, after Chad.
Wodaabe herders hold the Guérewol, a yearly traditional courtship festival.
The Cure Salée, or "Salt Cure", festival marks the rainy season's end with camel and horse races.

Nigeria.text: The most populous country in Africa, home to well over 200 million people.
Its film industry, nicknamed Nollywood, makes more films each year than any other country except India.
Its name, taken from the Niger River, was coined in 1897 by the British journalist Flora Shaw.
The ancient Nok people made nearly life-sized clay figures here, some of the earliest known sculptures in Africa outside Egypt.

North Carolina.text: The Wright brothers made the first controlled, sustained flight of a powered airplane here, near Kitty Hawk, in 1903.
Mount Mitchell, at 6,684 feet, is the highest peak in mainland North America east of the Mississippi River.
The insect-eating Venus flytrap grows wild in its coastal lowlands.
Many car number plates here carry the proud slogan "First in Flight".

North Dakota.text: Home to the Bank of North Dakota, the only general-service bank in the US owned by a state government.
President Harrison shuffled the statehood papers so nobody could tell whether North or South Dakota joined first.
The town of Rugby has long billed itself as North America's geographic centre, though newer calculations put it elsewhere.
