The KVLY-TV mast, a giant TV antenna finished in 1963, was once the tallest structure in the whole world.

North Island.text: Home to most New Zealanders, it's the most populous island in all of Polynesia.
New Zealand's capital, Wellington, sits at its south-western tip.
In Māori legend, the demigod Māui hauled it from the sea as a giant fish, so it's called Te Ika-a-Māui.
The legend says its mountains and valleys are the marks of Māui's brothers hacking at the fish.

North Korea.text: Around 80 percent of the country is mountains and uplands, cut by deep, narrow valleys.
Its ancient Koguryo tombs became the country's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004.
The name "Korea" comes from Goryeo, a medieval kingdom named after the even older Goguryeo.
Pyongyang's famous Okryu-gwan restaurant, known for cold noodles, sends research teams to the countryside to collect recipes.

North Macedonia.text: Shares Lake Ohrid, one of Europe's deepest and oldest lakes, with more than 200 species found nowhere else.
A school founded in Ohrid in 886 by Saint Clement helped spread the Cyrillic alphabet.
Since 1961 the lakeside town of Struga has hosted a famous poetry festival whose top prize is the Golden Wreath.
A landlocked country built around the Vardar river valley and framed by mountains.

Norway.text: Counting every fjord and island, its coastline is long enough to wrap more than twice around the Earth.
Hydroelectric plants make around nine-tenths of its electricity, powered by rivers and waterfalls.
Its English name comes from Old English Norþweg, meaning "northern way".
No country produces more salmon, thanks to the fish farms that line its fjords and coast.

Norwich.text: Wealth from the medieval wool trade left it with more medieval churches than any other city in Western Europe north of the Alps.
In 2012 it became England's first UNESCO City of Literature.
Flemish weavers brought pet canaries here in the 1500s, which is why the city's football club is nicknamed "The Canaries".
Revelations of Divine Love, by local mystic Julian of Norwich, is the earliest surviving book in English known to be written by a woman.

Notre-Dame de Paris.text: Begun in 1163 on an island in the Seine, this Gothic cathedral was largely complete by 1260.
A landmark of French Gothic, famous for its pioneering flying buttresses and enormous, colourful rose windows.
Its gargoyles do a real job: they are rain spouts that throw water clear of the walls.
Victor Hugo's 1831 novel, The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, sparked the interest that led to the cathedral's restoration.

Nyhavn.text: King Christian V had this canal dug in the 1670s as a gateway from the sea into the old city.
Fairy-tale author Hans Christian Andersen lived at No. 67, where a memorial plaque now stands.
Since 1977 it has been a museum harbour for historic wooden ships.
Today's busy café-lined quay was a car park until it was made pedestrian-only in 1980.

Ohio.text: Seven US presidents were born here, so it shares the nickname "Mother of Presidents" with Virginia.
The Wright brothers designed and built their first airplane in Ohio, before flying it in North Carolina.
Named after the Ohio River, whose name comes from a Seneca word meaning "good river" or "great river".
Its swallowtail-shaped flag is the only US state flag that is not a rectangle.

Oia, Greece.text: Perched on the lip of Santorini's volcanic crater, with houses built into niches in the cliff.
Famous for whitewashed Cycladic houses and blue-domed churches.
Many simple cave houses once used by sailors are now guest houses, hotels and restaurants.
Grand two-storey captains' houses recall the days when a merchant fleet made the village rich.

Oklahoma.text: More people here identify as American Indian than in any other US state, according to the 2020 census.
Its name joins two Choctaw words: "okla", meaning people, and "humma", meaning red.
Called the "Sooner State" after settlers who staked land claims before the 1889 Land Rush officially began.

Old Faithful.text: Famously predictable, this geyser erupts on average about every hour and a half.
Named in 1870, it was the first geyser in Yellowstone to get a name.
Early visitors used it as a laundry: clothes dropped in came out washed, though woollens were torn to shreds.
Each eruption can blast up to 8,400 US gallons of boiling water as high as 185 feet.

Oman.text: In the 1800s Oman's sultan moved his court to the island of Zanzibar, off East Africa, making it his capital.
Its rocky Musandam peninsula juts into the Strait of Hormuz but is cut off from the rest of Oman by the United Arab Emirates.
Summer monsoon rains turn the southern Dhofar region green, and frankincense, the ancient perfume resin, comes from trees in its hills.
Inside Madha, a patch of Oman surrounded by the UAE, sits Nahwa, a tiny village that belongs to the UAE again.

Oregon.text: Crater Lake, filling an old volcano's caldera, is the deepest lake in the United States.
A single honey fungus spreading under one of its forests is thought to be the world's largest living thing by area.
It became a US state on Valentine's Day, February 14, 1859.
Its flag is two-sided: the back shows a golden beaver, the state animal.

Orlando, Florida.text: Nicknamed the Theme Park Capital of the World.
Walt Disney World, which opened in 1971, lies about 20 miles southwest of the city, outside its limits.
Before it was Orlando, the settlement was called Jernigan, after its first permanent European settlers.
Nobody knows for sure where its name came from; one story points to a character in Shakespeare's As You Like It.

Osaka.text: It hosted the World Expo in 1970 and welcomed it back in 2025.
Back in the seventh and eighth centuries, it briefly served as Japan's imperial capital.
An old saying goes that people from Kyoto go broke on clothes, while Osakans go broke on food.
Its name means 'large hill' or 'large slope'; the area was once known as Naniwa.

Oslo.text: The Nobel Peace Prize is handed out here every year, at a ceremony in the City Hall on 10 December.
Frogner Park, the city's largest, holds hundreds of Gustav Vigeland's sculptures, the world's biggest sculpture park by a single artist.
Was called Christiania, later Kristiania, for three centuries until its original name, Oslo, was restored in 1925.
A famous ski jump, Holmenkollbakken, stands within the city, the country's main venue for Nordic skiing.

Ottawa.text: Queen Victoria herself picked it as the capital, and her choice took effect on the last day of 1857.
Before it was chosen, lawmakers held more than 200 votes over several decades trying to agree on a capital.
It began life as Bytown, named after Colonel John By, the engineer who built the Rideau Canal.
In winter, 7.8 km of the frozen Rideau Canal becomes a skateway people use to skate to downtown.

Palace of Versailles.text: Home of French kings Louis XIV, XV and XVI, with roughly 2,300 rooms.
Its dazzling Hall of Mirrors has 357 mirrors set in 17 arches, facing 17 windows and bouncing the daylight around.
It began as a modest hunting lodge, teased as a "house of cards" for its red brick, white stone and slate.
Louis XIV often ate his evening meal in public, while courtiers stood and watched him dine.

Palau.text: In 2009 it created the world's first shark sanctuary, banning commercial shark fishing in its waters.
Its Rock Islands, hundreds of uninhabited limestone islets, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.
Visitors get the "Palau Pledge", a promise to care for the environment, stamped right into their passports.
The capital is Ngerulmud, on the largest island, yet about two-thirds of Palauans live on Koror.

Palma de Mallorca.text: Capital and largest city of Spain's Balearic Islands, set on the Bay of Palma.
Its seafront Gothic cathedral, La Seu, was begun in 1229 and not finished until 1601.
The cathedral's rose window, nearly 14 metres across, is the second-largest surviving Gothic rose window.
In the early 1900s, the famous Catalan architect Antoni Gaudí led restoration work inside the cathedral.

Pamukkale.text: Its name means 'cotton castle' in Turkish, after its snow-white terraces.
The dazzling white terraces are travertine, a rock laid down by mineral water from hot springs.
The ancient Greek spa city of Hierapolis was built right on top of the terraces.
Visitors can bathe in Cleopatra's Pool, where ancient marble columns lie under the water.

Panama.text: Home of the Panama Canal, the shipping shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, completed in 1914.
Scientists think this land bridge was completed about three million years ago, letting animals cross between North and South America.
The Pan-American Highway runs from Alaska to Patagonia, except for one break: the dense Darién Gap jungle between Panama and Colombia.
One popular legend, among several theories, says "Panamá" was a fishing village whose name meant "abundance of fish".

Panama City.text: Its ruined first site, Panamá Viejo, was the first Spanish city founded on the Pacific coast of the Americas, in 1519.
After the privateer Henry Morgan's raid burned the original city in 1671, it was rebuilt on a new site.
Frank Gehry, architect of Bilbao's Guggenheim Museum, designed its Biomuseo, completed in 2014.
Inside the city, the Metropolitan Natural Park's tropical forest is home to over 200 kinds of birds and 45 kinds of mammals.

Papua New Guinea.text: Around 840 languages are spoken here, making it the most linguistically diverse country in the world.
People in its highlands invented farming on their own around 7000 BC, one of the few places on Earth where that happened.
Since 2015, sign language has been recognised as a national language alongside English, Tok Pisin and Hiri Motu.
The colourful bird-of-paradise appears on the national flag, and its feathers still decorate dancers at traditional sing-sing gatherings.

Paraguay.text: More than 90% of people speak Guaraní, an Indigenous language that shares official status with Spanish.
Thanks to the giant Itaipu Dam on its border with Brazil, it's one of the world's leading exporters of hydroelectricity.
Its flag looks different from each side: the front shows the national seal, the back a treasury seal with a lion.

Paris.text: Home of the Louvre, the largest and most-visited museum in the world.
Nicknamed the 'City of Light' mainly for its leading role in the 18th-century Age of Enlightenment.
The Romans called it Lutetia; its modern name comes from the Parisii, a Gallic tribe who lived here.
The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 world's fair, held to mark 100 years since the French Revolution.

Paro Taktsang.text: This cliffside monastery has become the cultural icon of Bhutan.
Built into a near-vertical rock face, it hangs about 900 metres above the Paro valley.
In one version of the legend, Guru Rinpoche flew here on the back of a tigress, hence "Tiger's Nest".
It's so precariously perched that it's said to cling to the mountainside like a gecko.

Parthenon.text: A temple to the goddess Athena, built 447 to 438 BC and a lasting symbol of ancient Greece and democracy.
It once housed a giant gold-and-ivory statue of Athena by the sculptor Phidias.
Its floor isn't flat: it bulges upward by about 10 centimetres in the middle.
Its gleaming marble carvings were originally painted in colour.

Pena Palace.text: A fairy-tale hilltop palace named one of the Seven Wonders of Portugal.
King Ferdinand II turned the ruins of a monastery into a summer palace for Portugal's royal family.
Its red and yellow walls faded to grey for many years until they were repainted in their original colours.
A sundial cannon on the Queen's Terrace used to fire every day at noon.

Pennsylvania.text: The Declaration of Independence was adopted in its city of Philadelphia in 1776.
Its name means "Penn's woods", honouring Admiral William Penn, father of the colony's founder, who was also called William Penn.
One of only four US states to call itself a "Commonwealth" in its official name.
The town of Hershey is home to one of the world's largest chocolate makers.

Perito Moreno Glacier.text: It flows from the Southern Patagonian Ice Field, the world's second-largest ice field outside the polar regions.
Its ice wall is 5 kilometres wide and rises about 74 metres above the waters of Lake Argentino.
The glacier can dam part of its lake until the water, up to 30 metres higher, bursts through in a spectacular rupture.
It has had other names: a Chilean Navy captain called it Francisco Gormaz, and a boundary surveyor named it Bismarck.

Persian Gulf.text: Its only link to the open ocean is the narrow Strait of Hormuz, less than 60 km across.
Very shallow for a sea: even its deepest point is only about 90 to 100 metres down.
During most of the last ice age it was mostly dry land – a flat floodplain where rivers met.
The ancient Assyrians called it the "Bitter Sea".

Perth.text: One of the world's most isolated big cities: the nearest city of over 100,000 people, Adelaide, is more than 2,100 km away.
In 1962 residents switched on their lights as astronaut John Glenn orbited overhead, earning it the nickname 'City of Light'.
Its Swan River was named for the black swans spotted by Dutch captain Willem de Vlamingh in 1697.
Kings Park, overlooking the city centre, is one of the world's largest inner-city parks.

Peru.text: The Inca Empire, builders of Machu Picchu, was the largest known state in the Americas before Columbus arrived.
Its ancient Caral–Supe culture is counted as the earliest civilization in the Americas, one of the world's cradles of civilization.
Farmers here grow more than 3,000 kinds of potato.
Around three-quarters of the country lies in the Amazon basin, and it holds about 4% of the planet's fresh water.

Petronas Towers.text: Counting their spires, these twin 88-storey towers were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004.
To finish on time, each tower was built by a different team: one led by a Japanese firm, one by a South Korean firm.
The double-decker skybridge linking the towers was built on the ground, then lifted into place over three days.
Each tower's floor plan is based on the Rub el Hizb, an eight-pointed star from Islamic art.

Philippines.text: An island nation made up of about 7,641 islands in the western Pacific.
A Spanish explorer named some of its islands 'Felipinas' in the 1540s after Prince Philip, who later became King Philip II of Spain.
The Christmas season here can begin as early as 1 September.
Basketball, played by amateurs and professionals alike, is considered the country's most popular sport.

Phuket (city).text: Capital of Phuket province, which is built around Thailand's largest island.
Its name probably comes from 'bukit', the Malay word for hill.
Its Old Town's Sino-Portuguese buildings date from the days when tin mining made the island prosperous.
Named a UNESCO City of Gastronomy in 2015, thanks to its multicultural cooking.

Plaza de España, Seville.text: Its sweeping half-circle of buildings was the largest and most famous showpiece of Seville's 1929 world's fair.
Colourful ceramic alcoves and benches line the plaza, each one celebrating a different province of Spain.
Star Wars fans may recognise it: it played the city of Theed on the planet Naboo in Attack of the Clones.
Film crews love it: scenes for the classic movie Lawrence of Arabia were shot here in the early 1960s.

Plitvice Lakes National Park.text: Its lakes step down the valley in a cascade, with sixteen of them visible at the surface.
One of Croatia's oldest and largest national parks, founded in 1949.
The natural dams between the lakes are made of tufa rock, and they keep growing, by up to 13 mm a year.
About 400 years ago a fast-growing tufa barrier merged two lakes into one, today's Lake Kozjak.

Plymouth.text: The Pilgrim Fathers set sail from here for the New World in 1620.
Home to HMNB Devonport, the largest operational naval base in Western Europe.
Legend says Sir Francis Drake insisted on finishing his game of bowls on the Hoe before facing the Spanish Armada.
Smeaton's Tower on the Hoe once stood far out at sea as the Eddystone Lighthouse, before being taken apart and rebuilt here.

Poland.text: In 1791 it adopted Europe's first modern written constitution, second in the world only to the United States'.
Birthplace of Marie Skłodowska-Curie, the first person ever to win two Nobel Prizes.
Around a quarter of all the world's white storks nest here.
Deep in the Wieliczka Salt Mine, miners carved whole chapels out of rock salt, near an underground lake.

Pompeii.text: Buried under volcanic ash, this Roman town offers a snapshot of daily life frozen at the moment it was covered.
Excavations here and at nearby Herculaneum in the 1700s helped give birth to modern archaeology.
In 2020 archaeologists uncovered a Roman snack bar whose pots still held traces of duck, goat, fish and snails.
In 2016 guitarist David Gilmour played to a crowd in its ancient amphitheatre, 45 years after Pink Floyd filmed a concert there with no audience.

Pont du Gard.text: One of the best-preserved Roman aqueduct bridges, built in the first century AD to carry water to Roman Nîmes.
Across its 456 m, the bridge drops just 2.5 cm, a slope of about 1 in 18,000.
Its huge stone blocks were cut so precisely that they mostly hold together by friction and gravity, without mortar.
Water took nearly 27 hours to trickle along the aqueduct from its spring to the city.

Port-au-Prince.text: Haiti's capital and largest city sits on a natural harbour on the Gulf of Gonâve, used since Taíno times.
The name means "Prince's Port", but nobody is sure which prince, or which ship called Le Prince, it honours.
Brightly painted pickup-truck taxis called tap-taps are its most common public transport.
Its national museum shows a rusty anchor said to come from Columbus's ship, the Santa María.

Porto.text: Port wine, one of Portugal's most famous exports, is named after the city.
Its ancient name, Portus Cale, has been suggested as the origin of the name "Portugal".
Locals are nicknamed tripeiros, tripe-eaters: the story goes that the best meat went to the fleet, leaving tripe behind.
Its historic centre on the Douro River became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.

Portugal.text: Its alliance with England, sealed by the Treaty of Windsor in 1386, is the oldest standing alliance in the world.
About half the world's cork, the bark used for bottle stoppers, comes from its cork oak forests.
In 1498 its explorer Vasco da Gama sailed all the way from Portugal to India.
Singer Amália Rodrigues, nicknamed the 'Queen of Fado', carried Portugal's soulful fado songs around the world.

Positano.text: This cliffside town is part of the Amalfi Coast, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997.
Mick Jagger and Keith Richards wrote the Rolling Stones song "Midnight Rambler" here while on holiday.

Potala Palace.text: Perched about 3,700 metres up, this vast palace was the Dalai Lamas' winter home for around 300 years.
From outside it looks 13 storeys tall, and inside are well over a thousand rooms filled with shrines and statues.
It has a White Palace and a Red Palace, the red part added in the 1690s.

Prague.text: Charles University, founded here in 1348, is the oldest university in Central Europe.
Nicknamed the "City of a Hundred Spires", its historic centre has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992.
On its medieval astronomical clock, a little skeleton representing Death strikes the hour while apostle figures parade past.
St. Vitus Cathedral, inside Prague Castle, was begun in 1344 but not finished until the 20th century.

Preikestolen.text: This "Pulpit Rock" towers 604 m above Lysefjorden, with an almost flat top about 25 m square.
Nepalese Sherpas helped rebuild the popular hiking path up to the cliff, starting in 2013.
Its old local name meant "Plane's Tooth", after a woodworking tool; the name "Pulpit" was coined around 1900 to attract hikers.
Tom Cruise and Henry Cavill dangle from its cliff face in the final fight of Mission: Impossible – Fallout.

Pretoria.text: One of South Africa's three capital cities, home to the government's executive branch and every foreign embassy in the country.
Nicknamed the Jacaranda City: around 70,000 jacaranda trees turn its streets purple each October.
Its first two jacarandas, grown from seeds gathered in Rio de Janeiro, were planted in 1888 and still stand in a school's grounds.
A 9-metre statue of Nelson Mandela, unveiled in 2013, stands with open arms before the Union Buildings.

Pyongyang.text: One of Korea's oldest cities, it was the capital of two ancient Korean kingdoms, Gojoseon and Goguryeo.
Its old nickname, Ryugyong, means "Capital of Willows".
Pyongyang naengmyeon, a famous Korean cold buckwheat noodle soup, was born here.

Qatar.text: In 2022 it became the first Arab country to host the FIFA World Cup.
Sits on some of the world's largest natural gas reserves.
Mostly flat desert, its highest point, Qurayn Abu al Bawl, is only 103 metres above sea level.
In the southeast, rolling sand dunes surround the Khor al Adaid, or "Inland Sea", an inlet of the Persian Gulf.

Queenstown, New Zealand.text: A hotspot for adventure sports like bungy jumping, jet boating and whitewater rafting, plus skiing in winter.
After gold was found nearby in 1862, settler William Rees turned his wool shed into a hotel, today's Eichardt's.
In Kāi Tahu tradition, Lake Wakatipu was dug out by the ancestor Rākaihautū with his digging stick.
A coal-fired heritage steamship, the TSS Earnslaw, still sails on Lake Wakatipu.

Quito.text: At about 2,850 metres up, it is either the highest or second-highest national capital in the world.
In 1978 its old town became one of the first 12 places ever named UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
No capital city is closer to the Equator, which runs through the north of its metropolitan area.
GPS later showed the real Equator lies about 240 metres north of the famous Mitad del Mundo monument nearby.

Rabat.text: One of Morocco's four imperial cities, with a historic heart listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Hassan Tower is a huge unfinished minaret from the late 1100s, meant for an enormous mosque.
In the 1600s it became a haven for the Barbary corsairs, the notorious North African pirates.
Its name comes from 'ribat', an Arabic word for a fortified base; its full old name meant 'stronghold of victory'.

Radcliffe Camera.text: The focal point of Oxford University, it appears in almost every picture used to sum the university up.
Nothing to do with photos: "camera" here is Latin for "chamber".
Built in 1737–49 as a library, paid for by £40,000 left by the doctor John Radcliffe.
Underground reading rooms and a tunnel link it to the Bodleian Library, a space nicknamed the "Glink".

Red Sea.text: Its warm, shallow shelves teem with sea life, including more than 200 kinds of soft and hard coral.
One of the saltiest seas on Earth – no significant rivers or streams flow into it.
It's still widening as Arabia pulls away from Africa, and may one day become an ocean.
The ancient Romans called it Pontus Herculis – the "Sea of Hercules".

Registan.text: Three grand tiled madrasas face this square, among Central Asia's finest Islamic architecture.
Registan means "place of sand" in Persian.
The Sherdar Madrasa's portal shows tigers with rising suns on their backs, unusual for showing living creatures.
The great Persian poet Jami studied at the square's Ulugh Beg Madrasa in the 15th century.

Republic of Ireland.text: James Joyce set Ulysses in Dublin, and Irish writers Yeats, Shaw, Beckett and Heaney all won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Its name, like the Irish name Éire, is thought to come from an ancient Celtic word meaning "fertile land".
In the 1800s, Halloween lanterns in Ireland and Britain were carved from turnips, often with grotesque faces, not pumpkins.
A harp is the state's symbol, stamped on Irish coins and official documents.

Republic of the Congo.text: A 2006–07 study suggested about 125,000 western lowland gorillas live in its swampy northern forests.
Its capital, Brazzaville, faces Kinshasa, capital of DR Congo, directly across the Congo River.
Nicknamed Congo-Brazzaville, after its capital, to tell it apart from its bigger neighbour, Congo-Kinshasa.
Its forest of Odzala-Kokoua became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

Reykjavík.text: The world's northernmost capital of a sovereign state.
Its name means 'smoke bay', after the steam rising from nearby hot springs.
Almost every building in the city is heated with geothermal hot water.
Legend says Iceland's first settler built his home wherever his high-seat pillars, thrown overboard, washed ashore.

Rhode Island.text: The smallest of all fifty US states by area.
On May 4, 1776, it became the first colony to renounce its allegiance to the British Crown.
It was the last of the original 13 states to accept the US Constitution, holding out until 1790.
Named after an island, even though most of the state actually sits on the mainland.

Riga.text: About a third of the buildings in its centre are Art Nouveau, which one historian calls the highest concentration anywhere.
Founded in 1201, it grew rich as a trading city of the medieval Hanseatic League.
The pavilions of its Central Market were built by reusing old German Zeppelin hangars.
One old explanation says the name comes from riverside warehouses that the local Livonian people called "Riae".

Rio de Janeiro.text: Above the city stands Christ the Redeemer, named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.
Its 2016 Games were the first Olympics ever held in South America.
From 1808 to 1821 the Portuguese royal court ruled its empire from here, a rare case of a colony hosting the capital.
Its name means "January River": Portuguese explorers first reached its bay on 1 January 1502.

Riyadh.text: The largest city on the whole Arabian Peninsula, sitting on a desert plateau about 600 metres above sea level.
Its name means 'gardens', after the date-palm orchards that once grew outside the old town walls.
On its outskirts lies Diriyah, original home of the Saudi royal family and site of the UNESCO-listed At-Turaif district.
Al Faisaliah Tower, Saudi Arabia's first skyscraper, wears a golden ball on top said to be inspired by a ballpoint pen.

Rock of Gibraltar.text: One of the two ancient Pillars of Hercules, which legend said marked the western edge of the known world.
Its upper slopes are home to Europe's only wild monkey population, the Barbary macaques.
A Neanderthal skull found here in 1848 was discovered years before the famous one in Germany's Neander Valley.
Its name comes from the Arabic Jabal Ṭāriq, meaning "Mountain of Tariq".

Romania.text: Romanian is a Romance language, a cousin of Italian, French and Spanish, and the most widely spoken of its Eastern branch.
Its Danube Delta is the largest continuous marshland in Europe, home to nearly 1,700 plant species.
Bran Castle is sold to tourists as Dracula's castle, yet there's no evidence the novel's author ever knew it existed.
Sculptor Constantin Brâncuși was Romanian; one of his "Bird in Space" sculptures sold for $27.5 million in 2005.

Rome.text: Home to the only country inside a city: Vatican City lies entirely within Rome's boundaries.
The Roman poet Tibullus was first to call it 'the Eternal City', back in the 1st century BC.
Its most famous founding myth tells of twins Romulus and Remus, who as babies were suckled by a she-wolf.
Nicknamed the 'City of Seven Hills', ancient Rome grew up across seven hills, including the Palatine and Capitoline.

Rwanda.text: Its Volcanoes National Park makes it one of only three countries where you can see mountain gorillas in the wild.
One of the few Commonwealth members with no historical link to the British Empire.
Its mountains earn it the nickname "Land of a thousand hills", or Pays des mille collines in French.
On the last Saturday morning of each month, adults join umuganda, a national session of community work such as cleaning streets.

Sagrada Família.text: Its central tower, which reached 172.5 metres in 2026, makes it the world's tallest church.
Antoni Gaudí devoted the rest of his life to it and is buried in its crypt.
Building started in 1882, but it only got an official building permit in 2019.
Though sometimes called a cathedral, it isn't Barcelona's cathedral; that title belongs to a different, much older church.

Saint Basil's Cathedral.text: Built for Ivan the Terrible between 1555 and 1561, it is one of Russia's best-loved symbols.
Nine colourful onion domes, each topping a separate church, rise like the flames of a bonfire.
Nobody knows for sure who designed it.
Its famous bright colours weren't complete until 1683, over a century after it was built.

Saint Petersburg.text: The world's northernmost city with over a million people living within its city limits.
In early summer its famous "White Nights" never get fully dark, and the city throws a festival to celebrate them.
Founded by Tsar Peter the Great in 1703, it was the capital of the Russian Empire until 1918.
Built on marshland among river islands and canals, it's often called the "Venice of the North".

Sakhalin.text: Russia's largest island, a long, narrow strip of land 948 km from end to end.
Its name comes from Manchu words meaning "island at the mouth of the Black River", the Black River being the Amur.
In 1890 the writer Anton Chekhov spent three months here interviewing thousands of people for a census.
It lies at similar latitudes to England, Wales and Ireland.

Salar de Uyuni.text: The largest salt flat in the world, covering more than 10,000 square kilometres high in the Andes.
So flat that its height varies by less than a metre, making it ideal for calibrating satellites that measure Earth's surface.
After rain, a thin film of still water can turn it into a giant mirror, often called the largest in the world.
Several kinds of flamingo come here to breed.

Salzburg.text: Birthplace of the composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart.
Its hilltop Hohensalzburg Fortress, begun in the 11th century, is one of Europe's largest medieval fortresses.
"Salz" is German for salt, and salt mining once helped make the city rich.
The 1960s musical film The Sound of Music was filmed here, and tours still visit its locations.

Samoa.text: European explorers called these the "Navigator Islands" because of the Samoans' brilliant seafaring skills.
Skipped a whole day, Friday 30 December 2011, when it changed time zone and the International Date Line moved east of it.
In 2009 the country switched from driving on the right to driving on the left, like Australia and New Zealand.
Traditional Samoan houses, called fale, have no walls; blinds of coconut palm fronds come down at night or in bad weather.

San Francisco.text: Its Chinatown is the oldest in North America and one of the largest outside Asia.
The Gold Rush swelled it from about 1,000 people in 1848 to around 25,000 within two years.
More than 50 hills rise within the city limits.

San José, Costa Rica.text: Costa Rica's capital and largest city, recognised by UNESCO as a "Design City".
In 2012 the city announced plans to put up its first street signs, about 22,000 of them.
Its grand National Theatre and Barrio Amón recall a coffee "golden age" in the late 1800s.
It has whole museums devoted to ancient pre-Columbian gold and to jade.

San Marino.text: Claims to have been founded in AD 301, which would make it the world's oldest surviving sovereign state and constitutional republic.
Has two heads of state at once, the Captains Regent, chosen afresh every six months.
Made Abraham Lincoln an honorary citizen; he replied that the little republic proved free government could be "secure and enduring".
Its postage stamps are mostly bought by collectors rather than letter-writers, and earn the country a significant income.

San Salvador.text: Home to the headquarters of the Central American Integration System, which links the region's countries.
Surrounded by volcanoes, with the Boquerón Volcano, nearly 1,900 metres high, looming over the city.
Has hosted the Miss Universe pageant twice, in 1975 and 2023.
Just to the east lies Lake Ilopango, a volcanic caldera and El Salvador's largest natural body of water.

Sanaa.text: Perched more than 2,200 metres up, it is one of the highest capital cities in the world.
Its Old City, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is famous for tall many-storeyed houses decorated with geometric patterns.
Old tower houses grew upward: families added new floors as sons married and had children of their own.
Its name comes from an ancient Sabaic word meaning 'fortress', first written down around 2,500 years ago.

Santiago.text: Chile's capital fills a valley squeezed between the Andes and the Chilean Coastal Range.
Founded in 1541, with a grid of streets laid out around today's Plaza de Armas.
The president's palace is here, but Chile's National Congress mostly meets in the port city of Valparaíso.
Snow in the city centre is rare: between 2000 and 2017 it was measured there only twice.

Santo Domingo.text: Founded in 1496, it is the oldest continuously inhabited European settlement in the Americas.
Its UNESCO-listed Colonial Zone holds the oldest cathedral still standing in the Americas, begun in the early 1500s.
Christopher Columbus's son Diego once lived in the Alcázar de Colón palace, now a museum.
The Ozama River splits the city in two, with the historic Colonial Zone on its west bank.

São Paulo.text: Brazil's biggest city is also the most populous city in the Americas, counting people living within city limits.
No city in the world has more Portuguese speakers.
Home to the largest Japanese community outside Japan, plus huge Italian and Arab ones, with neighbourhoods like Liberdade.
Founded by Jesuit priests in 1554, it's one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the Americas.

São Tomé and Príncipe.text: After the Seychelles, it's Africa's second-smallest and second-least-populous country.
In the early 1900s it was the world's largest cocoa exporter, earning the nickname the "Chocolate Islands".
Watching a 1919 solar eclipse from Príncipe, Arthur Eddington helped deliver one of the first successful tests of Einstein's relativity.
The equator runs right across a tiny islet here, Ilhéu das Rolas, just south of São Tomé Island.

Sarajevo.text: Hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics, with skiing on the mountains that ring the city.
One of a few major European cities with a mosque, Catholic church, Orthodox church and synagogue in the same neighbourhood.
The Sebilj, a wooden Ottoman-style fountain at the heart of Baščaršija square, was rebuilt in 1891.
The cable car up Mount Trebević, a landmark of the 1984 Olympics, was rebuilt and reopened in 2018.

Saudi Arabia.text: Its Rub' al Khali, the "Empty Quarter", is the world's largest continuous sand desert.
The only Arab country among the G20 group of major economies.
At Hegra, the Nabataeans carved 131 monumental tombs into the rock around 2,000 years ago.
Arabic coffee, served as a symbol of generosity, is UNESCO-listed heritage that Saudi Arabia shares with its Gulf neighbours.

Schönbrunn Palace.text: This vast Baroque palace on the edge of Vienna was the main summer home of the Habsburg rulers.
Its name means 'beautiful spring', after a well whose water the royal court drank.
Emperor Franz Joseph was born here and died here too, at the age of 86.
Its gardens hold a zoo founded in 1752, the world's oldest zoo still in operation.

Seattle.text: Named after Chief Seattle, leader of the Duwamish and Suquamish peoples.
The 1897 Klondike Gold Rush made it the main supply stop for miners heading north.
Its region is the cloudiest in the lower 48 states, averaging about 201 cloudy days a year.
The very first Starbucks opened at Pike Place Market in 1971, selling coffee beans.

Senegal.text: The westernmost country on the whole mainland of Africa, Europe and Asia.
In 2026 Dakar hosts the Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic event ever held in Africa.
Traditional wrestling rivals football as the country's favourite sport and has become a national obsession.
From 1979 until 2007, the famous Paris–Dakar off-road rally usually finished in its capital, Dakar.

Seoul.text: Its story stretches back over 2,000 years: by tradition, the kingdom of Baekje founded a capital here in 18 BC.
'Seoul' is a native Korean word simply meaning 'capital city', so unlike most Korean place names it has no Chinese characters.
The Cheonggyecheon stream, long buried under concrete, was uncovered and restored in 2005 as an open stream through downtown.

Seville.text: Some 80 km from the sea up the Guadalquivir River, its port is Spain's only commercial river port.
As the gateway for Spain's trade across the Atlantic, it became one of Western Europe's largest cities in the 1500s.
Bitter Seville oranges grow on its streets, and large quantities are shipped to Britain for marmalade.
In 2021 a pilot scheme began turning the gas from fermenting leftover oranges into clean electricity.

Seychelles.text: Africa's smallest country by area, and its least populated.
Its granite islands are bits of an old continent, which Alfred Wegener used as evidence for continental drift.
The islands are named after a French politician, Jean Moreau de Séchelles.
Aldabra, one of its atolls, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site where giant tortoises roam.

Shanghai.text: Its port became the world's busiest container port in 2010.
Its metro opened only in 1993, yet has grown into one of the world's longest, with nearly 900 km of lines.
Its airport maglev, opened in 2004, was the world's first commercial high-speed maglev, cruising at over 430 km/h until 2021.
The name Shanghai translates as "Above the Sea".

Shenzhen.text: Mostly rural villages until 1979, it has boomed into a giant city of well over 15 million people.
Sometimes called China's Silicon Valley, it's home to tech giants such as Huawei, Tencent and DJI.
Since 2018, every one of its more than 16,000 city buses has been fully electric.
Its name means "deep ditch", after the local word for irrigation ditches.

Shwedagon Pagoda.text: Myanmar's most sacred Buddhist pagoda, a gilded stupa believed to hold relics of four Buddhas.
Yangon caps new buildings well below the pagoda's height, so the golden stupa keeps ruling the city skyline.
Legend says it was built over 2,500 years ago while the Buddha was alive, though chronicles first mention it in 1362.
Visitors pray at the corner for their birth weekday, and Burmese astrology counts eight weekdays, splitting Wednesday into morning and afternoon.

Sierra Leone.text: Its name comes from the Portuguese Serra Leoa, 'lioness mountains', after the hills near today's Freetown.
Founded in 1827, Freetown's Fourah Bay College is the oldest Western-style university in West Africa.
Freetown was known as the "Athens of Africa" for its many excellent schools.
Nearly everyone speaks Krio, yet the Krio people whose language it is make up only about 1% of the population.

Sigiriya.text: A 5th-century king built his palace on top of this granite rock, which towers about 180 metres high.
Its name means "Lion Rock", after a giant lion-shaped gateway built halfway up the cliff.
Paintings once covered most of the rock's west face; in 1907 one writer called it perhaps 'the largest picture in the world'.
Its water gardens rank among the oldest landscaped gardens in the world.

Singapore.text: Its name comes from a Sanskrit word meaning "lion city".
It sits only about 137 kilometres north of the equator.
Thanks to land reclaimed from the sea, it's expected to be over 30% bigger in the 2030s than in the 1960s.
Its Botanic Gardens are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Slovakia.text: Nicknamed the "European Detroit", it makes more cars per person than any other country.
Became independent in 1993 when Czechoslovakia split peacefully in two, the "Velvet Divorce".
Hundreds of caves lie beneath its mountains, including Dobšiná Ice Cave, where the ice floor is about 25 metres thick.
Vlkolínec, a well-preserved village of wooden folk houses, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993.

Slovenia.text: About 60% of the country is covered in forest, one of the highest shares in Europe.
Its Karst Plateau gave the world the word "karst", for limestone landscapes riddled with caves.
The famous white Lipizzan horses are named after Lipica, a Slovenian village where a royal stud farm was founded in 1580.
Near Postojna, Predjama Castle sits half hidden inside a cave.

Sofia.text: Perched about 550 metres up at the foot of Vitosha mountain, it's one of Europe's highest capital cities.
Its medieval Boyana Church joined the World Heritage List in 1979.
The Roman emperor Constantine is said to have called it "my Rome" and thought of making it his capital.
The city's motto is "Ever growing, never ageing".

Solomon Islands.text: Made up of six major islands and around a thousand smaller ones in Melanesia.
Rennell Island is one of the world's largest raised coral atolls, and its eastern part is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Europeans named the islands after the wealthy biblical King Solomon, believing them to be the legendary Ophir.
Naturally blond hair is common here, especially in children, thanks to a gene variant found only in Oceania.

South Africa.text: It has three capitals: Pretoria for government, Cape Town for Parliament and Bloemfontein for the Supreme Court of Appeal.
Has 12 official languages, including South African Sign Language, added in 2023.
Another whole country, Lesotho, sits entirely inside its borders.
Cape Agulhas, not the Cape of Good Hope, is the true southernmost point of Africa.

South Carolina.text: Boeing's 787 Dreamliner jets get their final assembly at a factory beside Charleston's international airport.
In 1788 it became the eighth state to approve the US Constitution.
Carolina comes from Carolus, the Latin form of Charles, in honour of an English King Charles.
Its state dog, the Boykin Spaniel, was bred here for hunting wild turkeys and ducks in a river swamp.

South Dakota.text: Mount Rushmore, the giant carving of four presidents, is in its Black Hills.
The geographic center of all 50 US states lies here, in open country about 20 miles north of Belle Fourche.
When it joined the Union alongside North Dakota in 1889, the president shuffled the papers so nobody could tell which came first.
North America's pole of inaccessibility, the spot farthest from any coastline, is here, over 1,000 miles from the sea.

South Island.text: The larger of New Zealand's two main islands, covering 56% of the country's land.
Aoraki / Mount Cook in the Southern Alps rises 3,724 metres, making it New Zealand's highest peak.
Its Māori name, Te Waipounamu, means "the waters of greenstone".
Its dramatic scenery starred in films including The Lord of the Rings trilogy.

South Korea.text: Its pop culture of K-pop, TV dramas and films has swept the globe as the 'Korean Wave' since the late 1990s.
Its alphabet, Hangul, was created by King Sejong the Great to help ordinary people learn to read.
The Jikji, the oldest surviving book printed with metal movable type, was made in Korea in 1377.
Its highest point, Hallasan on Jeju Island, is a dormant volcano about 1,950 metres high.

South Sudan.text: On 9 July 2011 it became Africa's 54th independent country, the newest nation on the continent.
Its Sudd swamp on the White Nile is one of the world's largest wetlands.
Antelopes and gazelles around the Sudd swamp take part in one of the largest mammal migrations on Earth.
Before independence, other names considered for the new country included Azania, Nile Republic and Kush Republic.

Space Needle.text: Built for the 1962 World's Fair, it is now an icon of Seattle.
At 605 feet, it was once the tallest building west of the Mississippi River.
Its original paints had space-age names: Orbital Olive, Astronaut White, Re-entry Red and Galaxy Gold.
Up top, a revolving glass floor takes 45 minutes to carry visitors all the way round.

Spain.text: Home to the southernmost point of continental Europe.
Spanish, which grew up here, is the world's second-most spoken native language.
Its highest peak isn't on the mainland at all: it's Teide, an active volcano on Tenerife in the Canary Islands.
Two Spanish cities, Ceuta and Melilla, sit on the mainland of Africa.

Sri Lanka.text: In 1960 Sirimavo Bandaranaike became prime minister here, the world's first elected woman prime minister.
Famous for Ceylon tea, still a trademark export from its old plantation days.
The word "serendipity" comes from Serendip, an old Persian name for this island.
In the late dry season, herds of elephants meet on the bed of Minneriya reservoir, an event dubbed "The Gathering".

St Helier.text: Capital of Jersey, the largest of the Channel Islands, and home to the island's parliament and courts.
A statue of King George II in the Royal Square is the 'zero milestone' from which all distances in Jersey are measured.
Elizabeth Castle sits on a tidal island: walk there along a causeway at low tide, or ride an amphibious 'duck' ferry.

St Mark's Basilica.text: Its domes, vaults and upper walls glitter with gold-ground mosaics of saints, prophets and Bible scenes.
Until 1807 it was the private chapel of Venice's rulers, the Doges; only then did it become the city's cathedral.
Medieval chronicles say two Venetian merchants carried Saint Mark's body here from Alexandria, Egypt, in 828 or 829.
The bronze horses on its balcony are copies; the ancient originals have been kept safely indoors since 1974.

St Michael's Mount.text: A tidal island: between mid-tide and low water you can walk out from Marazion on a granite causeway.
In medieval times it belonged to the monks of France's Mont-Saint-Michel, another cone-shaped tidal island.
Its Cornish name means "grey rock in a wood", perhaps remembering a forest now drowned under the bay.
In one legend, a giant called Cormoran lived here until a boy named Jack trapped him: Jack the Giant Killer.

St. Peter's Basilica.text: The largest church in the world by interior measure, built over 120 years and completed in 1626.
Designed mainly by Bramante, Michelangelo and Carlo Maderno, it is a celebrated masterpiece of Italian Renaissance architecture.
The right foot of a bronze Saint Peter statue inside is worn away by centuries of pilgrims touching and kissing it.
Despite its size and fame, it isn't a cathedral, because it is not the seat of a bishop.

Stari Most.text: A graceful single stone arch commissioned by Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent and finished in the 1560s.
Mostar is named after its 'mostari', the bridge keepers who guarded the river crossing here in Ottoman times.
Every summer, divers compete by leaping about 20 metres from its hump into the chilly Neretva river below.
Rebuilt using traditional Ottoman building techniques, it reopened in 2004 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Statue of Liberty.text: A gift from the people of France, dedicated in 1886, with an inner metal framework built by Gustave Eiffel.
Her tablet is inscribed JULY IV MDCCLXXVI, the date of American independence in Roman numerals.
She started out a dull copper colour; a green coating called verdigris had covered her completely by 1906.
Her torch-bearing arm was shown off in a Manhattan park for six years to raise money, long before the rest of her was finished.

Stockholm.text: Spread across fourteen islands where Lake Mälaren flows out into the Baltic Sea.
Every December it hosts the Nobel Prize ceremony and banquet; only the Peace Prize is handed out elsewhere, in Oslo.
Its metro stations are so lavishly decorated that the network has been called the longest art gallery in the world.
The "stock" in its name means log in Swedish.

Stone Town.text: A UNESCO World Heritage Site whose buildings blend Swahili, Arab, Persian, Indian and European styles.
It is named for the coral stone it's built from, which gives the town a warm reddish colour.
Its famous carved doors come in two styles: Indian ones with rounded tops and rectangular Omani Arab ones.
The sultan's House of Wonders, built in 1883, was the first building in East Africa to have a lift.

Stonehenge.text: The monument lines up with sunrise on the summer solstice and sunset on the winter solstice.
Its smaller bluestones are generally thought to have been hauled about 150 miles from the Preseli Hills in Wales.
The giant stones are slotted together with mortise-and-tenon and tongue-and-groove joints, tricks borrowed from woodworking.
In 1915 a local man, Cecil Chubb, bought Stonehenge at auction and gave it to the nation three years later.

Sudan.text: Ancient Nubians here built about 255 pyramids, more than ancient Egypt ever did.
Kings from the ancient Kingdom of Kush here ruled Egypt as pharaohs for nearly a century.
Africa's third-largest country by area, and the largest until South Sudan became independent in 2011.
Ancient Egyptians called this land Ta Seti, "Land of the Bow", after its skilled Nubian archers.

Sugarloaf Mountain.text: A granite peak rising 396 metres above the harbour at the mouth of Rio's Guanabara Bay.
The Portuguese named it in the 1500s because it looked like a cone of sugar shaped in a clay mould.
Its cable car opened in 1912, and for its first 60 years it carried visitors in cars made of wood.
With two neighbouring hills, it forms one of the world's largest urban rock-climbing areas, with more than 270 routes.

Sulawesi.text: The world's 11th-largest island, with four long peninsulas that give it a sprawling, spidery shape.
Its twisting shape fooled the first European visitors into thinking it was a group of islands.
Its caves hold a painting of a warty pig at least 45,500 years old, among the oldest known figurative art.
Its old name, Celebes, may come from the Portuguese for "the famous ones", after some prominent rocks.

Sumatra.text: The largest island lying entirely within Indonesia, and the sixth-largest island in the world by area.
The equator runs right across the middle of the island.
Ancient Sanskrit names called it the "Island of Gold", thanks to gold in its highlands.
Its rainforests grow Rafflesia arnoldii, the world's largest individual flower.

Suriname.text: South America's smallest independent country, by both area and population.
The only independent country outside Europe where Dutch is the main language of government and schools.
In a 1667 peace deal the Dutch kept Suriname, while the English kept New Amsterdam, which they had renamed New York.
In the capital, Paramaribo, a synagogue and a mosque stand side by side.

Swansea.text: Wales's second-largest city, looking out over Swansea Bay and the Gower Peninsula.
In the 1800s it was a key centre of copper smelting, earning the nickname "Copperopolis".
In 1807 the Swansea and Mumbles Railway carried the world's first fare-paying rail passengers.
Poet Dylan Thomas was born here and fondly called it an "ugly lovely town".

Sweden.text: The most populous Nordic country, and the largest too, unless you count icy Greenland.
Alfred Nobel, the Swede who invented dynamite, founded the Nobel Prizes.
In Stockholm the sun is up for more than 18 hours in late June, but only about 6 in late December.
ABBA shot to fame in 1974 by winning the Eurovision Song Contest for Sweden.

Switzerland.text: Neutral for centuries, it hasn't fought an international war since 1815.
Swiss law names no capital: Bern is officially just the "federal city".
The Red Cross emblem was created by reversing the colours of the Swiss flag.
Solid milk chocolate was invented here by Daniel Peter in 1875.

Sydney.text: Founded in 1788 by the convicts and settlers of the First Fleet, it was the first European settlement in Australia.
The Harbour Bridge and the World Heritage-listed Opera House are its star attractions.
Dozens of surf beaches line its coast, with Bondi Beach the most famous of all.
Its Kingsford Smith Airport is one of the world's oldest continually operating airports.

Sydney Harbour Bridge.text: Nicknamed "the Coathanger", its great steel arch rises 134 metres from its top down to the harbour water.
About six million rivets, all driven by hand, hold it together.
At its 1932 opening, a man on horseback slashed the ribbon with his sword before the premier could cut it.
Its four granite-faced pylons hold nothing up; they were added for looks and to reassure a nervous public.

Sydney Opera House.text: Its daring design won an international competition in 1957 for Danish architect Jørn Utzon; it finally opened in 1973.
Became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007, just 34 years after it opened.
Those gleaming white sails are really 1,056,006 Swedish-made tiles in two shades: glossy white and matte cream.
Every curved roof shell is cut from the same imaginary sphere, a trick that let builders reuse the same moulds.

Syria.text: Its capital, Damascus, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.
Over 4,000 years ago the kingdom of Ebla here kept an archive of about 20,000 clay tablets.
The oldest surviving, nearly complete piece of written-down music, a hymn on a clay tablet, was found at ancient Ugarit.
Palmyra, a desert trading city here, grew into one of the richest cities in the Roman Empire.

Table Mountain.text: The only feature on Earth to give its name to a constellation: Mensa, meaning "the table".
Named one of the New7Wonders of Nature in 2011, its flat top is about three kilometres across.
Cable car cabins spin a full 360 degrees on the way up, so every rider gets the view.
The rare Table Mountain ghost frog lives nowhere else in the world.

Taipei.text: Taipei 101 became the world's tallest building when it opened in 2004, until Dubai's Burj Khalifa overtook it.
Just north of the city, Yangmingshan National Park sits on old volcanoes, with hot springs and sulfur deposits.
Its National Palace Museum, full of ancient Chinese treasures, shares its origins with Beijing's Palace Museum.
Its night markets, such as Shilin, usually open in the late afternoon and keep going well past midnight.

Taj Mahal.text: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan ordered this white marble tomb in 1631 for his late wife, Mumtaz Mahal.
An estimated 20,000-plus workers and artisans helped build it, from sculptors to calligraphers.
Teams of oxen and elephants hauled marble along a 15-kilometre earthen ramp to the building site.
Shah Jahan ended up buried here too, beside the wife it was built for.

Tajikistan.text: Much of the Pamir range, the mountains nicknamed the "Roof of the World", lies within its borders.
When completed in 1980, its Nurek Dam was the tallest dam in the world.
Its capital's name, Dushanbe, means "Monday", after the big Monday bazaars once held there.

Tallinn.text: Its Old Town is one of Europe's best-preserved medieval cities and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A tech hub: the ride-hailing app Bolt started here, and Estonian programmers in the city helped build Skype.
A weather vane shaped like an old warrior, Old Thomas, went up on the Town Hall spire in 1530 and became the city's symbol.
The Town Hall Pharmacy, already open by 1422, is one of the oldest continuously running pharmacies in Europe.

Tanzania.text: Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain, is the world's highest free-standing mountain above sea level.
Shares three of Africa's Great Lakes, including Lake Tanganyika, the continent's deepest.
On the Serengeti plain, wildebeest and zebra make a huge migration every year.
The name blends Tanganyika and Zanzibar, the two states that united in 1964 to form the country.

Tashkent.text: Uzbekistan's capital and largest city, which grew rich from its spot on the ancient Silk Road.
About a thousand years ago, the scholar al-Biruni explained its name as "Stone City".
Home to Central Asia's first metro, opened in 1977, where each station is designed around its own theme.
Its grand metro stations were off-limits to cameras: taking photos there was banned by law until 2018.

Tasmania.text: Australia's only state that isn't on the mainland, sitting about 240 km to the south across Bass Strait.
Home of the Tasmanian devil, which became the world's largest carnivorous marsupial after the thylacine died out in 1936.
Once called Van Diemen's Land, it was renamed in 1856 to honour Abel Tasman, the Dutch explorer who sighted it in 1642.
European sailors only proved it was an island when George Bass and Matthew Flinders sailed right around it in 1798–1799.

Tbilisi.text: Its name means "place of warmth", after the area's many hot sulphur springs.
In one version of its founding legend, a king's hunting falcon and a pheasant fell into a hot spring, so he built a city there.
English speakers called it Tiflis until 1936.
It was the capital of Georgia's medieval golden age, when Shota Rustaveli wrote the national epic, The Knight in the Panther's Skin.

Tegucigalpa.text: Shares the role of Honduras's capital with its sister city Comayagüela, across the Choluteca River.
Became the capital of Honduras in 1880, when the government moved there from Comayagua.
The name is often said to mean "hills of silver", though that version is uncertain.
El Picacho Hill rises above downtown, topped by the popular United Nations National Park.

Tehran.text: Home to Golestan Palace, a royal complex of the Qajar dynasty and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Its landmark Azadi Tower was built in 1971 to mark 2,500 years of the Persian Empire.
One theory says its name means 'bottom of the mountain slope', fitting its spot at the foot of the Alborz mountains.
At night, cool air sliding down Mount Tochal brings a gentle breeze into the city from the north.

Tenerife.text: Largest and most populous of the Canary Islands, lying in the Atlantic off northwest Africa.
Its volcano, Teide, is Spain's highest mountain and the highest point on any island in the Atlantic Ocean.
Measured from the ocean floor, Teide rises more than 7,500 metres.
At Santa Cruz's carnival in 1987, about 250,000 people packed into one outdoor concert, setting a Guinness world record.

Tennessee.text: Great Smoky Mountains National Park, partly here, is the most visited national park in the US.
Elvis Presley and Johnny Cash began their recording careers at Sun Records in Memphis.
Nashville's Grand Ole Opry is the longest-running radio broadcast in US history.
The name comes from Tanasi, a Cherokee town.

Teotihuacan.text: Around 1,500 years ago, this was the largest city in the Americas of its time.
Not an Aztec city: it was built and abandoned many centuries before the Aztec Empire rose nearby.
Its real name is lost; the Aztecs named it centuries later, and the name is often glossed as "birthplace of the gods".
Deep beneath the city, archaeologists found a miniature landscape with tiny pools of liquid mercury standing in for lakes.

Terracotta Army.text: More than 8,000 clay soldiers, plus chariots and horses, were buried to guard China's first emperor in the afterlife.
Farmers digging a well in 1974 stumbled upon the buried army.
The faces seem to differ for every soldier, built up from about 10 basic face shapes.
The soldiers were once brightly painted, but in Xi'an's dry air much paint can flake off within four minutes of digging.

Texas.text: The second-largest US state by both area and population.
Produces more wind power than any other US state.
Its name comes from a Caddo word meaning 'friend', and its state motto is simply 'Friendship'.
Before joining the US in 1845, it was an independent country, the Republic of Texas, for nearly ten years.

Thailand.text: The only Southeast Asian country never colonised by a Western power.
Known to the world as Siam, it was officially renamed Thailand on 24 June 1939.
Bangkok's full ceremonial name is listed by Guinness World Records as the world's longest place name, at 168 letters.
Before muay Thai boxing matches, fighters traditionally perform a ritual dance to honour their teachers.

The Bahamas.text: Columbus made his first landfall in the Americas here in 1492, on an island he named San Salvador.
A scattering of about 700 islands and more than 2,500 cays spread across the Atlantic north of Cuba.
One of just two countries whose official short name begins with "The"; the other is The Gambia.
Before Britain made it a crown colony in 1718, it was a haven for pirates, including the notorious Blackbeard.

The Gambia.text: Mainland Africa's smallest country by area, a narrow strip of land along both banks of the Gambia River.
Less than 50 km wide at its widest point, it is surrounded by Senegal everywhere except its Atlantic coast.
One of only two countries with an official 'The' in its short English name; the other is the Bahamas.
With Senegal, it shares the Senegambian stone circles, which UNESCO calls the largest concentration of stone circles anywhere in the world.

The Twelve Apostles (Victoria).text: Southern Ocean waves carved these limestone stacks, up to 50 metres tall, from the mainland cliffs.
Despite the name, there were probably never twelve of them, and only seven still stand.
Before "Twelve Apostles" caught on, the stacks were known as the Sow and Pigs.
Each stack began as a sea cave that became an arch, then collapsed to leave a lone pillar.

Timbuktu.text: In the 1500s, its three great mosque schools may have taught as many as 25,000 students between them.
Hundreds of thousands of handwritten manuscripts were gathered here over the centuries.
So legendary that English dictionaries use its name to mean any faraway place.
For centuries, camel caravans have brought salt here across the Sahara, each camel carrying four or five 30 kg slabs.

Times Square.text: Tens of millions visit each year, making it one of the world's busiest pedestrian crossroads.
Once called Longacre Square, it was renamed in 1904 when The New York Times moved in.
Its New Year's Eve ball drop has been a tradition since December 31, 1907.
Bright signs aren't just allowed here, they're required: since 1987, city rules have made building owners display illuminated signs.

Timor-Leste.text: On 20 May 2002 it became the first new sovereign state of the 21st century.
Its coral reefs lie within the Coral Triangle, a famous hotspot of ocean life.
In Tetun it is called Timór Lorosa'e, from a word meaning "east", literally "where the sun rises".
One piece of the country, Oecusse, is cut off from the rest by Indonesian territory.

Togo.text: A long, narrow sliver of West Africa, squeezed between its neighbours Ghana and Benin.
Its Koutammakou region, shared with Benin, is a UNESCO World Heritage landscape of traditional mud tower-houses, a national symbol of Togo.
Wealthy cloth traders called the "Nana Benz" got their nickname from the Mercedes-Benz cars many of them drove.
The name, from Ewe words for "water" and "shore", first belonged to a single town, now called Togoville.

Tokyo.text: In 1964 it became the first city in Asia to host the Summer Olympics.
Its name means "Eastern Capital"; until 1868 the city was called Edo.
By the mid-1700s, Edo had grown from a small fishing village into one of the world's largest cities, with over a million people.
Tokyo officially includes the faraway Ogasawara Islands, which stretch more than 1,000 km out into the Pacific.

Tokyo Skytree.text: In 2011 it overtook China's Canton Tower to become the world's tallest tower, finally topping out at 634 metres.
Its height of 634 metres is a pun: 6-3-4 can be read "Mu-sa-shi", the old name of the Tokyo region.
Its name was picked in a nationwide public vote, beating runner-up "Tokyo Edo Tower".
Completed on Leap Day, 29 February 2012, it is painted "Skytree White", based on a traditional bluish-white Japanese colour.

Tonga.text: Never gave up its sovereignty to any foreign power, even while under British protection from 1900 to 1970.
Nicknamed the "Friendly Islands" after the warm welcome Captain James Cook received on his first visit in 1773.
Between about 1200 and 1500, Tongan kings held sway across a vast stretch of ocean, from Fiji to Samoa and Niue.
Its only Olympic medal so far is a boxing silver, won by super-heavyweight Paea Wolfgramm at Atlanta in 1996.

Toronto.text: Canada's most populous city, and the fourth-most populous in North America after Mexico City, New York and Los Angeles.
About half of its residents were born outside Canada, and over 200 ethnic origins are represented.
Downtown hides the Path, 30 km of underground walkways and shops that Guinness named the world's largest underground shopping complex in 2016.
Nicknamed "Hogtown", after a big pork-processing plant that once stood near the harbour.

Torres del Paine National Park.text: Named after three jagged granite towers in Chilean Patagonia, the tallest reaching about 2,500 metres.
UNESCO named the park a World Biosphere Reserve in 1978.
In an 1880 travel book, Lady Florence Dixie called the three towers "Cleopatra's Needles".
Melting glaciers here revealed fossils of dozens of ichthyosaurs, dolphin-like reptiles from the age of the dinosaurs.

Tower Bridge.text: Opened in 1894, its road splits into two halves called bascules that lift to let ships through.
In 1952 a bus driver accelerated his double-decker and jumped the gap as the bridge began to open.
For Queen Elizabeth II's Silver Jubilee in 1977 it was painted red, white and blue.
It is sometimes confused with London Bridge, which stands about half a mile upstream.

Tower of London.text: Founded in 1066, it has served as a royal palace, an armoury, a treasury, the Royal Mint and even a zoo.
It guards the Crown Jewels, whose crowns, sceptres and orbs sparkle with around 23,578 gemstones.
At least six ravens are always kept here, because legend says the kingdom will fall if they ever leave.
In the 1250s King Henry III kept a white bear here, probably a polar bear, that fished in the Thames on a rope.

Tre Cime di Lavaredo.text: These three battlement-like peaks are one of the best-known mountain groups in the Alps.
Their German name, Drei Zinnen, means "Three Merlons", the raised blocks along a castle battlement.
The western peak was first climbed on 21 August 1879, exactly ten years to the day after the tallest one.
Climbers rank the partly overhanging north face of Cima Grande among the great north faces of the Alps.

Trevi Fountain.text: About 26 metres high and 49 metres wide, it is listed by Guinness World Records as the world's largest Baroque sculpture.
Tradition says that tossing a coin in, with your back to the fountain, means you'll return to Rome.
Thousands of euros in coins land in it every day, and the money goes to charity.
Legend says a young girl led Roman engineers to its water source in 19 BC; the scene is carved on the fountain.

Trinidad and Tobago.text: Birthplace of the steelpan, the limbo, and the music styles calypso and soca.
Pitch Lake, on Trinidad, is the largest natural deposit of asphalt on Earth.
Christopher Columbus named Trinidad "The Island of the Trinity" to keep a vow he'd made before his third voyage.
Unlike most Caribbean nations, which rely heavily on tourism, its economy runs mainly on oil and gas.

Tripoli, Libya.text: Founded by the Phoenicians in the 7th century BC, it has been lived in for well over 2,500 years.
Historically called 'Tripoli-of-the-West' to tell it apart from Tripoli in Lebanon.
Its most striking Roman survivor is the Arch of Marcus Aurelius, a triumphal arch built in AD 165.
In 1530 the city was handed, along with Malta, to the Knights of St John, who held it until 1551.

Tulum.text: Perched on cliffs above the Caribbean, this walled Maya city was a busy seaside trading centre.
It flourished late in Maya history, at its height between the 13th and 15th centuries, and was still lived in when the Spanish arrived.
Its name is the Yucatec Maya word for "wall" or "fence", fitting for a city guarded by thick stone walls.
One small shrine here seems to have worked as a beacon, guiding trading canoes through a gap in the reef.

Tunis.text: At its heart lies the Medina, a maze of centuries-old streets listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The ruins of ancient Carthage, once a mighty Mediterranean power, lie just north of the city.
Its grand tree-lined Avenue Habib Bourguiba is often called 'the Tunisian Champs-Élysées'.
In the old Medina, the Souk El Attarine is famous for perfumes, jasmine and rose water.

Tunisia.text: Home to Cape Angela, the northernmost point of mainland Africa.
Ruins of ancient Carthage, a mighty trading city founded by Phoenicians in the 9th century BC, lie here.
Its deserts and villages starred as the planet Tatooine in four Star Wars films, beginning with the 1977 original.
Its eastern coastal plain, the Sahel, is among the world's premier areas for growing olives.

Turkey.text: Straddles two continents: mostly in Asia on the Anatolian peninsula, with a smaller slice, East Thrace, in Europe.
Göbekli Tepe, among the world's oldest Neolithic sites, is close to 12,000 years old.
Two of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World stood here: the Temple of Artemis and the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus.
The American turkey bird borrowed its name from guineafowl, once called "turkey cocks" because they reached Europe through Turkey.

Turkmenistan.text: The sandy Karakum Desert covers well over two-thirds of the country.
Ancient Merv, an oasis city and Silk Road stop, was once among the biggest cities in the world.
In the desert, the Darvaza gas crater, nicknamed the "Door to Hell", has been burning for decades.
In 2013, the capital, Ashgabat, entered Guinness World Records for the highest concentration of white marble buildings.

Tuvalu.text: With about 25 square kilometres of land, it's the world's fourth-smallest country.
Its name means "eight standing together" – eight of its nine islands were inhabited.
Its internet ending, .tv, looks like "television", and leasing it out brings money into the government.

Uganda.text: Bwindi Impenetrable National Park is home to a population of rare mountain gorillas.
The Victoria Nile begins its long journey north here, flowing out of Lake Victoria.
Named after Buganda, a traditional kingdom in the south that includes the capital, Kampala.
Although it has no coastline, it contains many large lakes, including Victoria, Kyoga, Albert and Edward.

Ulaanbaatar.text: The coldest capital city in the world, measured by average yearly temperature.
Almost half of all the people in Mongolia live in this one city.
Founded in 1639 as a travelling Buddhist monastery, it changed location 29 times before settling for good in 1778.
Its name, given in 1924, means "Red Hero".

Uluru.text: This giant sandstone rock rises 348 metres above the desert, yet most of its bulk lies hidden underground.
Sacred to the local Aṉangu people, it was handed back to its traditional owners by Australia's government in 1985.
It seems to change colour through the day, glowing red at dawn and sunset.
During rare heavy rain, short-lived waterfalls pour down its sides.

United Arab Emirates.text: A federation of seven emirates, including Abu Dhabi, the capital, and Dubai.
In 2021 its Hope probe reached Mars orbit, making it the first Arab country to reach Mars.
In 2009, Abu Dhabi hosted Formula One's first day-night race, starting in daylight and finishing under floodlights.
Pearl diving was once a major trade here, until economic depression and the invention of cultured pearls wiped it out.

United Kingdom.text: Led the Industrial Revolution and became the world's first industrialised country.
The Prime Meridian, longitude 0°, was set at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London, in 1884.
Football, tennis, rugby, badminton, golf and cricket all originated or were largely developed here.
There's no single written constitution; its rules are spread across laws, court rulings, treaties and conventions.

Uruguay.text: Hosted and won the very first FIFA World Cup, in 1930.
South America's second-smallest independent country by area, after Suriname.
"La cumparsita", among the most famous tangos of all time, was written by a Uruguayan and first played in a Montevideo café.
More than half of all Uruguayans live in and around the capital, Montevideo.

Utah.text: Five national parks lie here: Arches, Bryce Canyon, Canyonlands, Capitol Reef and Zion.
The first railroad across the United States was finished at Promontory, Utah, with a golden spike on May 10, 1869.
Its dry, powdery snow inspired the slogan 'The Greatest Snow on Earth', used officially since 1975.
The dazzling white Bonneville Salt Flats appear in films such as Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End.

Uzbekistan.text: One of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world; the other is Liechtenstein.
Its cities Bukhara and Samarkand grew extremely wealthy from trade along the ancient Silk Road.
None of its rivers reach the sea; they all drain into inland basins.
Ulugh Beg, grandson of the conqueror Timur, built an enormous observatory in Samarkand in 1428 to study the stars.

Vancouver.text: Canada's most densely packed big city, with over 5,700 people per square kilometre.
So many films and TV shows are made here that it shares the nickname "Hollywood North" with Toronto.
The city grew around a tavern opened in 1867 by a bar owner nicknamed "Gassy Jack".
Despite the name, it isn't on Vancouver Island, which lies to the west across the Strait of Georgia.

Vanuatu.text: From 1906, Britain and France ran these islands jointly as the New Hebrides, until independence in 1980.
Mount Yasur volcano has erupted almost nonstop for centuries, earning the nickname "lighthouse of the Pacific".
On Pentecost Island, men leap from tall wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles, to celebrate the yam harvest.
Vanuatu's sand drawing is an art form recognised by UNESCO as a masterpiece of humanity's heritage.

Vatican City.text: The world's smallest country by area, and also the one with the fewest people.
The Swiss Guard, the pope's bodyguard, was founded in 1506 and still does that job today.
It has its own railway station, mostly for freight, with only about 300 metres of track inside the country.
Though not in the European Union, it uses the euro and issues its own euro coins inscribed 'Città del Vaticano'.

Venezuela.text: Home to Angel Falls, the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall, plunging off a flat-topped mountain.
Around Lake Maracaibo, local winds spark more lightning per square kilometre than anywhere else on Earth.
Its name probably means "Little Venice": in the best-known story, stilt houses on Lake Maracaibo reminded explorers of Venice.
The flat tops of its tepui mountains are home to carnivorous plants such as the marsh pitcher plant.

Venice.text: Built on more than a hundred small islands in a shallow lagoon, all stitched together by hundreds of bridges.
Capital of the Republic of Venice for almost a thousand years, from 810 to 1797.
Its medieval shipyard, the Arsenal, was one of the earliest large-scale industrial enterprises in history, churning out warships like a factory.
Baroque composers Antonio Vivaldi and Tomaso Albinoni were both born here.

Vermont.text: Makes about half of all the maple syrup produced in the United States.
Its capital, Montpelier, has fewer people than any other US state capital.
The name is a French translation of 'Green Mountains', the range running through the state.
Roadside advertising billboards have been banned here since 1968 to protect the country views.

Victoria Falls.text: Counting width and height together, it forms the world's largest sheet of falling water.
Its Lozi name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, means "the smoke that thunders", and is still widely used today.
Spray from the falls waters a small rainforest, home to plants rare for the dry region around it.
In 1855 explorer David Livingstone became the first European known to see it, from an island on its edge now named after him.

Victoria Harbour.text: Lying between Hong Kong Island and Kowloon, it's famed for its glittering night view of the skyline.
Its deep, sheltered waters helped Hong Kong grow into a great trading hub.
No bridge spans it: road traffic crosses through three tunnels beneath the water.
The Star Ferry has been chugging across it since the late 19th century.

Victoria Island (Canada).text: The eighth-largest island in the world and Canada's second-largest, by area.
Slightly bigger than the island of Great Britain, yet home to only about two thousand people.
One of its lakes holds an island with its own lake, which holds yet another island, like Russian dolls.
Named after Queen Victoria; local Inuit call it Kitlineq.

Vienna.text: Home over the years to Mozart, Haydn, Beethoven, Schubert, Brahms and the waltz-writing Strauss family.
One of the United Nations' headquarters cities since 1980, alongside New York, Geneva and later Nairobi.
Its Schönbrunn Zoo, opened in 1752 in the grounds of an imperial palace, is the world's oldest zoo still in operation.
One of the few world capitals with vineyards of its own, serving local wine in cosy taverns called Heuriger.

Vietnam.text: The world's second-biggest coffee grower, after Brazil.
Hang Sơn Đoòng, the largest known cave passage on Earth by volume, was first surveyed only in 2009.
So slender in the middle that, at its narrowest, it is only about 50 km from the sea to the Laos border.
Egg coffee, topped with egg yolk whipped with sugar and condensed milk, is a famous Hanoi speciality.

Vilnius.text: Its Old Town, one of the largest and best-preserved in Northern Europe, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994.
Gave its name to the Vilnian Baroque style, and is often called the largest Baroque city north of the Alps.
Legend says Grand Duke Gediminas founded the city after dreaming of a huge Iron Wolf howling on a hilltop.
On April Fools' Day 1997, its arty Užupis district declared itself an independent republic, complete with a constitution.

Virginia.text: Jamestown, founded here in 1607, began the first permanent English colony in the Americas.
Its legislature, set up in 1619, is the oldest law-making body still meeting in North America.
The famous Natural Bridge is the leftover roof of a limestone cave that collapsed.
The only US state where governors are not allowed to serve two terms in a row.

Wadi Rum.text: Nicknamed the Valley of the Moon, this vast desert valley in southern Jordan is carved from sandstone and granite.
A UNESCO World Heritage Site where ancient peoples, including the Nabataeans, left rock carvings and inscriptions.
Film-makers love its red landscape as a stand-in for Mars, as in The Martian.
Desert scenes for the 1962 epic Lawrence of Arabia were filmed among its towering red cliffs.

Walls of Dubrovnik.text: Almost two kilometres of unbroken stone walls still wrap around most of the old city, up to 25 metres high in places.
Carved over the gate of St Lawrence Fortress: "Freedom is not to be sold for all the treasures in the world."

Warsaw.text: Its Old Town was rebuilt almost from scratch after 1945, and that painstaking rebuild earned it a place on UNESCO's World Heritage list.
Birthplace of Marie Curie, who later founded a Radium Institute in the city.
Composer Frédéric Chopin's heart is sealed inside the city's Holy Cross Church.
One version of a folk legend says the city is named after Wars, a fisherman, and Sawa, the river mermaid he loved.

Washington (state).text: Grows more apples, pears and sweet cherries than any other US state.
Mount Rainier, an active volcano, is the most topographically prominent mountain in the lower 48 states.
Nearly named Columbia, it is the only US state named after a president.
Its Puget Sound ferries make up the largest ferry system in the United States.
