Washington, D.C..text: The capital of the United States isn't in any state: it's a special federal district of its own.
A planned capital, its layout was designed in 1791 by French-born engineer Pierre Charles L'Enfant.
A 1910 law keeps the skyline low by limiting building heights based on how wide the street is.
The "Columbia" in its name was a poetic name for the United States back then.

Wellington.text: The southernmost capital city of any country in the world.
Gales funnelling through Cook Strait make it the world's windiest city by average wind speed: "Windy Wellington".
Named after the Duke of Wellington, who took his title from a small town in Somerset, England.
The Lord of the Rings, King Kong and Avatar were all partly made here, and its film studios earned it the nickname "Wellywood".

West Virginia.text: The only US state that lies wholly inside Appalachia as officially defined by Congress.
The New River Gorge Bridge was once the world's longest steel single-arch bridge.
Almost entirely mountainous, it's nicknamed the Mountain State, and its motto means 'Mountaineers are always free'.
Home to the Green Bank Telescope, the world's largest fully steerable radio telescope.

White House.text: Home to every US president since John Adams moved in back in 1800.
Its Irish-born architect, James Hoban, modelled it on Leinster House in Dublin.
Its walls aren't white stone at all: they're Aquia Creek sandstone, painted white.
The residence packs in 132 rooms, 35 bathrooms and 28 fireplaces.

Whitehaven Beach.text: Its dazzling white sand is almost pure silica, stretching for about seven kilometres.
Silica isn't found in the local rocks, so the sand is thought to have drifted in on ocean currents over millions of years.
In 2010 CNN named it the world's top eco-friendly beach.
Gamers may spot it: Whitehaven Beach features in the racing video game Forza Horizon 3.

Windhoek.text: Perched about 1,700 m up on the Khomas Highland, near the geographical centre of Namibia.
The town grew up around a hot spring long known to local herding peoples.
Most think the name means "wind corner" in Afrikaans; another theory links it to South Africa's Winterhoek Mountains.
A pioneer in water recycling: it was the first city to pipe treated sewage water straight back into its drinking supply.

Wisconsin.text: Known as 'America's Dairyland', it makes more cheese than any other US state.
Grows more than half of all the cranberries harvested in the United States.
Green Bay Packers fans wear foam 'cheesehead' hats shaped like a big wedge of cheese.
Kringle, a flaky pastry brought by Danish immigrants to Racine, became the official state pastry in 2013.

Wyoming.text: The least populous US state, even though it's the tenth largest by area.
In 1869 it became the first US territory to give women the vote, and it kept that right on becoming a state in 1890.
Home to most of Yellowstone, which was set up in 1872 and is widely seen as the world's first national park.
Its name comes from a Native American language and means "at the big plains".

Yemen.text: For centuries a leading coffee producer, shipping its beans out through the port of Mocha.
The walled town of Shibam, with mud-brick tower houses up to eleven storeys, is nicknamed "the Manhattan of the Desert".
A third of the plants on its island of Socotra grow nowhere else on Earth.
The ancient kingdom of Saba, in today's Yemen, is thought to be the Sheba of the Bible.

York.text: Founded by the Romans as Eboracum in AD 71.
Constantine the Great was proclaimed Roman emperor here in AD 306.
As the Viking town of Jorvik, it grew to more than 10,000 people, one of the biggest towns in Britain.
The Kit Kat chocolate bar was created here by the sweet-makers Rowntree's.

Zagreb.text: Home of the Museum of Broken Relationships, filled with objects people donated after their break-ups.
Its old core grew from two medieval hilltop settlements, Kaptol and Gradec, which were united in 1851.
Since 1877, a cannon has fired from Lotrščak Tower every day to mark midday.
Its funicular runs on a track just 66 metres long, one of the shortest public-transport funiculars in the world.

Zambia.text: Copper is its great treasure: in 2019 it made up about 69% of the value of goods it exported.
Shares Lake Kariba, the world's largest artificial lake by volume, with neighbouring Zimbabwe.
Locally, Victoria Falls is called Mosi-oa-Tunya, meaning "thundering smoke".
Known as Northern Rhodesia until 1964, it took its new name from the Zambezi River.

Zhangjiajie.text: Its forest of towering sandstone pillars is part of the Wulingyuan area, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992.
In 2010 one pillar was renamed "Avatar Hallelujah Mountain" after the film's floating mountains.
The Bailong Elevator whisks visitors 326 metres up a cliff face in under two minutes.
When it opened in 2016, its canyon glass bridge was the world's longest and highest glass footbridge.

Zimbabwe.text: Named after Great Zimbabwe, a stone city begun in the 11th century that became a major African trade centre.
Victoria Falls, one of the world's largest and most spectacular waterfalls, lies in its far northwest.
Many sources say its name comes from a Shona phrase meaning "houses of stones".
